US death row inmate Christa Pike has released her first public statement since her botched execution in September.
"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," she said in a statement released by her legal team on social media on Friday.
"My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."
Pike, 50, was discharged from hospital at the end of last month after surviving two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital, which left her in a critical condition.
She has since been sent back to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995.
Pike is thought to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
Her lawyers previously said she had suffered from pneumonia following the attempted execution, had significant swelling on her arms and was also unable to swallow.
"I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger," she said in her statement on Friday. "But healing is not the same as being okay."
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
Shipp was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.

205a75a5a0d9.text: By — Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/aid-operation-and-evacuations-in-oleshky-amid-brief-truce-agreed-to-by-russia-and-ukraine Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Aid operation and evacuations in Oleshky amid brief truce agreed to by Russia and Ukraine World Oct 30, 2026 9:31 AM EDT KHERSON, Ukraine (AP) — A humanitarian mission entered the devastated city of Oleshky on Friday, officials said, as Russia and Ukraine observed the most significant truce of the 4½-year war that began with Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor. A convoy including 25 buses, ambulances and aid supplies was due to arrive in the Russian-occupied city to deliver food and medicine and evacuate residents wishing to leave for Russia or Ukraine. About 2,000 people remain in Oleshky, according to authorities and volunteers. A localized ceasefire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region has held for four days and is due to continue through Sunday evening to allow the operation to proceed. WATCH: News Wrap: Ceasefire in Oleshky holds for a third day "Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will have the opportunity to do so safely," Russia and Ukraine said in identical statements. "Those who choose to stay may remain and will receive all the humanitarian support they need." Officials from both countries worked together in a rare joint humanitarian effort, offering a brief bright spot in a grim war of attrition. The United States played a central role in the mission, which the White House said was brokered by first lady Melania Trump. Pope Leo XIV also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to help Oleshky. Fighting continued elsewhere, however. Russia's Defense Ministry said air defenses downed more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones overnight, while Ukraine's air force said Russia launched ballistic and other missiles, along with scores of drones. Residents fear what will happen in the evacuation The convoy assembled in Armiansk, a town in Russian-occupied Ukraine about 85 kilometers (53 miles) south of Oleshky, said Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's ombudsman and chief negotiator. Demining of designated routes into the city was completed late Thursday, officials said. Two people were killed during the work. Video posted by Lubinets' office showed him meeting older residents in Oleshky. One woman tearfully hugged him as others smiled. READ MORE: Melania Trump helps forge ceasefire deal in Russian-occupied Ukrainian city so aid can be delivered Lubinets said evacuations would continue until 2 p.m. local time, with aid distribution beginning 30 minutes later. It was unclear whether he meant Ukrainian time or western Russian time, which is an hour ahead. Ksenia Arkhipova, a volunteer who previously lived in Oleshky and remains in contact with residents, said large numbers of Russian military personnel were in the city. "They are currently checking empty houses, and in some cases, moving into them," she told The Associated Press. "They are also pressuring local residents to evacuate to Russia, rather than to Ukraine." WATCH: U.S. must put pressure on Russia so Putin ends the war, Ukrainian official says Arkhipova said Thursday that about 1,000 residents had told her they wanted to leave. She said the Ukrainian delegation's presence was important because many residents feared Russian authorities would interrogate or detain them. The evacuation route was not disclosed. Ukrainian-held territory lies just a few kilometers (miles) across the Dnipro River from Oleshky. But Ukrainian public television reported that those heading to Ukraine would travel hundreds of kilometers (miles), entering the country through its northern border with Belarus. Authorities have invited a small number of Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. media organizations to cover the operation in Oleshky. Associated Press writers Susie Blann and Derek Gatopoulos in Kyiv, Ukraine and Yuras Karmanau in Tallinn, Estonia contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press

7db822ac470a.text:
Yinkaâs view
There is no shortage of pessimism about Africaâs prospects in the AI race. The continent, we are regularly told, doesnât have the computing power, capital, or energy to compete. But investors and founders I spoke with in Lagos this week donât see this as another tech revolution that risks leaving Africa behind. Instead they see it as a chance to build new types of transformative businesses with AI, led by local founders and engineers.
The enthusiasm has some anecdotal evidence behind it: More than 1,300 companies applied to the inaugural cohort of African AI startups on the Askya Growth Platform, a VC-backed initiative which launched this month.
Their task is building the technology and infrastructure that make AI useful in African markets. As Babacar Seck, managing partner of Askya Investment Partners, put it, âAfrica cannot be renting AI, we must be making it.â That might mean developing smaller models adapted to African languages, but also systems that let governments and businesses keep control of sensitive data and apply AI to local problems in energy, agriculture, and commerce.
Marlon Nichols, a managing partner of Los Angeles-based MaC Venture Capital, which has deployed $20 million in early-stage investments in Africa, also sees an opportunity with venture capital shifting back toward physical infrastructure and technologies that are harder for AI to disrupt. âVCs are going back to atoms, to more physical things,â he told me on stage at Lagosâ Moonshot conference. He is less interested in data centers themselves than in the technology that runs them. That suggests African companies donât have to build the biggest models to share in AIâs value creation.
Enthusiasm wonât guarantee a generation of successful African AI companies as capital remains scarce on the continent, infrastructure expensive, and many startupsâ commercial prospects remain untested: Of the startups that applied to Askayaâs program, only 11 were picked this time. âThereâs almost no capital today for African AI, yet people are building,â said Seck. Overall, AI-native startups took less than 2% of the $1.36 billion that African startups raised in the first half of 2026, according to Digital Africa.
But you canât overlook the founders already building for markets that Big Tech has long underserved. The opportunity may be less about catching up with Silicon Valley than building an AI industry that works for Africa.

011cfdf813d9.text:
Tanzania and Angola have agreed to connect railways serving ports on opposite coasts of Africa, Tanzaniaâs president said. The move brings together multibillion-dollar infrastructure backed by Western governments and China.
The proposed connection of the Western-backed Lobito Corridor with China-backed TAZARA would stretch between ports on Angolaâs Atlantic coast and Tanzaniaâs Indian Ocean coast through Zambia and DR Congo, home to Africaâs richest deposits of copper and cobalt â minerals deemed vital to economic security amid the global energy transition.
The agreement complicates the geopolitical narrative around both railways because connecting them would turn rival corridors into a coast-to-coast network, putting Zambia and Congo in a position where they have access to both oceans without having to choose between China and the West.
The plan may be seen as illustrating an argument that developing countries are resisting pressure to choose camps in the growing competition between Washington and Beijing. The agreement comes days after the Africa Finance Corporation picked contractors for sections of the new Zambia-Lobito railway.

e9470ec6108d.text:
Uganda has called on the African Union to consider deploying its standby peacekeeping and humanitarian force to help contain an Ebola outbreak that has killed nearly 5,000 people in DR Congo. The call was made at a meeting of health officials from 45 African countries who came together to coordinate a continent-wide response to the outbreak, which has infected more than 10,000 people in DR Congo and now spread to Kenya and Nigeria.
Ugandaâs health minister told the summit on Wednesday that AU personnel could provide medical and logistical support, and help ease a shortage of health workers. He called on leaders to hold an emergency meeting to decide on financing and deployment.
Officials agreed to strengthen cross-border surveillance, share information, and keep borders open. The virus has now spread further across Africa than any previous Ebola outbreak, with cases in the continentâs central, eastern, and western regions.

26053fb38a90.text:
Lagos Fashion Week returned for its 15th edition this week, bringing together some of the continentâs best-known designers, including Lisa Folawiyo, Nkwo, Orange Culture, and Emmy Kasbit.
But the event is increasingly about more than runway recognition: This yearâs theme, âCrafted,â puts heritage, craftsmanship, and circular fashion at the center, say the organizers, and reflects Lagos Fashion Weekâs growing emphasis on building a commercially viable and sustainable African fashion industry.
The ambition is to turn global interest in African design into lasting economic opportunities for local manufacturers, artisans, and creative businesses.
âAfrican fashion doesnât have a creativity problem, it has an infrastructure problem,â Omoyemi Akerele, founder of Lagos Fashion Week, told Semafor. âAccess to finance, manufacturing capacity, and distribution remain significant barriers.â

055412977643.text:
The Africa Cup of Nations, the continentâs top football competition, will continue to be held biennially, reversing a plan to introduce a four-year cycle put forward by the Confederation of African Football.
Announcing the U-turn, CAF placed financial considerations at the heart of its reasoning. Patrice Motsepe, the South African billionaire who runs CAF and championed the shift, said the reversal was in the interest of the organizationâs 54 member nations and African players who ply their trade abroad.
AFCON games have risen in global recognition over recent editions, expanding revenue streams for CAF. The most recent tournament recorded a 61% growth in European, Asian, and South American audiences over the 2024 edition, and a 35% rise in revenue from media rights from those markets, CAF said in March.

ec4d3dbc1139.text:
South Africaâs third-largest lender, Absa, opened its first Gulf office, giving the bank a seat closer to Middle Eastern investors hunting for deals on the continent.
Absa joins South African rivals Standard Bank, Nedbank, and Investec, which have already established a presence in Dubai.
Absa CEO Kenny Fihla said the office, which is looking to benefit from advisory and credit-arrangement fees, would help âconnect capital from the region and from wider international markets with opportunities across Africa.â Gulf-backed ports, logistics, and energy projects are expanding along Africaâs eastern seaboard. The trend has incentivized continental banks to double down on East Africa and strengthen links with the Gulf.
Capital from that region has become more visible across the continent: Gulf Cooperation Council countries have pumped more than $100 billion into Africa over the past decade. The United Arab Emirates is now Africaâs fourth-largest foreign investor behind China, the EU, and the US.

f4cb2f63b31e.text:
- Published
Spain's transport minister says he won't resign over the high-speed rail collision that has left at least 69 people dead.
Ãscar Puente told a news conference in Madrid he had "nothing to hide" while repeating the government's vow to get to the bottom of the disaster, saying many questions needed to be answered.
"My duty right now is not to talk about whether I should remain in my position, but to resolve the problem," Puente said.
The transport minister has been facing calls to step down in the aftermath of the tragedy, including from political rivals, a trade union and demonstrators who protested outside the transport ministry on Wednesday night.
Dozens were killed and many more injured when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of another stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda, in the central Toledo province, on Wednesday morning.
A preliminary report released by transport investigators late on Thursday found the Renfe train was travelling between 160km/h (99.4mph) and 200km/h when the collision occurred, causing its front carriage to become embedded in the tail of the stationary train.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez said earlier on Friday that public trust in Spain's high-speed rail network had been broken and repeated it was "unacceptable" that there had been two similar tragedies within a year.
In January a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people in Adamuz in southern Spain.
Wednesday's tragedy was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Puente said on Wednesday a computer failure at about 08:30 that morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the crash.
Three audio recordings between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stalled on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Puente had said that the decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions, was "inexplicable".
The leaking of the audio recordings has been criticised by some Spanish politicians, with Alberto IbÃ¡Ã±ez, a member of Congress for the left-wing Sumar platform, writing on X that they were "despicable".
Meanwhile, Irene Montero - the prime ministerial candidate for the left-wing Podemos party - said responsibility for the crash should not be placed on one worker, adding that train drivers and experts have been warning against the liberalisation of the railway sector for years.
On Friday Puente said he was "not going to use any worker as a shield".
But he said "many questions" arose as a result of the tragedy and he wanted to look at them "one by one".
"If the investigation shows there is human error we will act in consequence of that," he said.
The country is observing three days of mourning, as the families of victims and the survivors of the crash struggle to comprehend how it could have happened.
The conservative People's Party joined calls for Puente's resignation after trade union CSIF called for the same earlier this week.
But Puente said on Friday he would not budge from his position.
"The easy thing for me would be to leave, but neither that fits with my character nor is it what the Prime Minister has asked me to do," he said.
"I feel immense pain and immense sadness for the victims and their relatives... I cannot let this pain paralyse me though. We have to find solutions to this problem."
Additional reporting by Sergi Forcada Freixas

e31066355db0.text:
A splash of pee could reveal bladder cancer.
Using a proof-of-concept urine test that decodes RNA molecules, it’s possible to pick out patients with the disease, scientists report October 2 in Nature Medicine. Because urine is in direct contact with bladder tumors, it’s “a very attractive fluid” to look for this type of cancer, says Stanford University oncologist Maximilian Diehn. The technology, still in its infancy, offers a glimpse of what future screening tests might entail.
Today’s liquid biopsies for cancer, which examine bodily fluids rather than tissue samples, largely focus on finding DNA that tumors shed into the blood. Diehn’s lab sought a different stream of information. The researchers analyzed RNA, DNA’s molecular cousin. RNA isn’t as stable as DNA, so it hasn’t been researchers’ top target. But it carries info that DNA lacks, such as which genes are turned on. That’s important, Diehn says, “because it can tell you what the cancer is doing at any given moment.”
Diehn and his colleagues previously developed a technique to analyze dribs of RNA floating in blood. In samples from people with lung cancer, the team could read RNA signatures of the disease. Now, the researchers have shown that their technique is a whiz at detecting cancer in urine. The team tested their technique using samples from 515 cancer patients and healthy people. It was sensitive enough to identify 95 out of 100 people with bladder cancer — even at early stages of disease. What’s more, the test also offered hints about cancer biology, such as the type of tumor and risk of recurrence. Those details could help doctors make decisions about treatments, Diehn says.
The researchers are now exploring their technique’s potential for picking up other cancers. Their evidence suggests that it can spot cancer in the kidney and prostate, organs also washed by urine. One day, Diehn says, he can imagine a multi-cancer urine test focused on tumors in the genitourinary tract. But there’s much to do before such a test makes it into clinics.
Because the technology is so new, the jury’s still out on whether RNA-based testing will find use in cancer screening, Diehn says. “But absolutely, I think the field needs to investigate it.”

fa7a00b69ff8.text:
- Published
A Swedish climate academic says he has been barred from entering the UK because he was due to speak on a panel with a co-founder of Palestine Action.
Andreas Malm told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he had received a letter from the Home Office notifying him that his presence was "not conducive to the public good", with no further details given.
He said he could not "see any other explanation" for being denied entry than his scheduled appearance with Huda Ammori, a founder of the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK.
The Home Office said it did not comment on individual cases.
Malm is a senior lecturer in human ecology at Sweden's Lund University, whose work includes the 2021 book How to Blow up a Pipeline and 2025's The Destruction of Palestine is the Destruction of the Earth.
He said he had asked the Home Office to explain its decision, but could not see a reason beyond the upcoming talk in London with Ammori organised by the left-wing magazine Tribune - calling the move a "severe restriction on the free exchange of ideas".
Malm said he was not a member of Palestine Action, had never publicly endorsed it, nor had he given it any financial support.
"The only link to Palestine Action is her as a person," he said, criticising the UK government for ascribing "guilt by association".
The academic acknowledged that he had previously described the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel - in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage - as "fundamentally an act of liberation".
Malm said it was possible that these remarks, during a December 2023 talk in which he also condemned the "deplorable" killing of civilians in the cross-border attack, had been the reason for the Home Office's decision.
But he argued that these views had been in the public realm for a long time, including when he was last allowed into the UK to deliver a talk in May.
"I don't expect the British state to agree with me on Palestine or climate or anything. What I expect the British state to do is to continue to let me enter the country and to discuss with colleagues, with people who disagree with me - as I have done for years."
The UK Supreme Court is due to review Palestine Action's controversial ban under terrorism legislation. The Home Office has said that it will robustly defend against the appeal.
More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK over alleged support of the group. About 2,500 have been charged, though none have gone to trial as the legal challenge to the proscription continues.
The government has broad discretion to bar foreign nationals from entering the UK if their presence is deemed to pose a risk to society.
In April, 11 people described by then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer as "far-right agitators" were banned from entering the UK ahead of a rally led by Tommy Robinson.
Kanye West was also denied entry that same month after backlash to his planned set at London's Wireless Festival, following a string of antisemitic, racist and pro-Nazi comments. He had previously apologised for the remarks and said his bipolar disorder had caused him to lose "touch with reality".
Left-wing political commentators Hasan Piker and Cenk Uygur claimed in June that their visas had been revoked ahead of planned appearances in London and Oxford, allegedly "for criticising Israel".

a5d40e07d20d.text: Democrats weighing 2028 presidential bids are piling onto the AI hate wave in their messaging, per an analysis shared exclusively with Axios. Why it matters: Democrats are turning AI anxiety into a political rallying cry ahead of 2028, while Republicans remain divided over how to respond. Driving the news: 2028 contenders including Gavin Newsom, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Kamala Harris, Pete Buttigieg, Jon Ossoff and more have all increased their AI commentary in recent months, per new research from Upswing, conducted on behalf of Reset Tech, a nonprofit advocating for tech regulation. Among 21 Democrats named as potential 2028 contenders, tech mentions on X nearly quadrupled, and press release mentions nearly tripled since the start of the year. Tech is now the second-most common topic in releases, trailing only jobs and the economy, with the highest concentration of mentions around data centers and phone bans in schools. To gather the data, Upswing analyzed nearly 30,000 X posts from 38 accounts associated with 21 potential presidential contenders and 3,868 press releases from 16 officeholders between Jan. 1 and Oct. 15. Between the lines: Democrats are galvanizing around AI as a winning issue. Democrats are "taking a meaningful advantage" on AI after the topic was initially seen as a "jump ball" for both major political parties, Rishi Bharwani, U.S. director of Reset Tech, told Axios. AI regulation has gone from the back burner to a top issue over the last six months, he added. While the economy is still what matters most to voters, AI is increasingly part of the financial conversation as it dominates markets and the macroeconomic backdrop. Zoom in: It's not just messaging. While data center bans have been proposed in Democratic- and Republican-majority states, New York is so far the only one to pass a moratorium. House Democrats drafted a resolution opposing government bailouts for AI companies if the so-called "bubble" bursts. There are also a variety of legislative proposals, including model transparency measures and kill switches. Zoom out: This comes amid a groundswell of anti-AI sentiment among voters. Most Americans across the political spectrum take the risks of AI causing harm seriously, per a September YouGov poll of nearly 1,500 voters. Likely voters trust Democrats more than Republicans to respond to artificial intelligence, the poll said. The other side: Republicans are caught between their base being concerned by AI and President Trump's unfettered embrace of the industry. Republicans are distancing themselves from Trump to varying degrees. Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-Fla.), for example, has been among the loudest about state-level regulation on the technology. The bottom line: Democrats are coalescing around a more critical stance on AI, but whether it meaningfully impacts elections remains to be seen.

b22c6f6b693c.text:
What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack
Binance, the world's biggest crypto exchange, has been hit by a $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) hack - thought to be the biggest in history.
Half of the assets have been frozen but many remain in the hands of the hackers, the cryptocurrency giant said. It later added that it has "begun recovering" some funds.
Two analytics firms have attributed the incident to a North Korean hacking unit, though no one has claimed responsibility. Binance did not directly respond to questions about the incident's potential links to North Korea.
BBC cyber correspondent Joe Tidy explains more about the hack and what to do if you are affected.

- Published
The evacuation of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky is under way, Russian and Ukrainian authorities have confirmed.
A ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined.
Residents of Oleshky who wished to leave had a four-hour window to do so. A convoy of 25 buses was brought in to allow up to 750 people to leave the town until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.
Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.
"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
"At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance."
Ukrainian territory lies 5km (3.1miles) from Oleshky, but the evacuees will first have to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa.
They will board a Russian government plane to Gomel in Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region.
Others are expected to choose to stay in Russian-occupied territory.
Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova travelled to Oleshky together on Friday, setting off from Armiansk, in the Russian-occupied Crimean peninsula.
Lubinets is the first Ukrainian official since the start of the war to visit Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine. He will also become the first to visit Russia when he escorts the evacuees back into Ukraine on Saturday.
The Oleshky ceasefire has required close cooperation with Lantratova, which Lubinets said he carried out in the interests of saving lives.
But some in Ukraine have recoiled at the sight of him standing beside a representative of the Russian occupying power which has killed so many of the city's residents and made life unbearable for the rest.
Both Lubinets and Lantratova posted videos from Oleshky on their social media channels, saying people were given the chance to form two groups depending on whether they wanted to be taken to Russian-controlled territory or to Ukraine.
In one video, Lubinets can be seen meeting tearful locals. "The problem is that a lot of people are staying," he can be heard saying. "I was told that it was their own choice, we will do everything possible for the humanitarian aid to arrive."
Russia said on Thursday that it had prepared "dozens of tonnes" of aid for the residents who do not wish to leave, including food, medicine, hygiene products and fuel for generators.
An Oleshky resident told the BBC she had decided against leaving because "they wouldn't take my animals, so that's it."
Olena, who now lives in Kyiv, said her grandmother and wider family in Oleshky were also staying behind.
"The older generation does not want to leave," she told the BBC. "I've barely managed to persuade my father - and only because I've just had a baby, who he would never see otherwise."
Olena's grandmother's sister died in Oleshky last winter.
"She lost her legs after stepping on a landmine, covered in snow... People took her to the hospital in a garden wheelbarrow," Olena said.
"That's how locals transport all wounded and dead people in Oleshky to the hospital and the hospital's morgue: in garden wheelbarrows."
The ceasefire is due to be in force until the end of Sunday 1 November. It has provided the first few days of peace in the Kherson region since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Residents of Kherson told the BBC they were "overjoyed" by the ceasefire. However, they are concerned the truce has given Russia time to build up its military presence on the banks of the Dnipro river, which could result in a renewed assault once the ceasefire expires.
On Friday, the Kremlin made it clear that the success of the Oleshky ceasefire should not be interpreted as willingness to extend the truce to the rest of Ukraine.
A handful of foreign journalists have been invited to witness the evacuation of the town, which Moscow is expected to present as a humanitarian mission conducted with mercy to protect the people of Oleshky.
Many Ukrainians suspect Russia's real intention is to earn credit with the White House, and to provide US President Donald Trump with a boost ahead of next week's midterm elections.

0639ab2a8358.text: President Trump's energy policies and investment deals could become major targets of Democratic investigations if the party wins control of either chamber of Congress. Why it matters: Congressional probes could expose new details about the administration's dealings with major companies and foreign governments. What they're saying: House Democrats are likely to take a "shotgun" approach of "throwing everything out there and then seeing what sticks in the realm of popular opinion," TD Cowen analyst John Miller said via email. Democrats will be looking for agencies that exceeded their authority, deals involving administration officials' families, or both, Miller said. The big picture: Scratch the surface of Democrats' biggest potential oversight targets, and energy is everywhere. Russia. Trump's dealings with Moscow will again be front and center — and so will the energy dimension. Democrats in both chambers are likely to investigate Trump's diesel deal with Moscow, which they claim violates a 2022 law barring imports of Russian fuels. The inquiries could also extend to U.S. banks and ports, which lawmakers have already warned could face congressional investigation. Venezuela. "We expect Venezuela to be the subject of a number of inquiries," RBC Capital Markets analysts said in a note. Democrats have already raised questions about whether any oil companies knew about plans to depose Nicolás Maduro. Investigations could also examine the legality of the Pentagon's 35% stake in the corporate parent North American Blue Energy Partners and the terms of the deal, the note states. The Iran war. High gasoline and diesel prices give Democrats another reason to scrutinize the decision to attack Iran, especially if pain at the pump persists. Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) have already pressed major oil and gas companies about their profits during the conflict. AI and data centers. Wider and intense oversight of AI will touch on data centers' energy use and power costs — a topic various Democrats have already been probing. The House Energy and Commerce Committee, with its expansive jurisdiction, will be the "center of gravity" on data centers, according to Alyssa DaCunha, who co-chairs the congressional investigations practice at the law firm WilmerHale. Oversight could also extend to Trump administration efforts to spur data center development on federal lands amid the public backlash. Investments and family ties. "We ... expect congressional reviews of the government's equity stakes in several critical mineral firms," RBC analysts write. Democrats in both chambers are very interested in how the deals may benefit the families of President Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Offshore wind deals. Several panels are poised to investigate Interior Department agreements to pay energy companies to relinquish offshore leases and redirect investment into fossil fuels. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), who would head the Natural Resources Committee, has signaled plans . So has Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), the top Democrat on the Appropriations panel that oversees Interior. Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who's likely to get the powerful Judiciary Committee gavel, has called it illegal, while Whitehouse, who's in line for Senate Judiciary if Dems retake, has also raised legal concerns. What they're saying: "The Democrats are already telegraphing that, once again, they have no agenda to improve the lives of Americans and will instead continue their decade-long obsession with investigating President Trump," White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said in a statement. What we're watching: Political space for legislation beyond messaging bills will be limited but not completely absent.

14e89a354055.text:
- Published
China has rejected allegations of a Chinese espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief executive, Jensen Huang, describing the claims as "groundless speculation".
US intelligence officials believe that Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, was gathering information for Beijing on the US chip-making giant, according to a report by The New York Times, external.
The report said Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was under investigation over the possible diversion of advanced Nvidia AI chips to China and had developed a close relationship with Jensen.
Nvidia said their interactions were routine business engagements, while Beijing accused Washington of attempting to smear China. Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.
The BBC has contacted Megaspeed and the White House for comment.
US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by The New York Times.
Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".
It remains unclear what information Alice Huang - who is also known as Huang Le - allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.
At a regular briefing on Friday, Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said: "The report in question is based on groundless speculation and is nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
The paper's report comes amid longstanding US concerns about China's access to advanced computing technology, which is considered crucial to developing artificial intelligence systems.
Jensen Huang has argued that allowing Nvidia to sell more of its products to China is important for maintaining US competitiveness in the global AI industry.
But Washington has restricted exports of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China since 2022, citing national security concerns and the risk that the technology could strengthen China's military operations. There have however been some loosening of restrictions during Trump's administration.
US officials said they had caught several firms illegally trafficking the chips across the Chinese border. They have also investigated whether companies operating through third countries are helping Chinese businesses access the restricted technology.
Nvidia has said it complies with applicable export laws and that there is no evidence its chips have been smuggled into China.
In response to the allegations made by the Times, John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, said: "Jensen's interactions with Ms Huang are not unusual or unexpected".
He said customers like Megaspeed "receive ordinary business information - not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets - and zero information relevant to national security."
He added that allegations the Singaporean company was smuggling chips to China "were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year".
Megaspeed told the paper its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation. The company also said it had informed the US government that it was willing to cooperate.
It is unclear how closely Alice Huang remains involved with Megaspeed.

ddcbaa51da49.text:
Oman is the standout among Gulf stock markets that have otherwise struggled this year. Still, as elsewhere, markets are not the economy: The IMF has forecast a 4.8% contraction in the Gulfâs GDP in 2026, but stocks havenât plunged as much, suggesting stronger-than-expected corporate earnings have supported valuations.
Within the relatively thin universe of equities, one name outshines all: Saudi Aramco accounted for about 72% of the combined earnings of Tadawul-listed companies in the first half of the year. Higher crude prices lifted its net profit 33%, and with oil up since Houthi attacks intensified on the kingdom, Aramco may have another strong quarter when it announces its results on Nov. 3.

b7209fd43882.text:
US artificial intelligence firms are expanding in the Gulf, a sign that some companies are not shying away despite increased risks to digital infrastructure. Oracle plans to build more data centers in Saudi Arabia and the UAE to meet rising demand, The National reported. And Scale AI, which is 49% owned by Meta and sells labeled data for model training, opened an office at the Dubai International Financial Center, following an agreement to work with a G42 unit to develop AI agents.
In Saudi Arabia, New York-listed Snowflake projects it will invest $300 million in the kingdom through 2030; its customers there include dairy company Almarai and PIF-backed developer Red Sea Global. Led by former Google Ads chief Sridhar Ramaswamy, it has plans for two more cloud computing regions and, with the communications ministry, AI training for thousands of Saudis.
So far, data center construction has âbarely moved the needle for Gulf economies,â according to Bloomberg economist Ziad Daoud. The Iran war makes building that infrastructure pricier and riskier; he wrote that hardened security adds 5% to 7% to costs. Still, it appears there is willingness to absorb the new premium.

8af7a2664b9b.text:
Prediction markets blew three big elections this week, a bad look for platforms pitching themselves to investors as hedges against global risk. Kalshi and Polymarket both gave Brazilian conservative FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro a 4-in-5 chance of winning; he lost to the progressive incumbent, costing anyone who traded Brazilâs currency and stocks.
The markets also overrated Netanyahuâs challenger in Israel, where the race is still too close to call â and where a series of suspicious bets elicited an investigation by Polymarket. In Serbia (emerging-market investors need good information, too!), Kalshi gave the heavily favored incumbent strongman 75% odds as late as election day. He lost.
Kalshi has touted the accuracy of its markets to win over institutional investors. A hedge that doesnât work is doubly bad: useless and expensive.

9fe05cf507b7.text:
Microsoft has protected its AAA credit rating â one of just two left in Corporate America, alongside Johnson & Johnsonâs â and is reaping the rewards for its financial discipline. Despite the spreading fears about AI-related debt, the company raised $25 billion Thursday in its first bond offering since 2017. The dealâs 10-year portion cost just 5.6%, barely more than the US government pays to borrow.
Further down the ratings ladder, investors are getting choosier and demanding higher yields to take on the risk of lending to companies in the AI sector. SpaceX, rated three rungs lower than Microsoft at BBB, will pay as much as 8.75% for its $40 billion haul this week, and neocloud CoreWeaveâs bonds, deep in junk-rated territory, have traded at yields above 15%. In the race to bankroll the AI boom, the bond market is drawing a stark dividing line between borrowing at a bargain and paying a punishing premium.

bae5e0f774ac.text:
- Published
For the last three decades, Novaya Gazeta has been one of the most high-profile independent news outlets in Russia.
Now it's shutting down - and it has accused the Russian authorities of the "murder" of a newspaper.
"They've killed us," reads a statement on the Novaya Gazeta website.
"The newspaper is no more. The Russian authorities and Russian special services have forced the paper to stop its work."
Novaya Gazeta has received an eviction order. Crucially, at the same time, the system that had allowed the paper to receive donations from readers was disabled.
That leaves no way to fund the publication.
Novaya Gazeta had developed a reputation for fearless investigative reporting on subjects such as corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power by officials and bureaucrats - dangerous topics in Russia.
The paper said that over time six journalists connected with the paper were killed for "fulfilling their professional and civic duty." Those reporters include Anna Politkovskaya, who was shot dead in the stairwell of her apartment block 20 years ago this month. Among the subjects she had reported on were the wars in Chechnya.
In the statement announcing its closure, Novaya Gazeta launched a stinging attack on the Russian authorities, claiming the newspaper was the victim of a "coordinated act" and blaming "the repressive state apparatus".
"Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated in the country and their protection has been equated to a crime," the statement said.
"The courts have been destroyed along with the law. Having personal convictions is now state treason."
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the pressure on independent journalism and independent Russian journalists has been growing.
Soon after the start of what the Kremlin calls the so-called "special military operation", new laws were adopted in Russia. Their aim: to punish dissent and silence criticism of the war and of those in power.
Novaya Gazeta itself and its staff had been facing a multitude of problems.
The authorities had already revoked the newspaper's licence and blocked access to its website. Several of its journalists and contributors had been designated "foreign agents", a label often used by the Russian authorities to punish critics.
Earlier this year there was a police search of the editorial office. A veteran investigative journalist, Oleg Roldugin, was arrested and charged with "unlawful access to computerised information".
In connection with the case, the newspaper's editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, was recently taken in for police questioning and his home was searched.
Despite increasing pressure, Novaya Gazeta had managed to continue operating, albeit in a reduced form.
Loyal readers used virtual private networks to circumvent official blocking of the website and access content. But the loss of its licence and other restrictions dealt a major blow.
One of the founders of Novaya Gazeta in the 1990s - and for many years its chief editor - was journalist Dmitry Muratov, external. In 2021, Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression, which is a precondition for democracy and lasting peace".
The award didn't stop the authorities from declaring him a "foreign agent" in 2023.
At the offices of Novaya Gazeta, they've already started packing.
The end of this newspaper is very much the end of an era.
In an increasingly authoritarian Russia, it's also a sign of the times.

a8adc0f228f6.text:
The US upped the pressure on its ostensible allies as part of its push for a truce in the Russia-Ukraine war. Kyiv has paused its strikes on Russian refineries at the behest of Washington, which is trying to corral runaway fuel prices, The Wall Street Journal reported, while Reuters said the Pentagon had urged European leaders to calm their rhetoric over the threat of Russian aggression.
The moves come as Russiaâs foreign minister entered the US to attend a meeting of G20 foreign ministers, and after the Trump administration waived new sanctions on Russian energy and reached a diesel deal with the Kremlin â decisions met with unease in Europe, which sees Washington as unnecessarily pressuring Kyiv.

892c3d8b18d1.text:
Chinaâs leadership doubled down on an anti-corruption drive that analysts say has variously sought to purge the top echelons of the Communist Party over graft and consolidate Xi Jinpingâs power. The Party said it had expelled 33 officials from its senior ranks and elevated the former head of the militaryâs anti-corruption body to its Politburo, following a meeting of its Central Committee.
The timing of the moves â the latest in a more than decade-long crackdown that âhas become a ceaseless wave of purges aimed at keeping officials loyal and on their toes,â The Wall Street Journal said â is key: A high-profile meeting next year is expected to confirm Xi to a new five-year term.

a8018d96dc22.text:
Amazon and Intel reported worse-than-expected figures, adding to a run of underwhelming Big Tech results that have weighed on markets.
Amazonâs $200 billion in third-quarter revenues were not enough to reassure investors, who have grown wary of the AI trade as surging debt and financing costs outpace revenues and push firms into negative cash flows. Intelâs fourth-quarter sales projections also disappointed markets, pushing its stock down 20% in after-hours trading.
AI investment recently became the single-biggest spending spree in American history, despite rising opposition to the technology and the data centers it relies on. The market is âscratching its head â how does all this pay off?â an investor told Bloomberg.

c938dac1df42.text:
Anthropic became SpaceXâs biggest customer, accounting for a third of sales last quarter, underscoring the intense concentration of the tech market.
Investors have grown concerned that the AI industry â and the economy writ large â is becoming overreliant on the performance of a small number of firms, thus increasing the risk of market destabilization if one fails.
Anthropic itself revealed in an IPO prospectus this week that almost half of its revenue comes from fellow tech giants Amazon, Google, and Microsoft.
âConcentration and acceleration are also risky in their own right,â Bridgewater said in a note to clients. âThey mean that more plain luck is needed to keep economies chugging.â

55663d89e740.text:
New figures showed Brazilâs debt picture is by some measures its worst in a decade, underscoring the scale of the challenge facing recently reelected President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva.
Brazilâs debt burden steadily climbed over Lulaâs third term and the deficit hit a record high; his reelection tanked Brazilian markets, reflecting investorsâ fears the countryâs fiscal picture will only worsen under his tenure as economic growth is forecast to cool in the years ahead and new benefits â including a reduction in the working week and an expansion of housing and education support â take hold. âAnother Lula government is unlikely to deliver the structural reforms Brazil needs,â a Bloomberg columnist argued.

6c3d25e6ef2b.text:
Franceâs economy unexpectedly contracted in the third quarter, adding to a pile of worries over the European powerâs fortunes in the run-up to divisive presidential elections. The latest figures come with investors already concerned over rising debt levels, a yawning budget deficit, and mounting public frustration over service provision; recent polls suggest the far right and far left are in the lead ahead of April elections.
The myriad issues have raised fears of contagion across the EU, and offer lessons for Washington, too: US federal debt recently crossed the symbolic threshold of 100% of GDP, with little sign of a slowdown in borrowing. âAmerica is getting a peek at its debt future, and itâs scary,â one Bloomberg columnist warned.

7c80b3a67962.text:
The News
Russiaâs offer to supply floating nuclear power plants to coastal African countries emerged as a major focus of talks held with African officials at a summit in Moscow this week. President Vladimir Putin hosted 48 country delegations, including 22 African leaders, at a Russia-Africa summit as he sought to deepen economic ties across the continent.
The summit, now in its third edition, produced a series of nuclear announcements involving at least six countries, with Russiaâs state-owned energy company Rosatom in advanced talks with Egypt, Togo, Namibia, and Tanzania over floating nuclear power plants, as Moscow seeks to become the worldâs first commercial exporter of the technology.
Africa remains the continent with the largest electricity access gap, holding back economic growth and industrial development. That shortfall has created opportunities for foreign suppliers, including Russia, which has spent years courting African governments with nuclear technology and state-backed financing to meet their growing demand for power.
The talks could lead to decade-long energy partnerships, giving Moscow an opportunity to extend its influence in Africa as China and Western countries pursue nuclear deals of their own. âRussia is definitely ahead of the other nuclear countries in terms of developing next generation reactors and providing state-backed finance,â Todd Moss, executive director of the US-based power think tank Energy for Growth Hub, told Semafor. Russia has about $200 billion in nuclear project orders worldwide, compared with $7.7 billion for the US, according to figures cited in July by former US deputy energy secretary Daniel Poneman.
Rwanda, which also signed a civil nuclear cooperation agreement with the US in May, agreed with Rosatom at the summit to assess and develop its nuclear infrastructure, building on an eight-year partnership that includes plans for small reactors and a research centre. Ghana also announced talks with the Russian company to build its first nuclear power plant.
Know More
Floating plants are attracting growing interest from African governments seeking faster ways to meet electricity demand, as conventional power plants are relatively costly and take a long time to build. Turkeyâs Karpowership now supplies diesel-generated electricity to eight countries from offshore vessels and is working with DR Congoâs state utility on a 134-megawatt plant to ease shortages in Kinshasa. Rosatom wants to bring nuclear power to that market, saying 38 of Africaâs 54 countries have coastlines suitable for its floating reactors.
But the promise of faster electricity comes with financial and political risks. âIf theyâre signing a deal for an emergency nuclear power plant on a ship, that is almost certainly going to be very expensive,â Moss warned.
Georgy Tikhomirov, a nuclear physicist at Russiaâs MEPhI university, said there is still too little operating experience to assess the actual cost of the electricity and power produced. Under Rosatomâs proposed model, the company would retain control of the vessels and handle their maintenance and refuelling in Russia.
Experts have long warned that floating power deals can leave African governments dependent on costly contracts with foreign suppliers. In Sierra Leone, Turkeyâs Karpowership cut electricity to Freetown in 2023 and sharply reduced supplies again in 2024 over unpaid bills, forcing the government to pay $17 million toward a $48 million debt to restore full power.
Russiaâs nuclear ambitions in Africa have yet to translate into much electricity. âAn agreement is not a power plant,â Moss told Semafor. According to a September report he co-authored, Rosatom has signed nuclear partnerships with at least 20 African countries, though most remain preliminary, with Egypt the only one currently building a Russian nuclear power plant.
Notable
- Nuclear power is key to bolstering energy security in Africa, but its rollout on the continent requires workforce training and safety regulations, said Daniel Poneman, former US deputy enerfy secretary.

7b03f708165d.text:
- Published
A search for survivors is under way after a helicopter carrying six people, including five pilgrims, crashed in the northern Indian state of Uttarakhand, officials say.
Uttarakhand's Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami said the helicopter had crashed near a village close to Joshimath in Chamoli district. Rescue teams have been dispatched to the mountainous area, but the condition of those on board remains unclear.
The aircraft reportedly took off from the Hindu pilgrimage site of Badrinath on Friday afternoon before losing contact.
The cause of the crash is also not yet known. The incident happened amid reports of heavy rain and poor visibility in the region.
Uttarakhand, a Himalayan state which borders China and Nepal, is home to some of Hinduism's holiest shrines and attracts millions of pilgrims every year.
Badrinath is one of four sacred sites on the Char Dham pilgrimage circuit, alongside Kedarnath, Gangotri and Yamunotri. Many devotees travel through steep Himalayan valleys to reach the temples, which are open for only part of the year because of harsh winter conditions.
Helicopter services have become increasingly popular among pilgrims seeking to avoid difficult mountain journeys, but their safety has come under scrutiny following a series of accidents.
Friday's incident happened amid heavy rain in the region. India's weather department had issued an orange alert for the area, warning of thunderstorms, hail and strong winds.
Dhami said, external a joint rescue operation was under way involving the district administration, disaster management department and State Disaster Response Force.
"I am continuously monitoring the entire incident," he added.
Dhami also said he had ordered that anyone seriously injured be airlifted for treatment.
In June 2025, seven people were killed when a helicopter carrying pilgrims crashed near Kedarnath. Another seven died in a crash on the same pilgrimage route in October 2022.
Several other helicopter accidents were reported during the 2025 pilgrimage season, prompting aviation authorities to tighten safety checks and restrict some operations.
