958625da654e.text: America's corporate titans greeted President Trump's 2024 victory with open checkbooks , 12-figure investment pledges and fawning tributes to his coming "Golden Age." Two years later, on the eve of a potential blue wave, Democrats are preparing to greet those same executives with a stack of subpoenas . Why it matters: The CEOs who staked their reputations and fortunes on MAGA's staying power could spend the final two years of Trump's presidency defending their dealings under oath. The big picture: A Democratic House would carry its campaign against billionaire power and corruption deep into corporate America, scrutinizing the relationships between Trump's White House and the executives who courted him . Corporate leaders now face a delicate balancing act: rebuilding ties with Democrats while avoiding retaliation from a president who still controls federal contracts, tariffs and regulators. Already, companies that scrambled to dismantle DEI programs or fund Trump's ballroom are hiring Democratic lobbyists , pushing back against the administration and rediscovering the virtues of bipartisanship. Zoom in: Elon Musk is taking a more confrontational approach. The billionaire, who has poured $445 million into Republican super PACs this election cycle alone, has threatened retaliation against Democrats preparing to investigate his sprawling business empire and tenure in the White House. DOGE: As head of Trump's short-lived cost-cutting initiative, Musk gutted USAID, drove mass federal layoffs and gave his team access to sensitive government systems. Investigators want to know whether his companies benefited from contracts or regulatory decisions while he wielded power inside the White House. Ukraine: A fierce critic of President Volodymyr Zelensky, Musk ordered Starlink restrictions that disrupted Ukraine's military satellite communications. Democrats are now demanding records of his communications with Trump and Vladimir Putin . Musk responds to reports that Democrats plan to investigate him. Screenshot via X. Zoom out: Across corporate America, the pursuit of Trump's favor has left a trail of donations, deals and concessions that Democrats are determined to follow. AI accelerationists: Trump has made the AI boom a centerpiece of his economic agenda, while giving industry leaders extraordinary influence over regulation and chip exports. Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, who set the template for corporate America's reconciliation with MAGA, is among the AI leaders likely to face scrutiny for pressing Trump to back off safety regulation. Media consolidation: Trump ally Larry Ellison helped finance his son David's rise to control of CBS and CNN, culminating in a $110 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery. Along the way, Paramount paid $16 million to settle Trump's lawsuit against CBS while seeking federal approval for its Skydance merger. Elite law firms: Trump's pressure campaign against the legal establishment yielded $940 million in pledged free legal services and concessions on diversity policies from nine major firms. Democrats are probing the terms of those agreements and whether the firms compromised their independence to appease the White House. Ballroom donors: Trump's massive White House construction project has drawn at least $333 million in private commitments , including $25 million apiece from Apple and Nvidia. Many donors — including some who kept their contributions secret — have lucrative business before the administration. Equity deals: Trump has transformed the U.S. government into a major corporate investor, striking roughly $30 billion in equity and warrant arrangements spanning more than 40 companies. Democrats are questioning how the beneficiaries were selected and whether political connections influenced the deals. Fossil fuel giants: Trump asked oil executives to raise $1 billion for his 2024 campaign while promising sweeping regulatory relief. His administration has since delivered major tax breaks and environmental rollbacks, prompting a Democratic probe of the industry's political contributions and the government benefits that followed. The bottom line: Corporate America's old instinct for bipartisan relationships existed for a reason. The same executives who spent the past two years seeking Trump's favor could spend the next two explaining exactly how they obtained it.

edcb6a017413.text: El Salvador's strongman president, Nayib Bukele , is sending thousands of troops to Haiti to boost the island's push to wipe out its gang problem — and find four of his military personnel who were captured in a recent ambush. Bukele called President Trump on Tuesday to make sure he had no problem with this major military escalation, to which Haiti's government has agreed. "Do what you have to do," Trump told him, according to sources briefed on the call. Why it matters: If it works, Bukele's troop surge could stabilize Haiti, a country 700 miles from Florida that has been devastated by deadly gang violence and has lacked a president since the last one, Jovenel Moise, was assassinated five years ago. If it doesn't work, it could increase Haiti's death toll well beyond the 5,700-plus killed in gang violence this year, embarrass Bukele and mark yet another failed international effort to restore stability to the country. Haiti also may be a test case for Bukele and security contractor Erik Prince — a Trump and Bukele ally also operating in Haiti — to act as public-private proxies for U.S. muscle in the hemisphere. El Salvador announced Wednesday it was deploying as many as 2,000 troops to Haiti. That number could double or triple, sources say. "We didn't come to Haiti to make money, because no one is paying us to do it. We came to Haiti to fight against the wicked," Bukele, writing in Haitian Creole, wrote Thursday on X . Zoom in: Along with other countries, El Salvador has been part of a UN-established initiative called the Gang Suppression Force, or GSF, operating in Haiti's capital city of Port-au-Prince. On Oct. 18, four Salvadoran aviation technicians were ambushed and remain unaccounted for, according to the Miami Herald . Three days later, Bukele posted a warning on X : "I want you, the gang leaders, to understand one thing very clearly: Today's attack is nothing compared to what is coming if we do not get all four hostages back alive." "We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too," he wrote. Zoom out: First elected in 2019, Bukele rose to political fame and infamy for wiping out the MS-13 gang in El Salvador in a campaign of brute military force and mass incarceration. Bukele's efforts transformed El Salvador from a murder capital to what's widely viewed as one of the Western Hemisphere's safest countries. Bukele, who has a strong relationship with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, endeared himself to the new Trump administration by agreeing to accept third-country migrants who were mass-deported from the U.S. and then locked up in Bukele's notorious CECOT prison. Driving the news: Bukele's force was authorized to operate on the island in a bilateral agreement with Haiti approved on Wednesday as Salvadoran special forces and hardware began pouring in. Also Wednesday, Haiti's electoral council postponed presidential elections until next year because of the gang violence. Between the lines: Bukele's force appears to be operating parallel to the GSF — to which it currently belongs — and Prince's private security firm, Vectus Global, a successor to Blackwater. Florida Rep. Brian Mast (R), chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said the UN-backed GSF is too bureaucratic and timid. The GSF's predecessor, led by Kenya, was too feckless and, at a cost of $1 billion, too expensive, he said. "We spent the equivalent of $1 million per Kenyan and the situation was worse at the end," Mast said. To show the butchery of Haitian gangs, Mast shared with Axios a video of a Haitian man who was hacked to death by machetes for helping the GSF. Rape, arson, extortion and kidnapping are rampant on the island. Beyond El Salvador finding its four missing personnel, Mast said, "I hope the mission is revenge, retribution and destruction of the gangs. Somebody needs to be there with motive and motivation." "Now the fight is personal to them and the fight will be taken to the gangs," he added. "The U.S. wants to be out of this and not spend millions on nothing." The intrigue: Bukele had proposed that the Trump administration let El Salvador pacify Haiti as a U.S. proxy force, but "Rubio wanted to stay away from that. He wants to keep Haiti off the radar," a source familiar with the discussions told Axios. Bukele had requested military equipment from the U.S., including drones and transport planes, but it was officially denied, according to another source who said that Colombia ultimately may act as an unofficial go-between to supply Bukele's force with no U.S. fingerprints on the mission. Inside the room : When Bukele called Trump on Tuesday, the president expressed sympathy and condolences over the plight of Bukele's missing military personnel, a White House official said. "Bukele doesn't want the U.S. to suddenly cut him off at the knees for going in," a source briefed on the call said. Trump's focus on Haiti is largely limited to making sure it takes back its citizens who were in the U.S. under temporary protected status, which Trump terminated last year. "Bukele told the president he was confidant he could do the job. But it might get messy," the source briefed on the call said. "The gangs f*cked with the wrong guy. He has something to prove."

e9a6c75b3fa2.text: A bipartisan deal to speed energy development is facing concerns it could favor natural gas over renewables because of President Trump's opposition to wind and solar. Why it matters: The worries from Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) could complicate efforts to pass the bill before year's end, highlighting divisions even among Democrats who have long supported permitting reform. Driving the news: Casten, a former energy executive and leading Democratic voice on permitting reform, said he isn't yet backing the bill and is negotiating changes with Senate Democrats to prevent it from disproportionately benefiting natural gas. "My test for the bill is: I talk to energy developers, and ask, 'What would you build in response to this bill?' And the answer I get overwhelmingly is a lot of gas," Casten told Axios on stage at a University of Chicago event Wednesday. "I think you have to look at the bill in the context of everything else that the Trump administration has done." The big picture: The AI boom is fueling demand for electricity, prompting a rush to build natural gas power plants alongside renewable energy projects. The permitting deal could help determine which technologies benefit most from that expansion. Catch up quick: The bill, sponsored by two Republicans and two Democrats who lead the Senate's energy and environment committees, would speed construction of power lines and other energy infrastructure. An initial procedural vote is scheduled for Nov. 9, shortly after the midterm elections, setting up a potential push to pass the legislation before the new Congress takes office. Threat level: The bill aims to prevent political favoritism in energy permitting, but Casten worries one provision could have the opposite effect. It would allow developers to challenge discriminatory permitting decisions in part by comparing them with decisions made over the previous five years. Casten argues that as Trump's second term becomes part of that historical benchmark, the administration's treatment of renewable energy could effectively become the new normal. What we're hearing: The five-year provision is emerging as a concern in negotiations over the bill. "This is definitely one of the key issues that folks are thinking about right now," said an industry official tracking the negotiations closely, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss congressional feedback. Clarifying or strengthening the language would "go a long way to reassuring folks who are on the fence," the official added. Zoom out: Divisions among Democrats are emerging about the overall bill. Former Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm and climate activist Tom Steyer are urging its passage, while four Senate Democrats are demanding the restoration of canceled clean-energy grants and Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) is calling for its defeat. Yes, but: Casten also praised the bill's overall structure and said relatively small changes could win his support. He's negotiating those changes with Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.). "I think the structure of the bill is good," he said. "I think there are modest changes we could make to it to make sure it works and doesn't sort of create like a gold rush for gas." He favors passing the bill before year's end, unlike some Democrats who have suggested waiting to see whether the midterm elections give their party more power next year. What they're saying: The White House said it supports the bipartisan deal and is pushing for a vote. "The text of the legislation has been published, and all that is left to do is vote. We are in direct conversations with the lead negotiators in the Senate," a White House official said. A Heinrich spokesperson said the bill "will expedite the approval of clean energy projects and put more clean, cheaper electricity on the grid." The bottom line: The midterms could upend these delicate negotiations just days before the Senate's procedural vote. Editor's note: Amy is a journalism fellow at the University of Chicago's Institute for Climate and Sustainable Growth and moderated Wednesday's event featuring Casten. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

4dc8fd337b08.text:
The News
A slew of top international sporting events is coming to East Africa, which governments are betting on to provide an economic boost and attract foreign investment. Despite a strong growth forecast for the region, unemployment among the fast-growing youth population remains stubbornly high, leading to political instability and leaving the authorities looking for ways to create more jobs.
The first sporting spectacle to land in the region will be the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, co-hosted by Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda. Then in 2029, Nairobi will welcome competitors for the World Athletics Championships. And in the early 2030s Formula 1 will return to Africa with an annual Grand Prix in Rwanda.
Travel, hospitality, construction, and entertainment are among the key sectors expected to benefit from the events over the next few years. World Athletics said the 2023 championships in Budapest generated $400 million when its overall impact was taken into account, which Kenya would hope to match. When it comes to AFCON, the hosts are eyeing the $2 billion in economic benefits that the Confederation of African Football said stemmed from the last tournament in Morocco, with Uganda alone targeting $500 million, according to a member of its organizing committee. And while Rwanda has not published official projections for the economic impact, it has confirmed that its new $2 billion Bugesera airport, currently under construction will sit adjacent to the planned Formula 1 circuit, along with hotels, apartments, and logistics facilities.
Peng Chen, co-founder of ticketing platform HustleSasa that operates in six African countries, said the events would serve as âproof pointsâ for investors looking at the sports ecosystem in Africa, including the long-term sustainability of investments in things like arenas.
âThe trickle down economy will also be massive,â Chen added. He told Semafor he expected visitors in host cities to spend âhundreds of dollars everydayâ between transport, food, accommodation, and entertainment including side events.
The desire to tap into the economic benefits is among factors driving new investments, especially in sports infrastructure, in Kenya and Uganda. Kenya revealed details last month of a partnership with pan-African sports investment outfit Zaria Group â led by Dallas Mavericks President Masai Ujiri â to build a 10,000-seater indoor arena in Nairobi. It is set to be part of a larger entertainment district that will also include the new $350 million Talanta Stadium being constructed for AFCON. Uganda has also unveiled plans for the Turkish firm Summa, which constructed one of its AFCON stadiums, to build a 15,000-seater indoor arena in Kampala.
Know More
The various plans come at a cost, with governments committing significant amounts to make the events happen. The three AFCON hosts, who each paid a $30 million fee for the right to host the tournament, have all invested in building new venues â along with Kenyaâs Talanta Stadium spend, Ugandaâs Hoima Stadium cost $112 million, and Tanzaniaâs Mama Samia Stadium has a $130 million price tag. This expenditure, along with the money for refurbishing old facilities, is putting pressure on national budgets.
Besides hosting events, Rwanda has also used marketing partnerships with global sports clubs to attract tourists with its Visit Rwanda partnerships. The country currently has multi-million dollar sponsorship deals with Aston Villa, PSG, and the LA Clippers.
Kenyaâs government expects to host an additional 1 million visitors in Nairobi during the month-long AFCON, growing the $3.85 billion earned from tourism in 2025. Rwandaâs strategy to boost this sector has partly leaned on sports events and sponsorship â with the country aiming to hit $1.1 billion in annual tourism revenue by 2029.
Martinâs view
Major international sporting events are welcome in East Africa, however, there is a piece missing. In order to ensure the long-term sustainability of major investments in stadiums and arenas, governments must first prioritise the development of the troubled local sports sector.
Kenyaâs own top-flight football league and national teams, for instance, have been riddled with challenges ranging from leadership wrangles to payment delays. Kenyaâs global athletics icons, including 1500m world-record holder Faith Kipyegon, have complained over the poor state of training facilities across the country. Uganda is one of the worldâs top-ranked netball teams, but its netball federation has faced allegations of corruption. Chronic underfunding and mismanagement have similarly affected several other sports and fueled their decline.
Once the international visitors have gone home, the question is whether the stadiums and facilities will lie empty and fall into disrepair. Supporting and investing in local sportsmen and women, clubs, leagues and venues is the key to ensuring the region develops lucrative sports ecosystems that create meaningful opportunities.
Room for Disagreement
Kenyan critics of the AFCON infrastructure developments have argued that the projects have been an avenue for corruption and risk escalating Kenyaâs $98 billion debt burden. Kenyaâs auditor-general in February flagged major financial irregularities in relation to the construction of the Talanta Stadium, saying that $83.7 million could not be properly accounted for.
âIt will leave us with a heavier debt burden at a time when the existing debt is crippling and critical sectors like education and health are struggling,â Nairobi-based economist Ian Mwangi told Semafor. He said that the $344 million infrastructure bond floated for the 60,000-seater stadium could balloon, echoing concerns shared by Rutoâs opponents.
Notable
- CAF President Patrice Motsepe called for a âheightened sense of urgencyâ in the development of facilities for AFCON 2027, even as he dismissed reports that a postponement of the tournament could be on the cards due to the state of some of the stadiums.

e07967243cae.text:
Medicare Drug Plans Are Hiking Premiums While Trump Claims Victory on Medicine Prices
Millions of Medicare enrollees who buy stand-alone prescription drug plans will see their average monthly premiums rise by 50% in 2027, a new analysis finds.
But enrollees can avoid the average increase — from $34 a month to $51 — by switching to lower-cost plans during the program’s open enrollment period, which runs through Dec. 7.
Robert Travis Scott of Abingdon, Virginia, did just that in late October after he received a notice that his AARP-UnitedHealthcare Medicare drug plan premium would be increasing from $39.60 a month in 2026 to $121.90 in 2027. With just a little work checking prices online, Scott found a Humana plan for $19.30 with similar benefits.
“Yes, I am quite happy about that,” he said of the new plan he just found. He said he was stunned his existing plan was going up so much and worried that other seniors won’t shop for plans to save money. He estimates he saved himself about $1,000 for next year.
“With some plans increasing premiums substantially, the stakes are higher this year for people with Medicare stand-alone drug coverage if they sit on the sidelines during open enrollment,” said Juliette Cubanski, a vice president and the director of the Program on Medicare Policy at KFF, which conducted the analysis. KFF is a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.
Rising drug costs are among the litany of affordability issues angering voters ahead of November’s midterm election. President Donald Trump, whose approval rating in some polls has dipped to the lowest level of his two terms in office, claims his administration has succeeded in negotiating lower prices from drug manufacturers.
“What we’re doing great with is pharmaceuticals, hundreds of billions,” Trump said at a campaign rally in Ohio on Oct. 28, ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms. “You should win just on this, everybody running. We have the lowest drug prices anywhere in the world. We went from the highest drug prices, we now have the lowest drug prices, favored nations, anywhere in the world.”
How much people actually pay for drugs varies widely, depending on what medicines individual patients need and their insurance coverage.
Medicare beneficiaries who get their drug coverage as part of private Medicare Advantage plans, which replace traditional Medicare coverage, will see much lower premium increases. The KFF analysis found these enrollees will pay an average of $9 for drugs as part of their overall monthly premium in 2027, or an increase of less than $2 per month.
More than half of Medicare beneficiaries are enrolled in Medicare Advantage health plans, which usually include a drug benefit, instead of the traditional program.
Nearly 25 million people are enrolled in Medicare stand-alone prescription drug plans, according to KFF. About 31 million get drug coverage through Medicare Advantage plans.
Premiums are just part of the higher costs Medicare enrollees are facing.
Most enrollees who buy a stand-alone drug plan or get drug benefits through Medicare Advantage plans will also have an annual deductible for drug coverage in 2027.
The average deductible in 2027 will be $643 for stand-alone plans, according to the KFF analysis, up from $540 in 2026. Drug deductibles will average $489 for those with Medicare Advantage plans, up from $360 in 2026.
In addition, most Medicare enrollees with drug coverage next year will have to pay coinsurance rather than copayments, the KFF analysis found. That can mean less predictable out-of-pocket costs because coinsurance requires paying a percentage of the cost of a drug, not a fixed amount.
One possible cause of the projected premium hikes is the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ decision in July to end early a three-year pilot program designed to keep down stand-alone premiums. The program paid subsidies to stand-alone plans in 2025 and 2026.
KFF said CMS’ decision to end that subsidy program after only two years could cause stand-alone premiums to rise in 2027.
CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz has called the subsidy program an insurance industry bailout.
KFF noted its analysis differs from CMS’ projection for a $1 increase in the national average premium, from $35 to $36, based on September 2026 enrollment. It said that CMS did not explain its calculation methods and that it’s possible CMS assumed people would switch to lower-cost plans.
CMS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the KFF findings.
About 10.4 million Medicare enrollees, or 76% of enrollees in stand-alone drug plans who don’t get low-income subsidies, will pay a higher monthly premium in 2027 if they stick with the same plan, KFF found.
This includes 4.1 million enrollees who are currently in a zero-premium plan. They’ll automatically pay more in 2027, because there will be no zero-premium plans available, the KFF analysis found.

Your Phone Knows You’re at the Doctor, and Data Brokers Do, Too — Then Profit From It
The sensitive information is used for targeted ads, often touting unproven treatments.
Chris McQueen finished treatment for leukemia a year and a half ago, but the ads for fake cures never stopped.
Juice cleanses to cure cancer, “natural” cancer treatments, clinics in Mexico promising full recovery with little chemotherapy — all appeared on McQueen’s mobile phone during routine oncologist visits and monthly bloodwork.
McQueen and others have taken to social media to vent about companies known as data brokers tracking their whereabouts via their smartphones’ location data, connecting it with other data gathered about them, and then drawing inferences about their health struggles to sell to companies hawking unproven treatments.
“It makes me feel sick to my stomach,” said McQueen, who lives in San Diego and fears some patients are putting themselves at risk, potentially fatally, if they try such untested treatments instead of following their oncologists’ advice.
More than 92% of patients in a 2022 American Medical Association survey said they believed their health data should not be available for purchase. But many people might not realize that when they are sitting in a hospital, an abortion clinic, or an Alcoholics Anonymous meeting in a church basement, the location data emitted from their mobile phones isn’t covered by the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, better known as HIPAA, which protects patient privacy.
That worries Eric Ellsworth, director of health policy and innovation at the Center for the Study of Services, a nonprofit focused on delivering consumers reliable information on local medical services and healthcare professionals.
“Data brokers typically are just hoovering up data from the open web and then buying it from anybody,” he said.
The U.S. government has begun to penalize some companies that track Americans when they visit health facilities and places of worship. But privacy and legal experts don’t think actions against a few companies will stop an entire industry built on scooping up Americans’ private data. They’re calling on more states or Congress to ban advertisers from tracking Americans’ locations via their phones.
But progress has been fitful. California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, on Sept. 27 vetoed a bill that would have blocked the sale and sharing of location and other sensitive personal data, saying it went “a step too far.” And a recent study from Stanford University showed that only 9% of data brokers are adhering to an existing California privacy law that gives consumers the right to delete their data, correct personal information, and learn what personal records the business is selling.
In January, Consumer Reports released model legislation giving state lawmakers a framework to ban or limit the sale of geolocation data, which uses GPS to identify a person’s movements in real time. Connecticut, Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, and Virginia have already banned the sale of precise geolocation data. But digital advertisers have also lobbied states to block such proposed limits.
The Money Behind Data Sales
Data brokers and advertisers argue that location data itself is not sensitive data, said F. Mario Trujillo, senior staff attorney at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a nonprofit that champions user privacy. “But location data is sensitive. It’s the comprehensive collection of location data that reveals sensitive things.”
Advertising trade groups say that targeted advertising saves consumers time and lowers the cost of searching for products, while also allowing websites and apps to offer digital services without paywalls or subscriptions.
“A national privacy law should protect consumers from harmful or unexpected uses of data without preventing businesses from providing the services consumers request and expect,” said Jim Potter, executive director of 4As Health, a subsidiary of the American Association of Advertising Agencies. “That balance is especially important in advertising, which is not merely a business model but a key part of the modern economy.”
The U.S. government has begun to look into industry practices. In August, the Federal Trade Commission warned retailers about using private consumer data to increase prices.
In May, the agency also placed limits on a data broker that the agency began investigating in 2022. That settlement prohibits Idaho-based data broker Kochava and a subsidiary from “selling, sharing or disclosing sensitive location data without consumer consent” following allegations that the companies “sold location data from hundreds of millions of mobile devices” that could be used to trace the movements of people when they visited hospitals, churches, abortion clinics, and other sensitive locations.
Kochava did not respond to requests for comment.
While privacy advocates have welcomed the government actions, they pointed out that the terms of individual settlements don’t apply to other companies, because settlements aren’t laws or regulations.
Meanwhile, digital advertising has become a major source of profits for big tech companies, which often offer consumers services such as apps, email, and cloud storage in exchange for monetizing personal data. A 2024 report by Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis economists on the economic implications of digital advertising showed that the profit margins for three of the four biggest tech firms — Google parent Alphabet, Facebook parent Meta, and Microsoft — were at least twice as large as the services sector average.
Other studies have shown that once data brokers build their collection systems, they face minimal additional costs to sell the same data repeatedly, including to AI companies. And their reach is wide: A 2019 study found that data brokers had data tied to more than 90% of Facebook accounts in the United States. And a 2020 report by the Electronic Frontier Foundatio

For Californians Drowning in Healthcare Costs, Governor’s Race Offers Few Answers
When Ashley Porter began slurring her speech one October day four years ago, doctors suspected a stroke. A spinal tap, an MRI, dozens of blood draws, another MRI, and a night spent at the hospital were followed, finally, by an answer: Porter had multiple sclerosis.
Her shock turned to outrage, she said, when she received the roughly $180,000 hospital bill, even though insurance covered most of it.
Porter and her husband have insurance through two separate employer plans yet have spent at least $75,000 a year — roughly a quarter of their gross income — on medical expenses since her diagnosis.
“It is terrifying,” said Porter, who works in transportation sales in the San Francisco Bay Area. “I can’t imagine having this disease and not making the kind of income that we make.”
With health insurance premiums and hospital prices rising faster than inflation, more than 40% of adults nationally struggle to afford their care and, like most, want the government to address it.
The average premium for a California family with employer-sponsored coverage has hit nearly $28,400 a year, up 24% since 2022, much more than workers’ wages. Amid skyrocketing healthcare costs, the gubernatorial candidates’ proposals remain short on specifics about funding or implementation to address this top priority for voters in the nation’s largest healthcare market.
“People are hungry for pretty aggressive action on healthcare spending,” said Kristof Stremikis, director of market analysis and insight at the California Health Care Foundation, a nonprofit philanthropic organization specializing in healthcare research and education.
“Regardless of who our new governor is and who our new state policymakers are in the next year, they have a mandate,” he said.
Nearly two-thirds of Californians worry about receiving an unexpected medical bill, surpassing financial concerns such as the cost of rent or food, according to a 2025 CHCF-NORC survey. Six in 10 said they or a family member had skipped care because of cost.
Democrat Xavier Becerra, the former U.S. health secretary who has a commanding polling lead in the race for governor, has vowed to negotiate lower drug prices and go after anticompetitive practices as he did as attorney general in a landmark antitrust settlement with hospital giant Sutter Health.
He has also said that Congress should restore an estimated $900 billion in federal Medicaid cuts and reinstate enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that President Donald Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress allowed to expire, causing insurance premium payments to increase for millions of Americans. Both are national Democratic priorities outside a governor’s purview.
Former Fox News host Steve Hilton, Becerra’s Republican opponent, has said he’d build on existing state laws governing price transparency and prescription drug middlemen known as pharmacy benefit managers to lower costs. And he wants to partially replace Medi-Cal, the state Medicaid program, with personal healthcare accounts of up to $10,000 a year — a concept unlikely to gain traction in a statehouse controlled by Democrats.
Both candidates declined multiple interview requests to discuss their health policies.
Healthcare Costs and Consolidation
From 1970 to 2025, U.S. health expenditures ballooned from $75 billion to a projected $5.7 trillion, rising nearly 40% from 2020. By 2032, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services predicts, health spending will account for more than a fifth of the U.S. economy.
Payments to hospitals, doctors, and clinics account for much of the inflation, along with rising prescription drug prices. Research shows that escalating mergers among physician practices, hospital groups, and insurers further stifled competition and raised prices.
In the 2018 lawsuit Becerra filed against Sutter Health, he accused the health system of using its market dominance to drive up hospital prices in Northern California, where procedures cost as much as 30% more than in other parts of the state.
The Sacramento-based not-for-profit system, which admitted no wrongdoing, paid an unprecedented $575 million fine and agreed to stop certain business practices, including imposing “all-or-nothing” terms on insurers that forced them to contract with the system’s entire network of clinics and hospitals.
“It was the biggest victory in antitrust and hospitals ever,” said Richard Scheffler, director of the Nicholas C. Petris Center on Health Care Markets and Consumer Welfare at the University of California-Berkeley. A report by the center, which conducts economic research on health policy topics, formed the basis of Becerra’s suit.
“But things change,” Scheffler said.
While the settlement likely discouraged similar practices by other hospital chains, he said, any relief has since been eclipsed by rapid consolidation in the healthcare industry.
At a press event in October, Becerra said he would work with the next state attorney general to “continue to look at the types of practices in healthcare that drive up costs.”
Hilton has said that he wants to increase competition by producing more generic drugs through California’s CalRx initiative, which aims to cut drug prices. He has said he wants to allow consumers to pick cheaper, pared-down insurance plans and force healthcare providers to make their prices more transparent.
Hospitals Under the Scope
Health economists say rising healthcare costs eat up money that employers might otherwise use for raises or new hires, depressing wages. That can be a double whammy for workers already struggling to meet basic needs and, consumer advocates warn, could increase medical debt, which 40% of California adults already report carrying.
Kia Frazier-Hill and her husband didn’t expect to be among them. She knew it would be expensive when he landed in the emergency room and was hospitalized at an out-of-network facility.

A proposed amendment to the Florida Constitution on the ballot this November is aimed at cutting property taxes. But the amendment would also affect funding for local governments and the state agencies responsible for flood control and water supply and conservation across this vulnerable, low-lying peninsula.
Amendment 3 would raise the homestead property tax exemption, available on permanent residences, from $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and to $250,000 in 2028, with further increases based on inflation. Tax hikes on non-homestead properties also would be limited. The Legislature approved the measure in June during a two-day special session called by Gov. Ron DeSantis, a term-limited Republican whose second term ends in January 2027. At least 60 percent of voters must approve the amendment for it to be added to the state constitution.
The amendment’s financial impact on local non-school property tax revenues is projected to be $5 billion in fiscal year 2027-2028 and $9 billion in fiscal year 2028-2029, according to a bill analysis prepared for the Legislature. The recurring impact is estimated to be $12 billion annually, affecting roads, public transportation and safety, libraries, parks and other services. The amendment has drawn a diverse array of detractors, from the Florida State Fraternal Order of Police, Florida Sheriffs Association and Florida Fire Chiefs’ Association to the League of Women Voters of Florida, Florida Library Association and 1000 Friends of Florida, a conservation group.
During an Oct. 21 roundtable discussion on Amendment 3 in Miami, attended by local officials and a representative of the Florida Realtors Association, DeSantis said the amendment would provide much-needed tax relief for Floridians and that local governments could afford it.
“If you have more money in people’s pockets, if they’re not having to pay more money to local governments just to live in their primary residences, that money is going to do better in the economy,” he said. “It’s going to expand the economic base, and then what will happen, you will end up getting revenue through the normal sources, not raising taxes, just like we’ve done in Florida. We’ve cut taxes. We’ve even eliminated taxes, and yet we continue to get more revenue every year. It’s because we’ve expanded the economic base.”
The state’s five water management districts, with boundaries defined by the watersheds they serve, are the stewards of Florida’s iconic water resources, from world-renowned springs to the vast Everglades. The fragile waters face growing pressures as the state’s population soars and the global climate warms, leading to hotter temperatures, rising seas and more damaging storms. Amendment 3’s financial impact on the water management districts, whose budgets are based on federal and state funds and local property tax revenues, is projected to be $89.5 million in 2027 and $160 million in 2028, climbing to $218 million in 2031, according to an analysis prepared for the Legislature by the Office of Economic & Demographic Research.
“The water management districts are one of those government functions that nobody pays attention to and everybody depends on. They help ensure that our communities don’t flood in storms. They are helping us to address the effects of climate change: blue-sky flooding in our coastal communities, crazy rainfall events that cause flooding inland. They are protecting our water supply, so making sure there is enough water to drink,” said Julie Wraithmell, executive director of Audubon Florida, which opposes Amendment 3. “They also help us with permitting of new development and making sure that sprawl is steered away from the most vulnerable wetland resources. And they are a really important part of the equation in how our state grows.”
At the South Florida Water Management District, the largest of the water management districts and the state agency charged with overseeing Everglades restoration, the impact in 2027 would amount to some 3 percent of the $1.6 billion budget for fiscal year 2026-2027. At the Suwanee River Water Management District, responsible for the more rural Big Bend region, the impact in 2027 would represent some 2 percent of the $70 million budget for fiscal year 2026-2027. The situation represents a continued “bleeding” of the water management districts, after cuts under former Republican Gov. Rick Scott, DeSantis’ predecessor and now a U.S. senator, said Jacqui Thurlow-Lippisch, a former board member for the South Florida Water Management District.

But it’s going to bleed us,” she said. “We’re going to watch our house go to hell in a handbasket, meaning it will still be there but it’s just not going to be as safe or as nice because there’s going to be a lot of pooling water and mildew and problems. PHOENIX— Koral Casillas’ American Dream was simple: Leave her corporate job to start a local business serving her community.
Five years ago, she did just that. She’s now the co-owner of two local Phoenix businesses—Monsoon Market, a purveyor of local goods, and Strip Mall, a coffee and wine shop. But this summer, Casillas said, she was rudely awakened from her dream when her August utility bill came in at $1,500—far higher than any bill she had received before; the next month, it rose again, to $1,700.
Casillas’ story quickly made the rounds on social media, and she’s using the recent attention to highlight a little-known elected office in Arizona tasked with regulating the state’s utilities, the Arizona Corporation Commission. The ACC is currently considering approving another 14 percent rate increase from Arizona Power Service—its third price hike from the utility in four years.
“It’s already pretty hard to operate a small business here in Arizona, and the risk of utility bills continuing to rise [is] probably [the] greatest one facing us today,” Casillas said at a press conference at Strip Mall featuring Clara Pratte and Jonathon Hill, Democratic candidates for the ACC. They are running against Republicans Kevin Thompson, a current commissioner, and Ralph Heap, a state lawmaker facing a campaign finance investigation, neither of whom responded to requests for comment.
“While I can shop around for cheaper costs for coffee beans and paper goods, I am sadly stuck with my utility provider, APS,” Casillas said. “This story isn’t unique, and I know that I’m not alone here. Our members on the ACC are supposed to negotiate and regulate companies like APS to ensure that they are providing safe and reliable power to all of us Arizona residents and small business owners. They have failed us.”
Created in 1912 under the state’s constitution, the ACC regulates the state’s water and power utilities, determining how much customers can be charged, how much profit utilities can make and how Arizona’s power grid is built and operated, among other responsibilities. The state is one of 10 where the commissioners are elected and are separate from the state’s other branches of government, meaning only elections and lawsuits can hold them accountable.
In the 2024 election, Republicans took control of all five seats on the commission. In the two years since, the commission has repealed the state’s energy efficiency standards and renewable energy standards. It also approved the first formula rate plans, which allow utilities to adjust their rates annually based on a pre-established formula, rather than go through a rate hearing process that involves more oversight and transparency about the need for the increase.
“Each of these decisions dealt a blow to consumers. Combined, it’s like a knockout punch,” said Diane Brown, executive director of the nonprofit Arizona Public Interest Research Group Education Fund. “In the upcoming year, the next commission will have major consequential decisions to make related to rate cases, data centers and energy resources, and the decisions of the next commission are extremely likely to impact ratepayer bills for years to come.”
Recent polling from The Nature Conservancy in Arizona and the Arizona PIRG Education Fund found about 80 percent of Arizonans said their electricity bills rose in the last two years. Over 60 percent said their summer bills are difficult to afford, and another roughly 60 percent said they keep their thermostat set above comfortable temperatures to save money in the hot summer months.
“The polling signifies a disconnect between what Arizonans want when it comes to energy efficiency programs provided by their utility, and what the Arizona Corporation Commission has done by repealing Arizona’s very successful energy efficiency standard,” which saved Arizonans over $1.7 billion dollars and over 2,000 megawatts in cumulative peak demand energy savings, Brown said.
Pratte and Hill have campaigned on bringing transparency and accountability to the commission, limiting excessive rate increases for ratepayers, requiring large energy users to pay their fair share and developing more renewable energy in the state.
“Arizonans are sick and tired of commissioners who will not fight for them,” said Pratte at the press conference. Pratte is a member of the Navajo Nation and co-founded Navajo Power, which partners with tribal communities to build renewable energy projects.
Pratte and Hill cite a recent analysis that shows between 2023 and 2025, homeowners and businesses paid $587 million for costs associated with the “large load” sector, such as data centers. In a statement, APS said the analysis “reaches false conclusions” and “oversimplifies a complex issue.”
But Pratte and Hill are calling on the ACC to require APS to open its books and launch an investigation into the claims. “Arizona ratepayers deserve an answer to this very important question” of whether ratepayers are helping pay for the surge of electricity costs driven by data centers in the state, Hill said.
“If small businesses, families, seniors are paying for billions of dollars of data center costs, we will demand an immediate reimbursement for those customers,” Hill said. “Arizonans are paying attention to these issues like they never have before, because it’s affecting them so much. Arizonans are realizing that something needs to change, because they’re seeing their utility bills every month, and the problem is only getting worse.”

A stalemate in the conflict between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo is raising fresh doubts about the Trump administrationâs ability to influence it.
The US imposed sanctions on Rwandaâs Ministry of Defense and a bank serving its security services earlier this week, accusing Kigali of backing and fighting alongside M23 rebels in eastern Congo nearly a year after US President Donald Trump declared the war over.
âIt will continue raising questions about US leadership within these matters, because the US is the guarantor of this particular agreement,â said Mvemba Phezo Dizolele, a senior fellow at Johns Hopkins Universityâs Foreign Policy Institute, of the stalemate.
Trump hosted Rwandan President Paul Kagame and Congo President FÃ©lix Tshisekedi in Washington last December to sign accords to end the war. But fighting never abated.
The State Department now says âthousandsâ of Rwanda Defense Force troops are fighting in Congo and that some âhave also brought in surface-to-air missiles and jamming equipment that endanger civilian aviation.â
In announcing the sanctions, the Treasury Department accused Zigama Credit and Savings Society of helping finance the Rwandan militaryâs support for Congolese rebels, including moving gold out of M23-held territory. The action follows sanctions on Rwandaâs army and four senior commanders in March and on a Kigali gold refinery in June.
The sanctions, however, are unlikely to have a major impact on Rwanda, argued Dizolele, though Kigali will be cognizant of the impact on its image in the eyes of the West. âThey will shrug it off, they will adjust, but it stings,â he said.

The CEO Signal
Any interference in next weekâs US midterm elections should be a âred lineâ that prompts business leaders to rally behind American democratic norms, Ken Chenault is warning his peers. But the influential chairman of venture capital firm General Catalyst worries that some leaders have lost sight of where to draw such lines, as theyâve retreated from a social responsibility agenda they espoused just a few years ago.
Chenault, who was one of the first Black CEOs to lead a Fortune 500 company and ran American Express for 17 years, says people concerned about meddling in Tuesdayâs election or damaging disputes over the results have been calling him to ask: âWill business stand up?â
In 2021, Chenault helped rally hundreds of executives in other companies to oppose restrictive voting bills. But he thinks it would be âvery challengingâ to muster the same response from executives now. Back then, businesses issued statements in favor of a peaceful transfer of power around the 2020 election and subsequent attack on the US Capitol.
But theyâve since âbacked down,â he notes. âThey said, âHereâs what weâre not going to do.â And then, in fact, they changed. And then the hammer came down.â
CEOs have pulled back from public comment on issues they fear will attract a costly backlash, having watched President Donald Trump go after law firms, universities, and corporations in his second term.
Some US officials have raised concerns about possible threats to the integrity of the midterms and campaigners have called on CEOs to express support for free and fair elections. Robert Rubin, the former Treasury Secretary, wrote recently that any manipulation of the process would have lasting economic effects. But very few active CEOs of large US companies have echoed such concerns publicly, and investors have been calm.
âPeople feel threatened by consequences,â Chenault says. Some executives see voting rights as too political a topic to touch, but âitâs not political; weâre talking about a fundamental right here. Weâre not saying Republican [or] Democrat.â
In Equal to the Task, a memoir that will be published next week, Chenault argues a point many CEOs wonât: that it is âvitally importantâ for business to protect the democratic process.
âAs the integrity of elections becomes compromised, segments of the population become alienated, communities become less stable and less prosperous, and individual businesses suffer,â he writes.
Chenaultâs stance seems an increasingly lonely one in corporate America. He does not believe that every CEO should have to take a public position on every social or political controversy, he stresses, âbut we need a few people.â
A call to get business off the sidelines
Warren Buffett, who appointed Chenault to the board of Berkshire Hathaway, has called him âthe gold standard for corporate leaders and the benchmark that I measure others against.â The onetime lawyer earned widespread respect in the upper reaches of US business for the way he led Amex through struggles including the September 11 attacks, the 2008 financial crisis, and a US antitrust probe.
âI think I confronted more major challenges than frankly, some of the CEOs of today,â he says. But he does not belittle the complexity of the environment facing this generation of executives, saying that âthe transforming impact of AI, the geopolitical environment, [and] the increasing movement to authoritarianism [are] existential challenges.â
Chenaultâs book is both a personal account of his âuniquely American storyâ and an attempt to guide his successors through those challenges. And it ends with a call for a broader ârebalancingâ of the relationship between business and society, which he implies will require a bolder stance from business leaders on issues from democracy to diversity.
âI canât recall a moment that has called for greater courage than today,â he writes, adding in an interview: âBusiness canât afford to just be on the sidelines.â
Chenault, who has mentored founders including Airbnbâs Brian Chesky in his role at General Catalyst, says he often asks CEOs what their core beliefs are beyond their strategy and which âred linesâ they would never cross in business. He has grown concerned that âpeople are increasingly uncomfortable with that question,â he says, adding that executives should see any election interference as one of those boundaries.
Organizations that know what behavior they would find beyond the pale have the advantage of being able to prepare for how to respond if they encounter it, Chenault says. The Harvard Corporation, the university governing body on which he served until earlier this year, discussed its red lines âbefore things happened,â he says, referring to the Trump administrationâs multi-front campaign against the institution.
Some people told him privately that they agreed with how Harvard responded, but said, âI could never do that; Iâve got to be silent,â Chenault says. âIâve said to people, you canât be silent about principles.â
A âproud capitalistâ makes the case for social responsibility
Chenault calls himself a âproud capitalist,â but he has long rejected Milton Friedmanâs argument that the only social responsibility a business has is to use its resources to increase its profits âwithin the rules of the game.â
âI believe that business exists because society allows it to exist. And, to me, that confers a level of responsibility,â Chenault says.

In what might have been his last hearing as chair of Pennsylvania’s House Environmental and Natural Resource Protection committee, long-time Democratic state Rep. Greg Vitali seemed to have little interest in soaking it all in.
During the October hearing, Vitali instead furrowed his brow as he watched a parade of witnesses discussing “roadspreading,” a practice in which some oil and gas companies dump waste brine from drilling on rural roadways, ostensibly to help control dust.
The regulations governing roadspreading are riddled with complex loopholes, and Vitali called the hearing after state officials issued a roadspreading permit he took issue with. That move proved the most recent example of a recalcitrance that may have contributed to ending Vitali’s decades-long career in Pennsylvania’s legislature earlier this year.
But if his loss in a competitive primary in his suburban Philadelphia district was humbling, Vitali seems determined to keep advocating for the climate and environmental issues he has always cared about. For the past 34 years, no one in the state legislature has spoken out more consistently or forcefully for fossil fuel regulation or clean energy alternatives in Pennsylvania, even as political polarization and the rise of the gas industry made those positions increasingly embattled. Vitali was the first Pennsylvania lawmaker to introduce climate change legislation and a chief advocate pushing for a “severance” tax on gas drilling in the state during the fracking boom.
David Hess, a former secretary of the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection, said what really sets Vitali apart is his willingness to act as a thorn in the side of even his own party’s leadership.
“I think, in some ways, he became sort of the conscience of the Democratic caucus on a lot of environmental issues,” Hess said. “Some people admired him for that. Some people didn’t admire him for that because he was very plain-spoken.”
Now Pennsylvania will find out what it’s like not to hear his voice in Harrisburg at all. Some of Vitali’s critics welcome his impending exit at the end of November, contending that his principled stands made it more difficult to forge the kind of compromises that are necessary to pass laws in a divided government. His allies think the state will be worse off without his dedication to the environment and sense of moral clarity.
With the House’s current term winding down, Democratic state Rep. Danielle Friel Otten said Vitali’s calling of the October hearing was like a teacher assigning homework on the penultimate day of school: Otten was one of just six lawmakers present from the 27-member committee. Even after Republican Minority Chair Rep. Jack Rader Jr. closed the hearing by thanking Vitali for his time in office, which began in 1992, Vitali signaled he still has miles to go.
“Oh, we’ve got almost two months left,” Vitali said with a wry smile. “You’re not done.”
Filling a Leadership Vacuum
Vitali’s career in politics began with a recycling regulation. In 1988, Pennsylvania passed Act 101, requiring large municipalities to provide curbside recycling for the first time. In Vitali’s view, his local Haverford Township was only doing the “bare minimum” the law required. He said he had an interest in environmental topics dating to when they rose to the top of the priority list for Democratic activists following the Vietnam War. Then a young lawyer, Act 101 became his personal call to action.
“I actually set up my mother’s card table by a recycling center and got signatures on a petition for the township to do more recycling, and took those to a township meeting,” Vitali said, adding the effort was ultimately successful. “It struck me that people wanted to make a contribution, but not be the prime mover or leader. And I felt I was filling a leadership vacuum.”
That solo effort grew into a drive to push surrounding Delaware County to establish a household hazardous waste collection program, which in turn provided the political base on which Vitali launched his first campaign for the State House in 1992. That year, he won the open seat for Pennsylvania’s 166th House District, previously held by a Republican. When the next session began, Vitali made the environment committee his first choice and got the assignment.
The first half of his career in Harrisburg was relatively fruitful. In 2004, he was among the Pennsylvania House members who voted for the Pennsylvania Alternative Energy Portfolio Standards, among the first regulations in the country to require electric utilities to purchase power from renewable sources like wind and solar. That same year, he introduced the legislature’s first-ever climate specific bill to require the state DEP to develop an inventory of greenhouse gas emissions, and in 2008 co-sponsored a similar bill that passed both chambers and became law.
That same year also saw the passage of Act 129, a so-called “smart metering” bill that supported statewide energy efficiency measures for utilities. John Hanger, then secretary of the DEP, said Vitali played a “significant role in its passage.”
Then came seismic shifts: Pennsylvania’s Marcellus Shale natural gas boom took off, enabled by advances in hydraulic fracturing, just as national political discourse began to polarize in the wake of the Obama presidency. Since then, even Vitali acknowledges his legislative track record has been more limited.
“It’s very difficult doing climate policy in Pennsylvania. Obviously, it has a lot of coal and oil and natural gas. So when you choose climate policy as the most important thing to work on, your life is not going to be filled with victories,” Vitali said. “It’s been frustrating. I like to give myself credit for being at the plate swinging.”

88855c740bf5.text: The people at the frontlines of the ongoing barrage of AI-enabled cyberattacks are being pummeled with attacks, vulnerabilities and false alarms. Why it matters: Humans are still at the frontlines of a fight enabled largely by AI — and they're struggling to wade through mountains of threat data to determine who's been hit and which attacks pose a real danger to companies. What they're saying: "The last month has been the longest year of my life," Justin Timothy, threat intelligence consultant at GuidePoint Security, told Axios. Even before "Black October," Timothy was already swamped and dealing with hacker gangs that returned from a seasonal summer lull. These groups specialize in ransomware, essentially attacking the networks of an institution and holding it hostage. While AI is playing a role in many new cyberattacks, the ransomware scourge has already been shutting down pipeline systems, hospitals, education software and other essential services for years. It's only expected to get worse this year as powerful new AI systems are amplifying the capabilities of attackers faster than defenders can insulate vast corners of the unprotected internet. The big picture: The people companies call when they're hacked are being swamped, piling onto the persistent burnout that has plagued the industry. Troy Bettencourt, who leads Palo Alto Networks' global digital forensics and incident response practice, told Axios that demand for his team's services has climbed by double digits over the last six weeks. Unlike past surges tied to historically harmful attacks like SolarWinds , this year's workload has been relentless. "It's just a continuous grind that increases," Bettencourt said. The same heavy workload is happening across the industry, and even Palo Alto Networks' incident response subcontractors are at max capacity, he said. Investigations that could once be handled by a single consultant now require teams of five to 20 people, he said. The company is also pulling employees off other projects and shifting staff into incident response as it braces for more attacks exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities disclosed last week. Zoom in: Samantha Lewis, head of threat intelligence at Armadin, said her team has been inundated with requests from customers scrambling to determine whether their systems are exposed to AI-discovered flaws in foundational internet code. "This week has been pure chaos," she said. "The burden of that has been tremendous." Her team spent days sorting through hundreds of purported exploits, many of which didn't work , to determine which posed real threats to customers. Between the lines: AI's ability to uncover more software flaws threatens to bury defenders in even more work. The mounting workload is pushing security firms to use AI and automation to identify weaknesses and accelerate investigations. "The number of people you would need to actually defend against this starts to become entirely untenable," Lewis said. Yet the shift comes with another headache: Palo Alto's Bettencourt said he's juggling workers who are both exhausted by the caseload and worried that the AI tools being developed to ease their workloads could replace them. "They're burning out, and they're hearing everything in the media that AI is going to take everyone's job," Bettencourt said. "It's a tough balance." The intrigue: Even companies that largely escaped the latest security scares haven't been spared. Jack Nelson, Ivanti's chief information security officer and deputy general counsel, said he got "less sleep than normal this past week," despite the company's limited exposure to the PHP vulnerabilities. "It's been busy, there's no doubt about it," Nelson said. What to watch: Cyber defenders can't keep working at this pace indefinitely, but many are hopeful AI will offer them more ammunition in a battle some expect to go on for 12 to 18 months.

In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents.
Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system.
On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.
Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges.
Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.
The intended loss in his case was $20,000 (Â£15,000), according to prosecutors.
Court documents say Mogambi received $2,000 a week and attempted to recruit another person into the scheme. He allegedly told the individual he needed a business that would allow him to cash larger cheques without paying taxes.
Mogambi was arrested shortly after the indictment was returned and is being held in custody pending trial. He has not yet commented on the allegations against him.
His case forms part of a wider US investigation, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, into the alleged use of stolen identities to enrol fictitious students at colleges and claim federal financial aid that resulted in a loss of $130m in taxpayers funds.
US authorities say the investigation has so far resulted in five indictments that involved Kenyan nationals, while a further 40 investigations remain open. Hundreds of people have been affected after fraudsters allegedly stole their personally identifiable information (PII) and used it to access federal student aid.
The stolen personal information was sometimes sold online for between $4 and $8, with fraudsters targeting low-income Americans who had never had the opportunity to attend college.
At a news conference on 29 October announcing the first charges in the investigation, Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald, who heads the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, vowed to pursue those involved.
"If you steal taxpayers' dollars, if you exploit a programme meant to help students, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.
The Justice Department says those behind the fraud use what is described as "super intelligence" to place fake students in classrooms and complete coursework, creating the impression that they are attending college and allowing financial aid payments to continue.
"The goal is to keep the ghost student in school as long as possible. Semester after semester after semester stealing money from the taxpayers," McDonald said.
But the consequences extend beyond the financial losses suffered by the US government.
People whose identities are stolen can find themselves facing unexpected student loan debts, even if they have never enrolled in college.
"His identity was stolen, his credit is now at risk, and his name is on the bill," McDonald said, describing the impact on one victim.
He also said that nearly a third of community college applicants in California in 2024 had been identified as fraudulent.
The scale of the suspected fraud is significant.
Investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent Federal Student Aid identification numbers associated with nearly $130m in September and October 2026. They recommended that the Department of Education disable them.
The figure represents financial aid associated with potentially fraudulent accounts, not confirmed losses.
"In a flash, the money vanishes, often overseas in places like Kenya," McDonald said.
The investigation has also exposed alleged financial links between the US and Kenya.
In September, US officials travelled to Kenya to work with local law enforcement on extraditions, prosecutions and the recovery of money allegedly stolen from American taxpayers.
With the help of Kenyan investigators, US authorities seized more than $750,000 from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the wider scheme. The Justice Department described it as the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya.
The seizure was not connected to Mogambi's individual case.
In a separate case in Virginia, prosecutors allege that a Kenyan national received more than 700 fraudulent student-aid refunds totalling approximately $1.44m. At least $1.3m was subsequently transferred through thousands of transactions to accounts in the US and Kenya.
Meanwhile, in New Jersey, three people have been charged with allegedly acting as money mules in a scheme to obtain more than $1m in federal student aid.
Prosecutors say they received the funds through US bank accounts, kept a portion for themselves and transferred the remainder to alleged co-conspirators in Kenya linked to a purported safari company.
If convicted, Mogambi faces a mandatory prison term of at least 10 years, according to the Justice Department.
Authorities say those convicted will also face appropriate orders for forfeiture of assets and restitution to victims, in addition to any prison sentences.

A Pakistani anti-terrorism court has sentenced human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari and her husband Hadi Ali Chattha to 10 years in prison, over an alleged security breach during a cricket tour in 2024.
The couple were accused of removing road barriers and obstructing police officers in Islamabad - charges that both have denied.
Mazari and Chattha were previously sentenced to up to 17 years in prison for social media posts criticising the military.
Pakistan's Supreme Court had suspended those sentences in August, but police re-arrested the couple before they could be released. They have been imprisoned in Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail for the past several months.
This latest case concerns an incident on 25 October 2024, when England's cricket team was touring Pakistan.
Prosecutors accused Mazari and Chattha of removing barriers from a road designated for the team's security convoy and obstructing police officers at Zero Point, a major cloverleaf road junction in Islamabad.
They were each sentenced to 10 years in prison under the Anti-Terrorism Act, as well as additional one-year and two-year terms for obstructing and using force against public servants. All sentences will run concurrently.
The court also fined each of them 200,000 Pakistani Rupees (Â£541:$723).
In statements recorded during the trial, the couple described themselves as "prisoners of conscience" who had faced state persecution.
"I am being punished for not only supporting my wife's work and activism, but for choosing this path of resisting injustice as our life journey together," Chatta said in his statement to Dawn News.
The couple had earlier said that they were "being made an example to further cement the chilling effect against those who stand (or want to stand) against tyranny, oppression, and injustice".
Amnesty International has criticised the proceedings, saying the couple were denied an open and fair trial.
"These convictions are an indictment of Pakistan's justice system." said Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International's Senior Director for Regional Human Rights Impact.
"Imaan and Hadi are being targeted solely because of their refusal to stop their fearless human rights work and for exercising their right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly."
The organisation also raised concerns that the trial had been moved inside the prison, where Mazari and Chattha were kept behind a cage-like structure during hearings.
The couple have faced several criminal cases in recent months.
They have been in custody since 23 January, when they were arrested in a separate case involving an alleged altercation outside the Islamabad High Court. A day later, they were sentenced to up to 17 years in prison under Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act over social media posts critical of the military.
Pakistan's Supreme Court suspended those sentences and granted them bail on 17 September - but they were arrested again the same day in connection with a separate case over a protest in March 2025, in which they were accused of chanting "anti-government slogans" and "blocking roads".
Mazari and Chattha are prominent human rights lawyers who have represented activists, journalists and marginalised communities subjected to enforced disappearances.
Mazari's mother, Shireen Mazari, is a former human rights minister who served in the government of former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan.
The couple's convictions have long drawn criticism from international human rights organisations, which have raised concerns about the treatment of lawyers and activists in Pakistan.

When BaRupOn LLC, a California-based developer, bought land in East Texas for a 700-acre industrial campus in 2023, the company received a warm welcome from the state. The developer set out to build numerous data centers and rare-earth manufacturing facilities at the site, as well as its own power plants.
At first, Gov. Greg Abbott’s office worked closely with BaRupOn, said Balaji Tammabattula, the chief operating officer.
The governor’s office staff would recommend site locations for future projects and which county officials they should get in touch with, Tammabattula said. Developers were encouraged to seek out incentives and tax breaks. The governor’s office, which was just a phone call away, even gave the planned industrial campus, in Liberty, Texas, the codename of “Project Tough,” Tammabattula said.
“Texas used to be the best place,” he said. “Fast forward to 2026, it’s impossible to have [the governor’s office] respond to our emails.”
The climate around data centers has soured so severely that new developments in Texas are essentially on pause until after November’s elections. The land, energy and water usage of the large warehouses filled with server racks have elicited strong protest across the country—even becoming a bipartisan issue among midterm election candidates, including in Texas.
Abbott has gone against his typical business-first approach and led some companies to rethink their major data center investments in Texas, analysts and developers said. Those seeking to keep their spot in the lengthy line for grid power are laboring to not only secure state permits but social permission from communities across the state.
The data center industry flocked to invest billions of dollars in the state to quickly construct the physical infrastructure required for tech companies to develop the most mature artificial intelligence and other advanced technologies. The developers, many of whom were new to the industry, saw a state not only open to doing business but a grid committed to connecting projects to power faster than anywhere else. Texas became the epicenter of A.I. development as Abbott willed last year. But that tune changed fast.
The state has long been seen as the best place for business development in the country, with its previously unfussy regulatory environment. It’s a reputation that’s carried throughout Abbott’s 11 years in office. Yet that’s changed amid the staunch opposition data centers have ignited and a race which could result in a Democrat representing Texas in the U.S. Senate for the first time in more than 30 years. And there’s another unanticipated outcome for Abbott: his own unusually tight race for reelection against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa from Austin.
Andrew Mahaleris, Abbott’s press secretary, said Abbott has taken decisive action to set clear guardrails to protect Texans against intrusive data center development.
In August, he ordered the state’s utilities regulator, the Public Utility Commission, and its grid operator, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, to audit how much power and water every data center project being developed would consume. In September, he ordered the Texas Water Development Board to enforce water-use reporting requirements on data center projects.
“Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water, and complete the ERCOT and TWDB audits,” Mahaleris said in a statement to Inside Climate News. “Until they do, no state agency will issue related permits, and any project that fails those standards will be denied.”
Abbott’s audit and directive to pause all environmental permits is on top of new regulations and planning processes implemented after the last legislative session, which seek to verify the validity of the massive amounts of data center projects trying to connect to the grid.
Six months ago, the industry in Texas was most concerned about how fast their projects could get interconnected to the grid, said Olivier Beaufils, a head researcher at Aurora Energy Research. Now, the industry is nervous, Beaufils said, because there’s more political uncertainty than there was earlier this year, when developers were solely dealing with the wave of new rules.
“Political backlash and political risk was sort of a remote risk that people weren’t considering as their core problem they had to deal with,” Beaufils said. “That has shifted very rapidly.”
There’s anguish within the industry over whether the political issues they’re facing today will subside after the midterms are over, or whether they will multiply during the legislative session in January, Beaufils said.
“I think there’s a recognition that this is not a risk that is going to disappear in November,” Beaufils said. “This is something they’re going to have to engage with over the next six months until there’s a bit more clarity.”
After Diode Ventures, a data center developer, withdrew its plans for a data center near a residential community in Henderson County as a result of Abbott’s directives and community pushback about its water usage, Abbott celebrated the company’s decision.
“Data centers that want to do business in Texas must meet a clear standard. This project did not,” Abbott said in a July statement. “Diode did the right thing by withdrawing their project. If other data center developments refuse to meet these standards, I expect them to do the same.”

Abbott stated that he plans to seek legislation to require large data centers to annually report electricity and water usage data to the PUC and repeal any sales tax exemptions or other outdated or unnecessary incentives for the facilities.
