841509f9c60a.text: A federal judge announced Friday she plans to appoint a special master to investigate whether Justice and Interior Department officials misled the court about the Trump administration's plans to renovate a D.C. golf course, according to news reports . Why it matters: The investigation could lead to professional sanctions, contempt proceedings or criminal referrals against administration officials over allegations government lawyers misled the judge. Driving the news: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes opened a hearing Friday by reading ethics rules requiring attorneys to be truthful with courts, then questioned Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. about the administration's conflicting accounts, according to news reports. Trump announced Oct. 18 the golf course would close Nov. 15 for roughly 15 months of renovations. Woodward told the court the next day there was "no plan to close the course." On Oct. 28, the Justice Department acknowledged Trump had directed the closure. Catch up quick: A preservation group and two golfers are suing the administration over what they say is President Trump's illegal plan to convert the historic, public East Potomac Golf Links into a championship-level golf course. After government crews cut down more than 400 trees, Reyes barred further tree removal without court approval and required 10 business days' notice before closing the park or making irreversible changes. The administration has appealed. What's next: Reyes said she intends to appoint a special master who could review documents, question witnesses under oath and hold hearings. The government would have five business days to object after a special master is selected, the Washington Post reported . This is a breaking news story and will be updated. Go deeper: Exclusive: Congress presses Trump on D.C. golf course plans

3d6f71384535.text: Pope Leo XIV voted in the 2026 Illinois midterm elections using a mail-in ballot, the Vatican confirmed Friday, becoming the first sitting pope known to vote in an American election. Why it matters: The pontiff, an American citizen, may be the first to vote in any secular democratic election. Joliet radio station WJOL first reported Oct. 23 that Leo had requested a mail-in ballot. What they're saying: The pope believes "in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Holy See Press Office said in a statement . The Vatican said Leo "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so" and that "in keeping with this long-standing practice of civic participation, he has submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago." Pope Leo also voted whenever eligible during his years living in Peru, the Vatican's statement said. Zoom in: The pope's ballot includes Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker 's reelection bid, the race to succeed Sen. Dick Durbin and a House contest between Democratic Rep. Jonathan Jackson and Republican Christian Maxwell. Jackson, the son of the late Rev. Jesse Jackson, won his district handily in 2024. The pontiff's ballot will have to travel from Vatican city to Joliet, Illinois. Worth noting : Leo has voted in both Democratic and Republican primaries in the last two decades. Leo requested Democratic primary ballots in 2008 and 2010 when he lived in heavily blue Cook County, per the AP. He then started voting in GOP primaries in subsequent elections when he moved to the more conservative Will County, where he is currently registered to vote. He's also voted as an undeclared voter off and on in recent elections, according to the Will County clerk's office. His party affiliation is currently undeclared. Zoom out: The pope, who has been recovering from lung cancer surgery , met with Chicago-area advocates Wednesday who are supporting immigrants at an ICE facility in Broadview , Illinois. He's also clashed with President Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who is Catholic, over the war in Iran and the treatment of immigrants in America. Go deeper: Pope Leo XIV discharged from hospital after lung cancer surgery Axios Chicago's Carrie Shepherd contributed.

9f96bcb90801.text: The U.S. naval blockade, sweeping economic sanctions and obstruction of overland export routes have crippled Iran's economy and intensified pressure on the regime, according to a new Treasury Department report obtained by Axios. Why it matters: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who is leading an economic pressure campaign dubbed "Operation Economic Outcast," is one of Trump's closest aides urging him to let the initiative play out rather than rush back into combat. Though the report doesn't argue that the Iranian regime is close to collapsing, it does lay out the Treasury Department's view that its efforts have crippled Iran's economy and limited its ability to generate revenue. Driving the news: As he did before Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025 and Operation Epic Fury in February, Trump is pursuing dual tracks — trying to reach a deal to restart peace talks while also preparing to possibly resume major combat operations after the midterms. The Treasury campaign, which launched in late August, is a third track. But U.S. officials say it needs more time to destabilize the regime and potentially convince the Iranian leadership to make concessions at the negotiations table. On Thursday, Trump met with his top national security and foreign policy aides to discuss the war. U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper, who commands forces in the Middle East, briefed Trump on the ongoing naval blockade . Bessent discussed the economic pressure campaign. "Bessent is telling the President the economic pressure campaign is working and that things are getting worse in Iran and that this could further destabilize the regime and push the Supreme Leader to agree to a deal," a U.S. official said. Zoom in: The Treasury report highlights several indicators of Iran's economic crisis: Currency collapse: The Iranian rial has lost roughly a quarter of its value since the operation began in August. In October, the unofficial exchange rate reached a record low of 2.687 million rials to the dollar. "The currency's decline reflects mounting pressure on Iran's economy and financial system, eroding purchasing power and making it increasingly costly for the regime to access goods and services abroad," the report argues. Soaring inflation: Iran's annual inflation rate reached 90% in September, compared to roughly 35% in early 2025. Oil exports: Iran has not loaded any oil onto tankers since Aug. 25 because of the blockade and sanctions, the report says. Tehran has also sold off its remaining oil stranded at sea, according to Kpler, which tracks maritime trade. Between the lines: The report details how the U.S. is seeking to cut Iran off not only from oil revenue but also from international trade routes, commercial aviation, banking networks and even digital currency alternatives. It states that Iran's effort to reroute trade overland around the U.S. naval blockade is facing major bottlenecks at borders with Pakistan, Turkey, Afghanistan, and Turkmenistan. Thousands of trucks are reportedly stranded at the Turkish border, facing delays of up to 20 days, while hundreds more are waiting at the Pakistani border, the report says. The UAE, Oman, Iraq, Georgia and Azerbaijan have barred Iranian airlines and canceled flights to Iran. Turkey has suspended all Mahan Air flights. Iranian banks have faced additional restrictions in Turkey, Lebanon and the UAE, while Treasury is targeting cryptocurrency exchanges used to evade sanctions.

845be682b087.text: By — Gary Fields, Associated Press Gary Fields, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/2-trump-attempts-to-change-the-d-c-landscape-play-out-in-the-courts-as-midterms-near Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter 2 Trump attempts to change the D.C. landscape play out in the courts as midterms near Politics Oct 30, 2026 2:34 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Hearings in lawsuits against two separate administration-backed projects were unfolding in a single federal court building Friday, revealing the breadth of President Donald Trump's attempts to mold parts of the District of Columbia as he wishes — and the underlying executive authority claims that lie beneath them. The cases involved are an impending shutdown and reconfiguration of a historic public golf course and the construction of the monumental arch that, at 250 feet (75 meters), would be 100 feet taller than the Statue of Liberty is from its base to the top of the torch. The two projects are barely three miles or five kilometers apart. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The hearing on the proposed golf course change began as other recent ones have: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes grilled Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward Jr. over how Trump's desires to turn the golf course, near the National Mall, into a world-class facility have become urgent plans that match his public pronouncements. At one point, Reyes read the code of conduct to government attorneys on presenting erroneous or false information during a hearing. Reyes ordered Friday's hearing after multiple Truth Social posts by Trump indicated that there were plans for the golf course and construction was expected to begin Nov. 15. Trump said the park would be closed 15 months while work goes on. A flurry of Trump posts sets off chaos The presidential posts, which began Oct. 18, created a tense dynamic in multiple court hearings afterward when officials from the Interior Department, Justice and National Park Service could not confirm the existence of the plans under questioning from Reyes. She eventually asked whom she should trust. The Justice Department filed notice Wednesday night that the plans were real. "On Friday, October 30, 2026, the National Park Service will submit to the National Capital Planning Commission for review a rendering designed by Tom Fazio for a World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events," the notice said. Reyes locked in on the filing and Trump's multiple Truth Social announcements as she questioned Woodward. READ MORE: Trump says he will close historic D.C. golf course for 15 months of renovations At one point, as they talked about plans that Woodward said only came about this week, he slipped and included tree cutting as part of the preparation for the closure. Reyes responded immediately: "News flash." She allowed him to correct himself that the tree cutting, which occurred earlier this month, was not part of the plan to close the East Potomac Golf Links. She said she intended to appoint a special master to investigate the administration's statements to the court. Another case is also a referendum on executive authority The golf course lawsuit was one of two cases in court Friday dealing with the Trump administration's push to expand its executive authority as the president remakes the federal areas of the capital near the National Mall and along the Potomac River. Three courtrooms away, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan was to hold a hearing on a motion asking that she call a temporary halt to plans to begin construction as early as Nov. 5 on the memorial arch. The arch is opposed by a small group of veterans and an architectural historian who sued in federal court in Washington, saying Congress must endorse the project. READ MORE: Trump's memorial arch faces a new lawsuit from Arlington County, Virginia "The public interest leans heavily against allowing defendants to blaze ahead," the plaintiffs said in seeking the injunction. "This court should enter a preliminary injunction blocking defendants from beginning construction on Memorial Circle in the hope that they can render the arch a fait accompli before this Court has made a final determination." Legal experts who have been watching the numerous cases underway say that what might appear at first glance to be vanity projects are in truth cases that test the limits of presidential power. Past administrations pursued legal theories that were sometimes legally sound, sometimes not, said David Super, law professor at the Georgetown University Law Center. "But there was always the assumption that you would try to do things that were legal," he said. "What we're seeing here now is that if you think the federal courts can't stop you, you can do things there indisputably illegal. He said that's "going to do long-term damage to the country." e6b7370770fe.text: A Texas grand jury indicted ICE officer Mario Alberto Morales with a charge of second-degree aggravated assault Friday after prosecutors said he deliberately drove his SUV into a fleeing immigrant in early October. Why it matters: This may be the first time an ICE agent has ever been indicted in Texas, making it a rare case of a federal immigration officer facing state charges. What they're saying: Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare announced the grand jury's charge of second-degree aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, namely a motor vehicle. Morales faces two to 20 years if convicted, Teare said. "Just because you have an ICE badge or any badge, if you are in Harris County and you are violating our community members' constitutional rights, there will be repercussions," he said. Catch up quick: Morales struck Miguel Parra Hernandez on Oct. 10 as Parra Hernandez fled on foot. Parra Hernandez, a Mexican national who has lived in Harris County for more than 30 years, had no criminal record and no pending immigration proceedings against him before the incident, Teare said. ICE has said Morales and other agents were looking for a different man identified as a deportation target, but that man's relatives say he died nearly a decade ago. Teare said Parra Hernandez is still rehabilitating from his injuries but is in ICE custody. The other side: An ICE spokesperson called the indictment "nothing more than a political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians" in a statement to Axios. "Federal officers acting in the course of their duties can only be investigated by other Federal agencies. Local governments do not have the authority to run such an investigation." "Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct." Zoom out: Teare said Morales was among the "surge hires" as part of efforts to speed up President Trump's mass deportation agenda. The DA declined to go into detail about the agent's prior work history, but said he could "unequivocally tell you that I've reviewed 1000s of job applications and resumes for law enforcement officers from around the state, and I'm not familiar with a single agency that would have hired this person based on his past." He also said he had "concerns about a number of the individuals that were hired during that surge" based on the investigation, and "concerns about the length of time that they're trained, and about what that training entails." What we're watching: Morales could attempt to move the case to federal court and argue federal law shields him from state prosecution. Teare said he was prepared to litigate such a move. Go deeper: Questions about Lorenzo Salgado Araujo's killing by ICE remain - Axios Houston

807d81990916.text: Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) is endorsing a trio of insurgent Democratic candidates who are challenging his fellow California House Democrats, Axios has learned. Why it matters: This is an aggressive move by a potential 2028 presidential contender who styles himself as one of the few Democrats willing to get into direct confrontations with the party establishment. He has backed members of the progressive "Bloc" who have refused to commit to voting for Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) as speaker. This is territory where even other high-profile House progressives — including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), another potential 2028er — have largely refused to tread. Driving the news: "Today I'm endorsing three new generation leaders Angela Gonzales-Torres, Eric Jones, and Mai Vang," Khanna said in a statement first shared with Axios. Gonzales-Torres, a former local elected official challenging Rep. Jimmy Gomez, "will join us in our fight against corruption, to stand up for survivors, and to lead with a moral vision," Khanna said. Khanna said he has known Jones — a venture capitalist running against Rep. Mike Thompson — "for many years," calling him "a change agent who understands the working class and building a better life for those left out." Vang, a Sacramento City Council member running against Rep. Doris Matsui, "will call out the genocide in Gaza, be for taxing billionaires, and stand for Medicare for All and the working class," Khanna said. Between the lines: Khanna said he has a "tremendous respect and admiration," for Thompson, 75, who has been in office since 1999. "But voters are crying out for change." Khanna said of Matsui, 82, who has held her seat since 2005: "I respect Doris Matsui's incredible service to our state and nation. This is the time to pass the baton." Jones is 35. Vang is 41. Khanna did not reference Gomez, who is under investigation by the House Ethics Committee over allegations of sexual misconduct. Gomez has admitted to "personal mistakes outside my marriage," but said his actions were "consensual" and denied breaking House rules. Asked about potential backlash from his colleagues for endorsing against fellow Democratic incumbents, Khanna said in a brief interview with Axios, "I think we need a new politics in this country, and we need a new party." "I've always been a reformer and independent-minded, that's what I believe," he added. The other side: A spokesperson for Gomez's campaign told Axios, "Instead of some Silicon Valley politician, the people of Los Angeles care a lot more about what Planned Parenthood thinks, what local teachers, nurses, and unions think – and they all support Jimmy Gomez." Said Thomas Dowling, a spokesperson for Thompson: "San Francisco venture capitalist Eric Jones and his Silicon Valley supporters are trying to buy our congressional seat, but it's not for sale. Mike's support comes from the people who actually live here." Matsui's campaign manager Bill Wong told Axios: "Voters in our district care about real results. Doris Matsui delivers. That's why the local teachers, firefighters, nurses, and women's and environmental organizations who see those results up close are standing with her." The intrigue: Khanna previously endorsed Thompson this cycle, which the latter congressman touted on social media as recently as May. The Thompson campaign even sent out a text to supporters, the content of which was shared with Axios, that reads: "This is Ro Khanna. I endorsed Mike Thompson for CA-4." Asked about the apparent discrepancy, Khanna told Axios: "I wanted to endorse [Gonzales]-Torres and then Mai Vang ... and I just thought, 'it's time for new blood,' and wanted to endorse Eric Jones." "I think very highly of Mike. I had, with the delegation, endorsed him earlier, so it's nothing against him. I just think it's a new generation and we're seeing bolder progressives win across the country," he added. Catch up quick: Matsui, Thompson and Gomez are each locked in Democrat vs. Democrat general elections with their rivals. All candidates ran in a single jungle primary in June, with the top two finishers — regardless of party — moving to the Nov. 3 general election. That means, unlike the rest of their colleagues who faced primary challenges, the trio will have to wait a little longer to find out if they will be returning to Capitol Hill next January. State of play: Jones and Gonzales-Torres both finished second in their respective primaries, while Vang narrowly came out ahead of Matsui. Polls have shown Jones leading Thompson and Gonzales-Torres essentially tied with Gomez. A senior House Democrat, speaking on the condition of anonymity to offer candid thoughts on Matsui's reelection, said party leaders "think she is gone" next Congress.

eaeaf25f6a65.text: By — Matthew Lee, Associated Press Matthew Lee, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-rubio-welcomes-g20-foreign-ministers-to-atlanta-at-critical-moment Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Rubio welcomes G20 foreign ministers to Atlanta at 'critical moment' Politics Oct 30, 2026 2:10 PM EDT ATLANTA (AP) — The top diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies opened two days of meetings in Atlanta on Friday after European objections to Russia's participation forced the U.S. to cancel a photo of the foreign ministers, underscoring deep rifts among the group over global crises. Secretary of State Marco Rubio pulled the plug on the traditional group photo after several European officials threatened to boycott or walk out of the snapshot that usually helps kick off such diplomatic gatherings. But he still opened the talks, which otherwise went ahead as planned, with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "We are in a critical moment — I would call it a moment of choosing, and I would say not just for my country, the United States of America, but frankly, for the world," Rubio told his colleagues. "We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises," he added, pointing to disruptions to global energy and food supplies, trade and freedom of navigation. Many are posing "severe threats to essential foundations of the global economic order." Yet there was no sign that the G20 diplomats could come to consensus on many of the most contentious issues they face. Among them are the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, U.S. tariffs and Chinese machinations in the South China Sea. All have contributed to spikes in the global cost of fuel as well as uncertainty about trade. Russia's presence at G20 gathering roils European allies Concerns about any prospects for the talks escalated when the Europeans balked at being photographed with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. Rubio decided to scrap the picture because he thought the controversy would be a distraction, according to two U.S. officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter. Some G20 countries had already expressed concern that the U.S. invited Russia during its heightened attacks on Ukraine, especially after Trump pushed ties with Ukraine to new lows by waiving fresh sanctions on Moscow and temporarily limiting logistical and intelligence assistance. The British foreign office said in a statement that the United Kingdom "has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that." Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski said the cancellation of the group photo was "the right decision" by the U.S., telling media in Atlanta that "I am not the only one who does not want to be photographed with Lavrov." READ MORE: Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes after call with Rubio German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said "there is no normality with Russia" but "we must exchange the controversies at the table here," the German news agency dpa reported. He added that "we also must not send falsely optimistic signals." Lavrov has traveled only infrequently to NATO member states since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and resulting severe sanctions were imposed on Moscow. His presence in Atlanta could cause domestic political problems for Trump just days before the U.S. congressional midterm elections as well as roil the G20, according to Ian Kelly, a U.S. ambassador to Georgia during Trump's first term. "It seems politically boneheaded to invite him," said Kelly, who now teaches international relations and diplomacy at Northwestern University outside Chicago. The meeting in Atlanta is meant to set the stage for a G20 leaders' summit hosted by President Donald Trump at his Miami golf club in December. It is unclear if Russian President Vladimir Putin will accept Trump's invitation to that gathering. G20 member South Africa was not invited Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous such meetings, was not invited this year as U.S. officials said they made a conscious choice to include only formal members of the group. But missing from the invite list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top U.S. officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted. READ MORE: Rubio says U.S. pressure on NATO allies to boost defense spending is 'not hostile' "We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary," said Phindile Kunene, spokesperson for South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola. Kunene welcomed support from other G20 members that had expressed reservations about the exclusion and said South Africa was ready to participate "on an equal footing with other members" when Britain takes over the presidency next year. The Iran war hangs over the G20 event The U.S. has said a top priority for the meeting is resolving differences over issues related to freedom of navigation, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the South China Sea. The topic will include discussions on Iran, Russia-Ukraine and China and its smaller neighbors. But hanging over the meeting is the prospect of new U.S. military intervention in Iran, which has put the region, including G20 member Saudi Arabia, on edge. The Associated Pr

136f386e40d0.text: By — Anna Wilder, Associated Press/Report For America Anna Wilder, Associated Press/Report For America By — Lekan Oyekanmi, Associated Press Lekan Oyekanmi, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/an-ice-officer-has-been-charged-after-striking-a-man-with-a-car-in-houston Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter An ICE officer is charged with assault for striking a man with a car in Houston Nation Updated on Oct 30, 2026 2:41 PM EDT — Published on Oct 30, 2026 1:53 PM EDT HOUSTON (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer accused of intentionally ramming his car into a Mexican construction worker in Houston was indicted by a grand jury Friday on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, prosecutors said. The officer, Mario Alberto Morales, was driving an unmarked SUV on Oct. 10 when he struck and ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez, 48, who was running away during a pursuit through a parking lot, the Harris County District Attorney's Office said. Parra Hernandez broke his leg and remains in federal custody at a rehabilitation facility, District Attorney Sean Teare said. READ MORE: ICE officer appeared to intentionally hit a man with a vehicle in Houston, Texas prosecutor says ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of the vehicle, an account that Teare said is contradicted by video. "The evidence we have in this case is as clear as any that I've ever prosecuted or investigated," Teare said. Morales, 33, of Brownsville, Texas, is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, although other encounters have come under investigation, including a fatal shooting by an ICE officer this summer in Houston. Morales' attorney, David Lindenmuth, said his client didn't commit a crime and he accused Teare of indicting Morales "for political gain." Morales had worked as an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little more than a year, Lindenmuth said. "Mr. Morales is truly a good man, a former member of our military, that has given his entire life to public service either for his country or in or adjacent to law enforcement," Lindenmuth told The Associated Press. "To have him charged for what was so clearly just an accident — the DA's office, the DA himself, has invented a crime out of thin air." WATCH: ICE shooting of man in New York with child in his car sparks outrage Teare hinted at concerns over Morales' background but would not provide details. Morales, who is charged with a second-degree felony, was not in custody Friday and a warrant will be issued for his arrest, according to Teare. ICE asserted that local officials do not have the authority to investigate federal officers acting in the course of their duties. "Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE," the agency said in a statement. The district attorney played Morales' body camera footage Teare has said video clearly contradicts the ICE account. Surveillance video shows a Jeep Cherokee speed over a median and drive toward Parra Hernandez as he runs away. During a news conference Friday, he played Morales' body camera footage, which shows him driving and talking about pursuing someone. The video shows Morales making a few sharp moves with the steering wheel before the SUV shakes. Morales stops the vehicle, then gets out and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is several feet away. The video then shows Parra Hernandez on the ground and grabbing his leg, yelling in pain. Morales is heard saying, "He got hit with a car, bro." It is not clear to whom he is talking. "I was coming in and I hit him with the car," Morales says. Family says ICE was looking for a dead person during operation Parra Hernandez has lived in Harris County for more than 30 years and did not have a deportation order or criminal background, according to Teare. Other aspects of ICE's account have also been called into question. READ MORE: New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops, memo shows After Parra Hernandez was taken into custody, ICE released a photo of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, and said he was the target of the operation that day. ICE said he was seen entering a vehicle with Parra Hernandez. Family members of Parra Hernandez said they had never heard of him. FIEL, an immigrant rights group in Houston that has been working with the family, said Mendoza-Cervantes' daughter told them her father has been dead since 2017. Teare's office has previously said its investigation has not found that Parra Hernandez and the man ICE identified as Mendoza-Cervantes were in a vehicle together, contrary to ICE's statement. ICE has not responded to claims that the suspect they were looking for has been dead for years. Fatal summer Houston shooting also under investigation Teare has said the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, has not cooperated with his investigators and accused ICE of destroying evidence "either intentionally or through gross negligence." He has said Morales left the scene before the vehicle could be impounded. In July, Teare said DHS also ignored his requests for information after an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in his van. DHS has said Salgado Araujo had "weaponized his vehicle" before the shooting and that an officer fired in self-defense. Other passengers in the van have disputed that account. Wilder reported from Austin, Texas. Wilder is a corps member for The Associated Press/Report for America Statehouse News Initiative. Report for America is a nonprofit national service program that places journalists in local newsrooms to report on undercovered issues. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. This story was originally published by Civil Beat.
The Maui Department of the Prosecuting Attorney is expected to soon have an investigator working full-time on contractor fraud cases targeting survivors of the deadly 2023 Lahaina wildfire, county officials say.
Mayor Richard Bissen asked Maui County Council Chair Alice Lee to introduce legislation to authorize the new hire after the department experienced a rise in the number of reports related to post-disaster contractor fraud. Last week, the council unanimously voted to advance the bill, with final passage expected on Nov. 13.
“This was an underreported crime at one time, where people may have felt embarrassed or didn’t know who to go to, or didn’t want to say what happened to them,” Bissen told Civil Beat Wednesday. “But I think since more people have come forward, others feel comfortable coming forward, especially if it’s the same individual whose name is brought up.”
The mayor’s request came in the weeks after Civil Beat and Inside Climate News co-published a joint investigation revealing that even though dozens of wildfire survivors have reported serious problems with the contractors they hired to rebuild their homes, government officials had not announced any actions against contractors for post-wildfire misconduct.
Contractors stopped showing up, were unable to account for large sums of money paid to them or performed work so poorly it had to be redone. Civil Beat and Inside Climate News reviewed hundreds of pages of public and private records, including police reports, court filings, contracts and text messages exchanged between contractors and property owners. Many community members said they believe contractor fraud and misconduct in the Lahaina burn zone is a far bigger problem than documented in official reports.
Maui prosecutor Andrew Martin told Civil Beat that he believed the story was among the factors that helped people feel more comfortable speaking to officials about their negative experiences with contractors.
“I think it’s all helpful,” he said, adding that the increase in reports also followed a Lahaina community meeting during which he and other county officials gave a presentation on post-disaster contractor fraud. “There is this segment of the population that, for a variety of different reasons, are not comfortable coming forward, and the more we get it out there, I think it puts people in a position to say, ‘OK, someone out there is going to listen.’”
The investigative services division of the prosecutor’s office currently employs six investigators. The legislation would amend the Fiscal Year 2027 budget to let the department hire a seventh. This would allow Martin to assign one of his office’s investigators to work full-time on active contractor fraud investigations, he told council members last week.
“These cases — because of the need to be able to distinguish between whether or not this is a civil complaint or a criminal complaint — are complex and involved,” Martin said at the meeting Friday. “I need to be able to assign an investigator to this full time.”
Martin has said his office had a deputy prosecutor and an investigator dedicating most of their time to reports of contractor fraud targeting wildfire survivors. He said this week that a recently hired deputy prosecutor — a former assistant U.S. attorney with complex white-collar experience — will also be assigned to the project full-time when they begin work on Nov. 6.
“When I talked to my team about what their needs are right now, they indicated they needed another investigator,” Martin told Civil Beat Wednesday. “That’s just where we’re at in terms of the current workload.”
There would be no immediate cost associated with adding the additional salaried staff position, according to an Oct. 15 letter to the council from Maui Budget Director Lesley Milner. Martin said during Friday’s council meeting that the new investigator would be funded through cost savings.
The need for another investigator “arises from the unforeseen scope and complexity of investigating potential contractor fraud related to the 2023 Maui wildfires,” Milner said in the letter. “As the investigations progressed, the department identified significant workload demands involving the review of financial records and contractual documentation, interviews with witnesses and victims, and preparation of cases for potential prosecution.”
The prosecutor’s office began referring tips related to contractor fraud to the Maui Police Department in May 2025, and the prosecutor’s office eventually opened its own investigation in an effort to more quickly move cases forward, according to Martin.
“We’re now moving on to a second one,” he told council members last week. “These investigations are incredibly time-consuming. The number of financial records that we are gathering through search warrants and subpoenas … are voluminous.”
Martin added that the new hire would also be in support of his efforts to improve his office’s ability to investigate other white-collar crimes, including elder abuse — “one of the fastest-growing areas of fraud-related, financial-related crimes in the country,” he said. “We’re going to need to be able to address that in a meaningful way and do it quickly.”
Bissen was glad to see council members unanimously support adding another investigator to Martin’s staff, he said.
“I really do think it’s prioritizing the needs of the folks who are already struggling and going through a difficult time,” Bissen said. “The question for us is: How do we help recoup people’s money? How do we hold people accountable? How do we stop them from doing this to others? Those are all the goals behind this bill, and I’m grateful that the council took it up.”
Council member Tamara Paltin, who represents Lahaina, said she personally knew fire survivors who had lost hundreds of thousands of dollars to the contractors they hired to rebuild their homes after the fire.

Tech stocks tumbled for the second day in a row as concerns rise over the hundreds of billions of dollars firms are investing in artificial intelligence (AI).
Shares in Intel plummeted by as much as 30% on Friday, following Google owner Alphabet's stock price plunging by more than $500bn (Â£374bn) in the previous day's trading.
Other tech stocks including Reddit and Amazon also fell, while the Nasdaq index of the largest tech firms listed in the US, sank more than 3.5%.
While tech firms are spending big on AI, their earnings are not always meeting analysts' expectations, spooking investors and creating fears of an AI bubble.
Major tech companies have ramped up artificial intelligence spending, with Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon, and Microsoft committing to spending $800.6bn between them in 2026.
Alphabet's stock market value plunged on Thursday after it revealed the AI summaries it now provides as the top answer to search queries were affecting its core search advertising revenue.
At the same time, Alphabet expects to spend up to $205bn this year on investments, almost entirely related to AI.
Alphabet stock continued to fall in early trading, down 2.2% after Thursday's slide of more than 12%.
The bigger losses on Friday were elsewhere, with Intel on track to lose more than $130bn in value as its shares continued to fall in Friday trading.
The chip maker said it planned to increase spending on AI despite weaker demand for computers, a major source of demand for its micro-processors.
On Thursday, Intel's finance chief David Zinsner said the firm did not expect to bring in more cash than it spent this year and forecast lower-than-expected revenue for its fourth quarter.
"Looking ahead, we see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," he said in the chip maker's third quarter earnings report.
In the earnings call, he said the firm had significantly ramped up investment in equipment in the third quarter and expected that to be "even more significant" in the following three months.
Amazon and Reddit down
Amazon shares fell as far as 6% in overnight trading after the company's reported earnings fell short of investors' expectations.
Amazon on Thursday revealed it had also spent more cash than it was making, and that spending had increased six-fold over the span of three months.
The company has committed to spending $220bn this year, putting the money towards investments such as AI data centres, network equipment, and servers.
Shares recovered slightly from the overnight fall but were still down about 1.6% in Friday trading.
Reddit stock was down by 26%, after the social media platform revealed weaker-than-expected daily user figures and warned that Google's growing AI-driven search was hurting referral traffic.
Stock in online game platform Roblox also fell, down by nearly 20%, as its daily active user numbers dropped.
Several major tech firms have reported earnings this week, including Microsoft, and analysts said there were questions about the payout from the huge investments in AI.
Chris Low, from investment management firm FHN Financial, said the bulk of what was happening in the stock market was in reaction to some of the biggest tech players such as Amazon and Google.
He told Reuters the companies were "showing some pretty significant growing pains as they aggressively pursue the AI build-out".
"The thinking is that these signs suggest that the entire sector is going to slow down."
'Investors have turned ruthless'
Many analysts have been debating the possibility of an AI bubble in the stock market.
The worry is that some tech firms will not be able to justify their sky-high valuations because the cost of building AI data centres and developing the software will end up being greater than the money they can make from it.
Kathleen Brookes, research director at trading firm XTB, said there have been many ups and downs in AI trade in recent months.
"Investors have turned ruthless, punishing any signs of disappointment in [third quarter] earnings," she said.
"The AI trade has had a good run in recent years, but now investors want payback, and companies like Alphabet and Intel are in the crosshairs."
However, stock market values for many of these companies remain well above where they were a year ago.
While the Nasdaq is down 3.5% in Friday trading, it is up 7.6% over the last year. Similarly Amazon is up nearly 7% over the past 12 months, while Alphabet is down 1.6%.
Brookes noted that November is typically a strong month for stocks.
"If we see AI stocks continue to struggle in the coming days, it could suggest the AI trade is past its peak, and investors will be looking for a new theme to drive markets," she said.

e3c018871337.text: By — Joshua Barajas Joshua Barajas By — Bryan Gallion Bryan Gallion Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-election-night-2026-pbs-news-special-coverage Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Election night 2026 PBS News special coverage Politics Oct 30, 2026 1:42 PM EDT President Donald Trump might not be on the ballot, but this year's midterm elections will set the stage for the final years of his presidency. PBS News' live special coverage of the 2026 midterms will begin at 6 p.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 3. Watch in the player above. Democrats have been gaining ground with voters on issues such as affordability and the Iran War as Americans weigh how Trump-led policies are affecting their daily lives. In the final PBS News/NPR/Marist poll before Election Day, Democrats hold an 8-point lead among likely voters in the fight for control of Congress. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Despite his own approval ratings at historic lows, Trump has been criss-crossing the nation from Kansas to New York to far-flung Alaska to help give a last-minute boost to his party's candidates. The president has been targeting key races in many states long considered Republican mainstays in the hopes his party can maintain its grip on both chambers of Congress. Meanwhile, elections and state officials are bracing for possible meddling from the Trump administration as the Justice Department prepares to deploy 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states on Election Day. Trump, who has continued to push the lie that the 2020 election was rigged and repeatedly railed against early voting, cast his vote in person in West Palm Beach, Florida, more than a week before Nov. 3. Around 1,000 vote-entry clerks will answer calls from those AP workers to enter candidates' vote totals into the news agency's election night reporting system. That data is then matched to election returns posted on county and state websites or delivered by electronic feeds to ensure accuracy. 4ba4e2846733.text: By — Kim Chandler, Associated Press Kim Chandler, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/christa-pike-says-she-feels-constant-pain-in-first-public-statement-since-failed-execution Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Christa Pike says she feels constant pain in first public statement since failed execution Nation Oct 30, 2026 1:40 PM EDT Christa Pike said Friday that she remains in constant pain and struggles to speak a month after surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee, a failure she blames on "incompetence." In her first public statement since the execution, Pike said she never contemplated a life beyond her execution date and was prepared to die in peace, but woke up alone and confused in a hospital bed. "There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul," Pike said. READ MORE: IV team warned Christa Pike's vein might have 'blown' during failed execution, court filing says Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 stabbing death of 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed Slemmer, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death. "I'm deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position," she said. "I continue to think about my victim's family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured." Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has called for an investigation into what happened during the failed execution and postponed the state's other lethal injection scheduled this year. The state's prison chief resigned. Pike said she's thankful for the medical workers who saved her life and the people who showed her kindness. "I don't know why I survived that night. I don't know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone," she said. WATCH: Botched execution reignites debate surrounding death penalty The failed lethal injection left her arms burned and blistered, according to her lawyers. For the first few days of her hospitalization, Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator. Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on the possibility that a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue rather than entering her bloodstream. Pike's attorneys have urged the governor to reduce her sentence to life imprisonment. Lee told reporters this week that, "I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts." Friday's statement was dictated to Pike's legal team from the infirmary at the prison where she is housed. Pike was hospitalized in the immediate aftermath of the failed execution and then moved back to prison at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center. The outer solar system is yielding its secrets to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.
Less than five months into the observatory’s decade-long survey of the sky, a potential new dwarf planet has already popped up in its data, astronomers reported this week at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division of Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.
Another team reported a handful of new Neptune Trojans, icy objects that share an orbit with Neptune, at the meeting and in the Astrophysical Journal Letters. The findings are filling in astronomers’ picture of the Kuiper Belt at the solar system’s frigid fringes.
“It feels a little bit like we’re replicating the 1800s and early 1900s, discovering what the solar system even looks like in general,” says Sam Deen, an amateur astronomer based in Simi Valley, Calif. “We’re finding out what there even is in the first place that makes up most of the Kuiper Belt.”
A possible dwarf planet hid in historical data
Perched on a mountaintop in Chile, the Vera Rubin Observatory is on a mission to map the entire southern sky every couple of nights, searching for faint and fast-moving cosmic objects. The observatory took its first images in June 2025 and officially began a decade-long survey in June 2026.
Even before the official survey started, Rubin had detected the motion of an object orbiting billions of kilometers beyond Pluto. Rubin observed the object 30 times on 20 nights from March 4 to July 11. But no one knew it was there until October 13, when astrophysicist Matt Holman of the Smithsonian Astronomical Observatory in Cambridge, Mass., ran a search for moving dots of light in the data.
The object, called 2026 ED138, appeared to be about 47 times as far from Earth as Earth is from the sun. Its brightness suggests it’s between 600 and 1,500 kilometers wide, potentially as large as other dwarf planets like Ceres and Makemake. That’s probably big enough to be spherical, making it a dwarf planet.
“It’s really big. It’s damn huge,” Deen says. “No matter what you call it, it’s still the biggest thing we’ve found in the entire solar system in 19 years.”
When Holman realized what he had found, he was thrilled but doubtful. “It’s quite an exciting thing,” Holman said in a news briefing at the meeting on October 27. “But one of the things that you need to do when you discover something potentially of this size is to try to verify that it’s true.”
Holman and colleagues were able to find observations of the same object in archived data from the Dark Energy Camera, located on an adjacent mountaintop in Chile, taken in 2016.
Deen was able to trace it back even farther, to photographic plates taken as part of a sky survey at Palomar Observatory in California in 1954. Other amateur astronomers independently found the same sightings.
“They took an image from Palomar in 1954, and another about half an hour after the first one, that both by pure chance happen to point at where ED138 is,” Deen says. “And it’s really obvious. If you know it’s supposed to be there, it’s not particularly faint.”
So why didn’t anybody notice it until now? It’s partly because ED138 practically crawls across the sky, orbiting the sun once every 280 years. It was also moving against a dense background of Milky Way stars, where it blended in.
By combining observations spanning decades, astronomers can calculate the object’s orbit with more precision.
Deen is hoping to observe the potential new dwarf planet pass in front of a distant star on Halloween. That sort of observation, called an occultation, can help reveal more details of the putative dwarf planet’s size and shape, and even whether it has moons or rings. Usually, it takes years to understand an object’s orbit well enough to predict an occultation, Deen says. “Getting to do it immediately is like being a kid in a candy shop, really.”
Icy objects could offer clues to solar system beginnings
A crop of newly spotted Neptune Trojans were masked by the Milky Way, too. These asteroids gather in the same orbit as Neptune, but offset from the planet at 60 degrees. Astronomers think they were some of the original building blocks of the solar system and contain an ancient record of planetary formation and evolution.
Other planets have Trojans, too. Jupiter has thousands. Astronomers think Neptune has many more, but so far they have seen only 30 in the cluster of space objects that orbit ahead of Neptune, and just two in the cluster behind it.
“We would expect these [groups of Trojans] to be symmetric in numbers, so you have to get more than two,” planetary scientist Meg Schwamb said in a news conference at the meeting on October 28.
The trailing cloud happened to have been moving in front of the Milky Way from the perspective of Earth for the last 15 years. Spotting individual Trojans against that crowded background was “like finding a needle in a sequined dress,” said Schwamb, of Queens University Belfast in Northern Ireland.
Schwamb and colleagues examined Vera Rubin data taken from the commissioning phase — the period when engineers were testing the telescope. In this early data haul, the team found two more trailing Trojans, plus one candidate. They seem to be similar in composition to the leading ones, which matches theories of how the solar system formed.
“It just kind of got lucky,” Schwamb said. “These objects photobombed the commissioning survey.”
“This is really the appetizer for what Rubin Observatory is going to do in its mission for the next ten years,” she added. “There’s hundreds more of these objects likely to be found.”
Some of the excitement about these discoveries is dampened by fears of losing observations to bright satellites crisscrossing the telescope’s field of view, says astronomer Sam Lawler of the University of Regina in Canada.
“I have to put in the constant downer of how the increasing numbers of satellites will make these discoveries harder,” Lawler says. “There are one hundred new satellites launching every week,

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist.
The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider.
Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (Â£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit.
The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds.
America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.
While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.
The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle â cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar.
Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".
It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected".
Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person. Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."
Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate".
Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach.
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody.
A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.
The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.
But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.
Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them.
Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".
Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.
Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack.
In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers.
In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor. The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.
North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.
North Korea has always denied this, but the wealth of evidence from cryptocurrency flow analysis and insider interviews from defectors is compelling.
It makes North Korea likely to be the only nation that uses hacking as a way to raise public funds.

Reedâs view
In August, I wrote about the use of AI in guest columns published in major news outlets, including by Dartmouth Provost Santiago Schnell. This week, he resigned.
The thing is, he shouldnât have lost his job.
Schnellâs was one of 50 guest columns that included AI-generated text that were published in The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and the Washington Post over a one-month period. An (AI-assisted) analysis showed that AI use in writing has become incredibly common, even in publications that prohibit it.
My hope was that the reporting would lead to some smart questions, not a shame-and-blame witch hunt that would result in a resignation: Does it make sense to have a blanket ban on something that has become so prevalent and can fool some of the worldâs most renowned editors? Will that even be technically possible in the future?
If the Dartmouth provost did anything wrong, it was failing to disclose that he used AI in the process of writing columns and academic journal articles for publications that prohibit its use. But it appears all of Schnellâs writing was based on his own ideas and work. He didnât just prompt a chatbot and pass the output off as his own.
âI develop ideas and arguments, conduct the research, evaluate the evidence and sources, determine the structure, prepare drafts and decide what appears in the final text,â Schnell told The Dartmouth newspaper, which did its own investigation into more of Schnellâs work.
I get why students are mad, and why Schnellâs resignation might seem appropriate. Students are often prohibited from using AI in class and subject to punishment if theyâre caught.
But forced resignations just perpetuate the current situation, where we are fighting against a current of technology use thatâs become so commonplace itâs impossible to fight. Years from now, weâll look back on this time with regret and wonder why we were so outraged by people using a new tool that was so obviously useful.
Room for Disagreement
âIf true, Provost Schnellâs use of AI in academic publications is arguably a graver violation,â Eli Moyse, a columnist for Dartmouthâs student newspaper, wrote in an op-ed.
âHe repeatedly outsourced his intellectual labor and then tried to pass off work that wasnât his under his name. Even if it wasnât human work, passing work that is not your own off under your name still constitutes clear plagiarism â probably the very worst academic violation a faculty member can commit.â

European diplomats have refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in the US, leading to the American hosts cancelling the planned picture.
Two officials confirmed to the BBC the cancellation of the so-called family photo scheduled for Friday morning, which would usually include representatives from all the nations in attendance.
The meeting, which gathers top diplomats from the world's biggest economies, is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Ukraine is not not a G20 member but has been invited to similar meetings in recent years. However, Ukraine was not invited to this meeting.
Relations between Ukraine and the US have been particularly tense this month, with a diplomatic standoff between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over Kyiv's strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is present and a diplomatic source confirmed the UK was among the countries which refused to participate in the picture.
One British official said: "The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that".
A US official said the photo was cancelled "after it became clear some of the delegations were unwilling to participate in a joint photo".
"Rather than allow a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction, the US decided to forgo the photo and keep the focus on the substantive discussions," the official said.
In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market.
The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of mid-term elections at the start of November, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".
Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory.
Moscow has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

Scott Ward can still recall the relief he saw on parents' faces when a search and rescue dog he was working with found their children safe in Canada's vast and heavily wooded Banff National Park.
Another time, his canine partner led him hiking up a steep mountainside for two hours until they reached a man with a broken leg who was close to dying from hypothermia.
Now 73 and retired, Ward spent 17 years as a dog handler in the wilderness of the Canadian Rocky Mountains, work he described as gratifying.
Over the years, the rescue programme was cut back to just one person in the role, and Ward was shocked when he heard recently that Parks Canada will end the programme entirely as of this month.
Prime Minister Mark Carney's government is making broad funding cuts to Canada's public service, and Parks Canada announced last week that hundreds of their employees will soon be laid off.
The agency confirmed the news to the BBC, calling it a "difficult decision" to axe its sole dog handler position out of Banff National Park, one of the most rugged parts of Canada that welcomes more than four million visitors each year from around the world.
It added it is part of its efforts to modernise its law enforcement branch, and that "search and rescue operations will continue to be delivered" through other means.
Cutting this one role has stirred public outrage, with more than 5,000 people signing a petition since Tuesday to restore it.
William Stevenson, the Conservative Member of Parliament for the Banff area who started the petition, says he welcomes tighter government spending, but that this cut could harm public safety.
"How could they possibly make such a bad choice in where to cut?" he told the BBC.
The BBC has asked Parks Canada about how much the canine search and rescue programme cost to administer.
For 55 years, the government used rescue dogs in the Canadian Rocky Mountains who were trained to trace "everything", Ward said, from a small paper clip to shell casings to a human body.
After avalanches, a common winter hazard in the area, they were called upon to search for trapped hikers or skiers underneath heavy mounds of snow.
"It saves probers hours and hours of standing shoulder to shoulder and poking in the snow, and also exposing themselves to secondary avalanche hazards," Ward said.
In the summer, they helped find children who got lost, often after wandering away from their parents' campsites.
"We lost a huge public safety and staff safety resource," he said.
Other countries still rely on canines, often called "avalanche dogs", for mountain search and rescue, including Italy, external.
The last dog in Parks Canada's programme, a German Shephard named Leroy, was retired in August.
For the seven years that he was on the job, Leroy helped track 156 people, find 57 who were lost in the wilderness, and solve two murders in Banff.
A new canine was trained and ready for duty before Parks Canada gave notice last week that the programme would be eliminated as part of recent C$145m ($104m; Â£78m) budget cuts to Parks Canada, local newspaper Rocky Mountain Outlook reported.
Along with his petition, Stevenson also raised the issue in Canada's parliament during a late sitting on Thursday.
In response, Ryan Turnball, a Liberal MP and the parliamentary secretary for finance, said the government is focused on reducing Canada's deficit and "ensuring public funds support growth, resilience and the well-being of Canadians".
Stevenson said he will continue to push on the issue, and has asked for a sit-down meeting with Parks Canada's CEO.
As for Ward, he hopes that the programme will soon be restored.
He recalled a quote that was often uttered by an old park warden who trained him: "You can make an armpit smell like a lilac bush and you can put a man on the moon, but nothing can replace the nose of the avalanche dog."

011ce0dac3d9.text:
Exhumed
Aaron Mahnke
Running Press, $30.00
October is my favorite month. I love when the leaves change colors and the air gets brisk. My hunger for media that sends a shiver down my spine is at an all-time high. This spooky season, I found satiation in Exhumed, a new book by historian Aaron Mahnke.
Mahnke draws on rich science-based history and folklore to show how fear of the unknown has shaped culture throughout history, even into the present day. He cites Taylor Swift, Twilight and other pop culture phenomena in his analysis — a choice that injects fresh air into the otherwise miasmic atmosphere. And thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down.
Exhumed kicks off with the true story of America’s first “vampire.”
Walk with me for a moment back in time to Exeter, Rhode Island in 1892. Rampant tuberculosis is killing scores of people, including three members of the Brown family: matriarch Mary and her daughters, Mary O. and Mercy L. Then a son, Edwin, falls ill with the same symptoms — sparking concern that one of the women is an undead vampire who is sucking his life away. The town exhumes the bodies.
Mercy is surprisingly well-preserved. Her hair and nails appear longer and blood dribbles from her skin when it is pierced, “evidence” that confirms everyone’s worst fear: Mercy is indeed a vampire. (Nevermind that she perished in the dead of winter, when temperatures were probably cold enough to substantially slow decomposition.) The town burns Mercy’s heart, though it doesn’t save poor Edwin. These events helped inspire Bram Stoker’s Dracula, which was published five years later.
Interestingly, the cause of tuberculosis — a bacterium — was discovered a full decade before Mercy’s story unfolded. But news doesn’t always travel fast and entrenched beliefs can be difficult to change, even in the face of hard evidence. Exhumed explores this idea far beyond Mercy’s tragic tale.
Fear has led people to do some extremely odd things by today’s standards: burning hearts to kill “vampires,” setting boobie-traps in graves to prevent the dead from rising or drinking the blood of freshly hanged men to “cure” epilepsy. Without modern science to explain the unexplained, people often filled in the blanks with stories, Mahnke explains.
He implores readers to withhold judgement. After all, storytelling is one of the main ways that humans make sense of the world. “All of us, both then and now, are simply making the best of what we have, trying to find a way to improve our lives,” Mahnke writes.
Perhaps this practice continues today in different shades.
At one point, eating mummies, or “mumia,” was considered cure-all for most ailments —headaches, stomach troubles and general sickness. Is it too far from the expectations some people have of buying a “health shot” from Whole Foods? Not really!
More than a century after Mercy Brown’s heart was incinerated, we’re still clinging to stories and rituals that offer us a sense of control over the thing we fear most: death. Exhumed makes it clear that we haven’t outrun this instinct, we’ve just given it different packaging.
Macabre Trivia
If you are the type of person who has 50 tabs open at any given moment, then you will appreciate Exhumed’s myriad quirky facts. Here are three of my favorites:
- Leonardo da Vinci was a fan of corpse medicine, the practice of reusing body parts from dead people for medicinal purposes. Like many of his peers, da Vinci believed the human body contained “vital spirits.” When someone died, there’d be leftover spirits for the living to make use of.
- In 17th century Europe, the tomato was known as the “poison apple.” Many people became sick after eating tomatoes and some even died. For two centuries, society wrongly blamed the fruit. The real killer turned out to be lead leached out of pewter dishes by tomatoes’ acidic juice.
- The spinning red, white and blue poles on barbershops were born out of the business’ former specialty, bloodletting. Red stripes stand for blood, blue for veins and white for the rags used for clean-up. The ball on top is said to represent the bowl that captured the blood. And the pole itself represents the wand patients squeezed during the procedure. Feeling sick in 1705? Head to the local barber with the spinning pole outside.
