8f278f779948.text: By — Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Nicole Winfield, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/leo-xiv-has-become-the-first-pope-in-history-to-vote-in-a-u-s-general-election Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Leo XIV has become the first pope in history to vote in a U.S. general election Politics Oct 30, 2026 12:53 PM EDT VATICAN CITY (AP) — Leo XIV has become the first pope to vote in a U.S. general election, casting a mail-in ballot in a contest that will decide America's future as the Trump era slowly comes to an end. The Vatican confirmed Friday that the Chicago-born pontiff had submitted a mail-in ballot in Chicago ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, citing his long-standing belief in civic participation. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen" and has done so "whenever he was eligible to do so," the Holy See press office said. The statement said he had also voted while living in Peru whenever he was eligible. Leo lived in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop for over 20 years. "The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," it added. Leo holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship, and is also the head of state of a foreign country, the Holy See. The city-state is an absolute monarchy with no political elections. WATCH: 'American Pope' traces Leo's journey from Chicago to the Vatican U.S. federal law allows citizens living abroad, even those working for foreign governments, to vote via absentee ballot. Americans working for foreign governments aren't automatically at risk of forfeiting their U.S. citizenship, though the U.S. State Department says on its website that it may "actively review" the citizenship status of Americans who "serve as a foreign head of state, foreign head of government, or foreign minister." This election, Illinois voters are deciding whether to elect Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker to his third term, and they're also filling an open U.S. Senate seat after longtime Catholic Democrat Dick Durbin's retirement. There are no statewide ballot issues on the Illinois ballot. President Donald Trump is not on the ballot but he has campaigned hard to try to preserve Republican control of the U.S. House and Senate for the final two years of his second term. Leo's vote was first reported by the Chicago Sun-Times, which quoted the chief of staff at the Will County clerk's office as saying the pope, registered at a New Lenox address, requested a mail-in ballot on Oct. 3. The request was made just 10 days before Leo underwent surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. Leo has been slowly resuming his activities at the Vatican after being released from the hospital Oct. 17. It is unclear how Leo returned the ballot. The pope's older brother, John Prevost, was in Rome this week accompanying parishioners from St. Jude's, an Augustinian-run parish in New Lenox, Illinois. The elder Prevost attends Mass there, and Leo gave a talk at the parish in 2024 while still a cardinal. Prevost's past votes have gone Democratic and Republican Since 2000, Robert Prevost has voted in five primary elections, requesting Democratic ballots twice and Republican ballots three times, according to records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections. The records do not show which candidates he supported. Illinois voters must declare a party preference to receive a primary ballot. No such declaration is required in general elections. READ MORE: Cardinal Prevost elected next pope, first American pontiff While registered in heavily Democratic Cook County, Prevost requested Democratic primary ballots in 2008 and 2010. After moving to the more conservative suburban Will County, he requested Republican primary ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016. The records also show that he submitted ballots in every general election since 2000 except those in 2020 and 2022. Clashes with Trump Since becoming pope, Leo has drawn criticism from Trump for repeatedly condemning the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran and calling for dignified treatment of immigrants. Earlier this year, Trump called Leo "weak" and captive to the "radical left," kicking off a remarkable back-and-forth public argument that dominated Leo's April trip to Africa. Responding to Trump, Leo told reporters en route to Algeria: "I'm not afraid of the Trump administration or of speaking out loudly about the message of the Gospel, which is what the church works for." WATCH: Rubio attempts to mend relations with Pope Leo in Vatican meeting after Trump's criticisms "I will continue to speak out strongly against war, seeking to promote peace, promoting dialogue and multilateralism among states to find solutions to problems," he said. The public dispute has subsided in recent months. "We try to let things pass if there are misunderstandings," the Vatican foreign minister, Archbishop Richard Paul Gallagher, told reporters this week when asked about the spring feud. "With anybody we would be looking to approach it and say, 'OK, there may be a misunderstanding, let's move on and try to rebuild trust and confidence.'" Leo and Trump have not spoken by phone since the pope's May 2025 election. Last week, however, the pope spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the humanitarian crisis in the Ukrainian city of Oleshky. Asked why Trump and Leo haven't spoken, Gallagher said the Holy See has found a capable conduit in the U.S. ambassador to the Holy See, Brian Burch, and hadn't needed to elevate any issue higher. "There hasn't been a feeling that there was the necessity of more direct contact," Gallagher

d0b3b7a9e71d.text: By — Tia Goldenberg, Associated Press Tia Goldenberg, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/israels-election-results-are-in-heres-what-could-happen-next Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Israel's election results are in. Here's what could happen next World Oct 30, 2026 12:27 PM EDT TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — Israeli election results are in, showing the makeup of the country's next parliament but leaving open the question of who will be prime minister. Party leaders will now hold high-stakes negotiations as they try to cobble together a 61-seat coalition in the 120-member assembly, known as the Knesset. WATCH: What's next for Israel after election produces political gridlock It's a tough path ahead for both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Neither of their camps won a majority, and Arab-led parties, which won a historic 19 seats, could play a decisive role. Any possible coalition would require candidates to make tough compromises that could outrage their own voters. If they are unable to do so, new elections would be held early next year, with Netanyahu's government staying on as caretaker until then. Here is a look at the possible scenarios: Eisenkot and the Arab parties On paper, the most straightforward solution would be for Eisenkot to join forces with the Arab-led parties in a solid, 67-seat coalition opposed to Netanyahu. Even if they don't join his coalition, they could provide crucial backing for a minority government. But that would be politically risky for Eisenkot and his Jewish allies. READ MORE: A historic vote born of fear and frustration for Palestinian citizens of Israel Israel's Arab citizens, who make up 20% of its population, are Palestinians whose families remained in Israel after the 1948 war surrounding its creation. They have close ties to Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza and largely support their cause, leading many Jewish Israelis to view them with suspicion. Only once has an Arab party joined a governing coalition, in 2021, and that government only lasted around 18 months. Netanyahu is already portraying any such alliance as a betrayal of Israel's Jewish identity and a national security threat, raising the pressure on Eisenkot's allies, particularly those on the right, to reject it. Unity government Netanyahu could try to convince Eisenkot and his right-leaning allies to instead ally with the prime minister. This constellation could give Netanyahu a 67-seat majority and would send Arab-led parties, as well as ultranationalist and ultra-Orthodox Jewish factions, to the opposition. Such a government could tackle pressing issues like military exemptions for the ultra-Orthodox or work to shore up Israel's economy. It would require a lot of promise-breaking, though. WATCH: Retired Israeli general on what the election results tell us Eisenkot and his allies have vowed not to sit in government with Netanyahu after blaming him for the security failures surrounding Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023 attack, accusing him of undermining Israel's democratic institutions and highlighting his ongoing corruption trial. A government led by Netanyahu is unlikely to approve an official inquiry into the Oct. 7 attack, a central demand of opposition voters. And in the past, when Israeli opposition leaders have defied their voters to join Netanyahu, their political support has plummeted. The arrangement would also require Netanyahu to jettison far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies who stood by him after the attack and through multiple wars and other crises. Poaching defectors Netanyahu is likely looking for weak links in the opposition bloc, which spans Israel's political spectrum. He could try to lure some of his former allies, like right-wing party leaders Naftali Bennett or Avigdor Lieberman. Both strongly support nationalist policies like expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank, and would find it particularly difficult to partner with Arab parties. WATCH: Projections show no clear winner in Israel's election But they have clashed with Netanyahu, often on personal terms, for years, and had vowed not to partner with him. They are also deeply opposed to the military exemptions that are a make-or-break demand of Netanyahu's ultra-Orthodox allies. Eisenkot has fewer possibilities, as Netanyahu's right-wing Likud, and his far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies, have been fiercely loyal to him over the years. New elections If neither side manages to secure a majority, the country could be headed toward another election, likely early next year. Netanyahu's government would remain in a caretaker role until then. This scenario could be disastrous for Netanyahu's opponents, who had momentum heading into this election, even though the outcome fell short of their expectations. They enjoyed a boost from tens of thousands of Israelis who flew in from abroad to vote but might not travel a second time. READ MORE: Why it could be weeks or months before Israel's election winner is known Netanyahu would meanwhile buy time to shore up his coalition. Smaller right-wing parties that failed to meet the threshold for entering parliament essentially wasted pro-Netanyahu votes. They might not run a second time, or their supporters might switch over to the bigger far-right parties, strengthening the prime minister. After a similar stalemate in 2019, Israel held five elections in 3 1/2 years. Tia Goldenberg has been covering Israeli politics for nearly two decades. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Tia Goldenberg, Associated Press Tia Goldenberg, Associated Press

bb37e6a17b2a.text: By — Sam Metz, Associated Press Sam Metz, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/a-historic-vote-born-of-fear-and-frustration-for-palestinian-citizens-of-israel Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A historic vote born of fear and frustration for Palestinian citizens of Israel World Oct 30, 2026 12:03 PM EDT SAKHNIN, Israel (AP) — For Palestinian citizens of Israel, it was a rare moment of political triumph. Hundreds of thousands voted in record numbers, giving two Arab-led parties their largest-ever number of seats in Israel's parliament. Many boycotted past elections, seeing little point. But after years of their communities being demonized or neglected, some of Israel's most marginalized citizens turned to the ballot box to fight back against the most right-wing government in the country's history. "We are here and we're not on the sidelines," declared Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra'am party, as supporters cheered in a wedding hall Tuesday night, watching the exit polls. WATCH: What's next for Israel after election produces political gridlock The surge makes them a major political force that could enable opposition parties to assemble a coalition to oust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. But the question is whether Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, and other opponents will ally with them. Only once has an Arab-led party ever served in an Israeli government. During the campaign, Netanyahu had accused his main opponents of planning to form a coalition with them, which Eisenkot denied. Netanyahu and his allies are now turning up the anti-Arab rhetoric even further, making unproven claims that foreign powers bribed voters to back Arab-led parties. In a Thursday post on X, Netanyahu warned against any party forming a government with them, saying it would lead to the "Islamization of Israel." Palestinian grievances fueled the surge Nearly 840,000 people on Tuesday voted for Ra'am and the Joint List, a coalition of three Arab-led parties, a 64% increase from the last elections in 2022, according to final results from the Central Election Committee. The parties won 19 seats in Israel's 120-member Knesset, surpassing the previous record of 15. Crowds packed polling places in Arab communities from the Negev Desert to the northern Galilee. In Tarabin, a Bedouin village in the Negev, Netanyahu's party had won majorities the past two elections. Turnout nearly doubled on Tuesday and Ra'am won 93% of the vote. WATCH: Retired Israeli general on what the election results tell us The northern town of Sakhnin had Israel's highest voter turnout, at 87%. Mayor Mazen Ghnaim said voters saw it as an emergency measure to fight rising violent crime in Arab communities and incitement by Netanyahu's far-right allies. "I want to protect my constituents from being killed, my children from being attacked at their universities and Arab doctors getting attacked at hospitals," said Ghnaim, a Ra'am supporter, referring to recent incidents of anti-Arab violence. The parties worked hard to overcome past reluctance to vote among Palestinians, who have long felt ignored in the halls of power. They held community meetings in cities and towns that Jewish-led parties mostly ignored. A grassroots movement went door-to-door in Bedouin villages to encourage women to vote. A reaction to Israel's most far-right government ever Voters and candidates said their heightened participation did not reflect faith in Israeli democracy — it was a sign of desperation to unseat Netanyahu. Two of his far-right allies, Itamar Ben Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, are responsible for some of Israel's most extreme policies and anti-Arab incitement. WATCH: Projections show no clear winner in Israel's election Ben Gvir, the national security minister, raised alarm on Election Day over Arab turnout, telling his supporters, "If you want this country to remain Jewish and Zionist … then get out and vote!" The rhetoric, also echoed by Netanyahu and Smotrich, may have only galvanized Arab voters. "We see the government going from bad to worse," 52-year-old Awni Zoabi said after voting in Nazareth. "We want to live, we want a future for our children, and we want a future for ourselves." The parties offer different visions Palestinians who managed to stay in Israel after the 1948 war surrounding its creation — when hundreds of thousands were expelled or fled — today, along with their descendants, make up more than 20% of the population. They have Israeli citizenship, including the right to vote, but also feel deep solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank. Ra'am and the Joint List both campaigned on combating crime and securing investment for Arab communities. But they offered different visions for how to approach the wider conflict. READ MORE: Israelis await final election results as Netanyahu rivals weigh joining forces with Arab parties Ra'am made the advantages of joining a coalition government central to its pitch to voters and said little that could alienate potential Jewish allies. It placed a Jewish former police official second on its candidate list. In contrast, members of the Joint List called Israel's campaign in Gaza a genocide and compared the occupation of the West Bank to apartheid South Africa. Most Jewish Israelis ardently reject both accusations. "People are clever enough to see what's happening. Of the two options, one is proposing a genocide, and the other is proposing apartheid. These are the choices: bad or worse," said Sami Abou Shehadeh, the leader of one of the slate's parties. Strong showing doesn't guarantee a role in government Mainstream Israeli parties have long resisted partnering with Arab-led parties elected to the Knesset, portraying them as threats to Israel's Jewish character or questioning their loyalty to the state. Netanyahu's opponents welcomed Ra'am into a short-lived coalition government in 2021, in return offering investment

ad0456ef8fea.text: By — Cara Anna, Associated Press Cara Anna, Associated Press By — Ibrahim Hazboun, Associated Press Ibrahim Hazboun, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/difficult-negotiations-lie-ahead-in-israel-after-netanyahus-bloc-lost-its-parliamentary-majority Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Difficult negotiations lie ahead in Israel after Netanyahu's bloc lost its parliamentary majority World Oct 30, 2026 11:23 AM EDT JERUSALEM (AP) — Israel's final election results confirmed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies lost their parliamentary majority and that weeks of difficult negotiations among very different parties, from ultra-Orthodox Jewish to secular to Arab-led, lie ahead. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The results released early Friday showed Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday's election. The main opposition bloc won 48. Arab-led parties secured the other 19, a historic showing. Now parties must meet, bargain and seek a way to team up for at least 61 seats in the 120-member Knesset. Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, remains in charge. "Now comes the truly hard part," centrist politician Yair Lapid said on X, urging patience and adding: "If you want to know if something's happening behind the silence you're hearing now, the answer is yes." The president will task someone with forming a government Difficult decisions lie ahead. Will the main opposition parties that campaigned hard to unseat the divisive Netanyahu make the politically sensitive choice to partner with Arab-led ones? Or will they toss their vows aside to team up with Netanyahu in a potentially fractious unity government? Israel largely shuts down on Friday for the Jewish Sabbath, and it was not clear who might be meeting with whom. Israelis debated possible coalitions and challenges, as some expressed traditional wariness around Arab parties and others insisted it was time for Jewish-led parties to embrace them. WATCH: What's next for Israel after election produces political gridlock "There are options for all of this, not like in the United States, where there are only two parties," said Beny Engalrd, a resident of Tel Aviv. The election results still need to be certified and submitted to the president next Wednesday. Then President Isaac Herzog will task someone with forming the new government. That could be the leader of the party that received the most votes — Netanyahu — or whoever leaders of the various parties believe is best suited. If multiple attempts to form a government fail, Israel faces a new election early next year. Herzog this week said he will do everything in his power to avoid that scenario. Netanyahu and Likud target Arab parties without evidence In the hours before final results were announced, Netanyahu and his Likud party amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had "stolen" the election, potentially with foreign assistance. The opposition quickly accused Netanyahu of demonizing Arab citizens, who make up 20% of the population and showed up at the polls like never before in outrage over his far-right government. On Friday, Netanyahu again warned against forming a coalition with Arab parties. READ MORE: Netanyahu's party claims Israeli election 'stolen' as results show him losing majority The head of Israel's election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, had said "serious suspicions" of foreign interference had been brought before him. In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims but asked the agency to investigate. Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu's party accused Qatar of involvement, allegations the Gulf state dismissed as "ridiculous and dangerous." Many Israelis view Qatar as a patron of Hamas, while Qatar says its relations with the militant group are part of its U.S.-backed mediation efforts in the region. The election commission said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. Acting Director General Dean Livne did not elaborate but warned that reports about the investigation had been "entirely unfounded." "It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population," he said. WATCH: Projections show no clear winner in Israel's election By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be trying to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab-led parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for chief rival Gadi Eisenkot or others to join with them. The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to "cast aspersions" on an entire section of the population that "exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner." The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament, saying that "allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless." The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week. Opposition could assert control in the upcoming Knesset Even as coalition negotiations begin, the new Knesset is expected to be sworn in Nov. 10. Once it convenes, Eisenkot's bloc could join forces with the Arab parties to elect a new Knesset speaker, giving them control over the parliamentary agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed. Already, hundreds of Israelis have been holding rallies urging Eisenkot and others to join forces with the Arab-led parties, a step that has happened only once before, briefly, in 2021. d858ea077f4f.text: By — Steve Peoples, Associated Press Steve Peoples, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/a-midterm-crossroads-for-both-parties-eyeing-the-beginning-of-the-end-of-the-trump-era Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A midterm crossroads for both parties eyeing the beginning of the end of the Trump era Politics Oct 30, 2026 11:21 AM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — The nation's major political parties are at a crossroads. A decade after he began to remake the Republican Party in his image, President Donald Trump is facing the prospect of a voter rebellion Tuesday that could force conservatives to rethink their undying allegiance to the 80-year-old lame-duck leader and his "Make America Great Again" movement. Already, some Republican candidates have begun to distance themselves from him. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. And Democrats, who remain unpopular despite midterm momentum, are speeding toward a tug-of-war between establishment leaders and emboldened progressives demanding nothing less than transformative change. Whether either party wins or loses Tuesday, the end of the 2026 midterms marks the beginning of a high-stakes fight over the country's political future in the twilight of the Trump era — a fight that will swiftly surge to the forefront of American politics as new members of Congress descend upon Washington and the 2028 presidential contest takes off. "When President Trump leaves office, it's going to create a tremendous vacuum. And I ask the question, where does the country go next?" said former Republican Sen. John E. Sununu, who is running for the New Hampshire Senate seat he lost in 2008. WATCH: Where key Senate races stand in the final days of campaigning Republicans start to envision a party after Trump More than any policy or principle, the most powerful unifying force in the modern-day Republican Party has become Trump himself. And so, as the party looks to the end of the Trump era, major questions loom over who or what will guide it. Trump long ago smashed Ronald Reagan's three-legged stool of conservatism that defined the GOP for generations: fiscal conservatism favoring small government and free trade, conservative social values and a muscular foreign policy. What remains today is a fluid populism that changes with the whims of the outgoing president. The brash businessman helped move the Republican Party away from the country club and toward a much broader coalition of working-class voters, including a growing slice of the traditional Democratic base, including Hispanics, African Americans and young people. Republican strategist David Urban said he's closely watching whether the Trump coalition holds up Tuesday. WATCH: Democratic and GOP strategists assess midterm landscape in final week "When we see that, that'll tell you a lot about the future," Urban said. "Look, if all those folks stay home — they're disaffected because of the economy, or the war, or pick your exit polling issue — that then leaves a lot of questions of who's going to be the next standard-bearer for the party." Most of the Republican Party's 2028 buzz has focused on Vice President JD Vance. The 42-year-old former Ohio senator went from a Trump critic to a Trump acolyte, and he could face the usual challenges of establishing an independent political identity while serving in the nation's number two role. Should Republicans have a bad night Tuesday, Vance's presidential stock could take a hit. Another popular 2028 prospect, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, could face a similar challenge. But that could open the door for Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, or perhaps even a vocal Trump critic like former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie, who is 64 years old and weighing a comeback. Democrats can't agree on what comes next With few exceptions, Democratic officials are anticipating a good night Tuesday, even if they do not win both chambers of Congress. They do not agree, however, on what comes next. The establishment is cheering the ascendance of Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become the nation's first Black House speaker should Democrats win the majority. Frustrated progressives, however, believe Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer are part of the problem. And they're demanding sweeping change in the people and policies guiding their party. Such demands are especially pronounced among the Democrats aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America. Currently, just two DSA-backed members serve in the House of Representatives. Their numbers are expected to swell to at least seven in the new Congress thanks to the success of the slate of candidates backed by New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani in the primaries. Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed would give the far left another vocal champion, although he is not endorsed by the DSA, nor does he identify as a democratic socialist. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, a Democratic presidential prospect facing reelection next week, declined to say he welcomed DSA into his party when asked directly. Instead, he told The Associated Press that he wanted "commonsense leaders that are prepared to disrupt the status quo and know how to move fast in order to get things done." He said over and over that Democratic leaders must act with urgency. "I don't want to be a party of no and slow. I want to be a party of yes and now," Moore said. "I want to be a party that is deeply impatient to be able to deliver the kind of results that we're hoping for and the things that we're hoping to see for our families." A top Democratic senator has blamed a crackdown on independent journalism in Egypt on a decision by the Trump administration to waive human rights conditions on US military funding to the country.
Chris Murphy, who sits on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, accused the US government of "abandoning" the Egyptian people after it lifted restrictions relating to more than $300m of defence assistance.
Over the last month a series of arrests has taken place of journalists at two of the few remaining independent news outlets in Egypt, where newspapers and TV stations are closely controlled by the authorities.
The US State Department told the BBC it waived conditions on a portion of military aid to Egypt in September due to the country's "importance to US national security interests".
Murphy, speaking at the Middle East Institute (MEI) in Washington this week, said he was in no doubt the two were linked.
"The minute that money was released, the crackdown began in an absolutely devastating way," he said.
On Tuesday a court in Cairo ordered the closure of the news website Madr Masa and fined its editor-in-chief Lina Attalah in what Amnesty International called "a crushing blow to press freedom".
Earlier this month, authorities arrested six journalists at the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh and charged them with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The Egyptian Embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.
Cairo has remained a close regional ally of the US despite what human rights groups say are widespread abuses under President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's government, including torture and enforced disappearances.
Sisi denies there are political prisoners in Egypt. He has previously said stability and security are paramount, adding authorities have promoted rights by trying to provide basic needs such as jobs and housing.
Washington sends Egypt Â£1.3bn ($1.73bn) per year, making it one of the world's biggest recipients of US military assistance.
US law allows up to Â£320m of the funding to be withheld, conditioned on Egypt meeting democracy and human rights requirements. But these restrictions can be waived by the administration on national security grounds.
In September, Secretary of State Marco Rubio waived human rights conditions on $320m of military aid in light of Egypt's role since the launch of the US war with Iran, according to a letter addressed to various Congressional committees. Egypt assisted negotiations between the US and Iran.
Exercising the waiver authority was "essential" for the US-Egypt relationship, "particularly in light of Egypt's helpful role following Operation Epic Fury," according to the September 4 memo seen by Reuters which bore Rubio's signature.
Asked by the BBC about the move in light of this month's arrests of journalists, the State Department said the waiver was "due to Egypt's importance to US national security interests, the concrete security cooperation Egypt provides to the United States, and the need to maintain that cooperation to address regional security challenges".
It added it maintained dialogue with Cairo on a "full range of issues" but would "not comment on private diplomatic conversations".
Rubio's move followed a similar decision by the Biden administration in 2024, when then Secretary of State Anthony Blinken waived human rights conditions to grant the full military aid allocation to Egypt as the US sought Cairo's role in mediating between Israel and Hamas in the war in Gaza.
Under Biden prior to 2024, the US withheld portions of the annual military allocation over Egypt's human rights record.
Murphy, who chairs a congressional committee on the Middle East and counterterrorism, said he had been a critic of both the Biden and Trump administrations over the issue.
"To the extent that there was any glimmer left of political speech in Egypt, it is gone for one proximate reason: The United States government abandoned the people of Egypt and decided to remove all conditions on our funding," Murphy told the MEI.
"Any hope of a true, meaningful political opposition rebirthing in Egypt has been shattered by this decision," he added.
US military aid to Cairo began after the 1978 Camp David Accords and the peace treaty that followed between Egypt and Israel. Successive administrations have viewed the world's most populous Arab country as a critical US ally in the region.
The group Reporters Without Borders describes Egypt, external as one of the world's biggest jailers of journalists.
The conviction of Lina Attalah and the closure of Madr Masr marked an unprecedented escalation in repression of press freedoms in Egypt, according to Timothy E Kaldas, Deputy Director of The Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, a Washington DC-based think tank.
He said both the US and European Union had been prioritising their strategic relations with Egypt over human rights and the rule of law in the country.
"It's been fostering a sense of impunity on the part of the Egyptian authorities that we're seeing play out," he told the BBC.
"Egypt is getting signals from both sides of the Atlantic that human rights and the rule of law are no longer a priority, and they're testing the limits of that."
He added: "The fact that they're not getting more robust pushback reinforces the wrong message."

Mature Scots Pine trees may be lost from a Highland landscape hit by a huge summer wildfire, experts fear.
Forestry and Land Scotland say the blaze around Glenmore in the Cairngorms may have led to the loss of many so-called "granny pines" which have matured over centuries.
They say their loss removes important seed sources and makes it more difficult for the species to regenerate.
However, the Scottish government agency said there were many encouraging signs of natural recovery among other species following the fire.
It burned through about 10 sq miles of forest and moorland near Aviemore in July and August.
Forestry and Land Scotland staff who have been monitoring the site have recorded birch, rowan and willow regenerating from surviving stems and root systems.
Large areas of hillside have also been observed turning green again as grasses, bracken and blaeberry begin to make a comeback.
The agency said this was particularly apparent where moisture had remained in the soil or where fire intensity was lower.
Deer and capercaillie are now being regularly spotted in the fire damaged area, attracted by the new grass growth.
FLS forestry management and stewardship forester Eelco de Jong said the recovery of broadleaf vegetation was promising with lots of birch, rowan and willow expected to grow back quickly.
However, he warned that there were "significant challenges" ahead because of organic soil layers being badly affected and due to damage to the area's renowned Scots pine.
He said: "The concern is many of the oldest 'granny pines' could be lost, removing important seed sources and habitat for species such as capercaillie."
"Some of these veteran trees were more than 100 or 200 years old and, where losses occur, it could take centuries for trees of a similar stature to return to the landscape."

For two decades, when the high-energy universe called, NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has answered. But now, the spacecraft’s science tenure is ending, just when its skills might be more valuable than ever. The Swift spacecraft is falling uncontrollably, destined to burn up in Earth’s atmosphere in just a few days.
The telescope launched in 2004, tailored to reveal the secrets of gamma-ray bursts. These outbursts are the most powerful kind scientists have ever seen, but they often faded before earlier telescopes could respond. Swift took its name from its ability to jump to work when a flash went off. That talent both illuminated these elusive bursts and made the observatory a cornerstone of modern astronomy for far longer than scientists ever dreamed.
“This was designed to be a two-year mission,” says astrophysicist Brad Cenko of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md. “We’re coming up on year 22. We are so fortunate to have had the opportunity to do all the things that we have.”
Over the decades, the spacecraft has lost about half its original altitude as it constantly slammed into molecules in the atmosphere. Those minuscule impacts infinitesimally slowed the observatory, pushing it closer to Earth. The sun’s relatively high activity in recent years has accelerated the process, leaving the spacecraft unable to continue into the 2030s as engineers hoped. A spacecraft commissioned by NASA to loft Swift out of danger launched in early July, but by late August, technical issues made a boost attempt impossible.
Swift is doomed — with nothing lined up to replace its unique capabilities.
Glimpsing gamma-rays
When scientists dreamed up the Swift mission, the massive energy and elusive nature of gamma-ray bursts made them one of the most tantalizing phenomena out there. Astronomers desperately wanted to understand how they worked.
Swift was equipped with three instruments. Its Burst Alert Telescope gave scientists eyes on gamma-ray emissions from up to half the visible sky, with the resolution to pinpoint where light is coming from. The agile spacecraft could then swing itself and its other instruments — one tuned to X-rays and the other to visible and ultraviolet light — to quickly give scientists a view of a patch of sky across a swath of types of light. It was a combination unlike any observatory before or since.
“It’s such a unique telescope,” says astrophysicist Wen-fai Fong of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill., who is not part of the mission team. “It has all these views of the universe, all in one observatory, which by itself is rare, but it can also rapidly point any of these instruments.”
Swift’s roster of accomplishments speaks to the power of that recipe. “Almost immediately after launch, Swift started discovering things,” says astrophysicist Lynn Cominsky of Sonoma State University in Rohnert Park, Calif. That’s not an exaggeration: One record-breaking observation, taken just the month after launch, revealed that stellar corpses with powerful magnetic fields undergo outbursts that create a distinct kind of gamma-ray signature.
That observation pushed back against scientists’ existing categorization of gamma-ray bursts. Before Swift, the bursts fell into two buckets. Long gamma-ray bursts lasted as long as minutes, and scientists believed they stemmed from exploding stars triggering supernovae. Short gamma-ray bursts, in contrast, lasted less than two seconds and were believed to originate in merging neutron stars, the superdense remains of a star large enough to explode but too small to create a black hole.
Swift confirmed this basic sketch, but also complicated it by finding bursts that didn’t cleanly fit into this binary. “The more data you get, the more confused you get,” Cominsky says. Other notable bursts the telescope observed included the brightest (gamma-ray burst) of all time, nicknamed BOAT, the highest-energy photons from such a burst, and multiple claimants to the title of most distant burst.
Notably, all of Swift’s data was public right away, even as team scientists were still working to understand what the telescope had seen. “That was very new,” Fong says, crediting the mission with inspiring other observatory teams to follow suit.
Beyond gamma-rays
As other astronomers heard about Swift’s work, they realized how powerful the observatory might be for their own interests as well. As Swift’s tenure unfolded, astronomers started asking to borrow the nimble observatory to study a whole range of objects changing on the sky.
“With scientists, if you give them a tool to do something, they will other find other things that you can do with that tool,” says astrophysicist Phil Evans of the University of Leicester in England. In its later years, Swift observed between five and 10 “targets of opportunity” most days, tallying hundreds or even thousands in a year.
Perhaps its most ground-breaking collaborations were partnerships with observatories hunting for ghostly neutrinos that travel nearly as quickly as light but don’t interact often, and for gravitational waves, the ripples in spacetime triggered by massive objects. In 2017, Swift participated in back-to-back discoveries: the unique explosion caused by two neutron stars merging, then the first neutrino traced back to its origin.
Since then, all efforts to observe light affiliated with a neutrino or gravitational-wave signal have come up empty. “We had these two really close together and then nothing since,” Evans says. “Which is frustrating, but also kind of fun.”
A grand finale
A range of current and future observatories will be able to take over some of Swift’s work, but not all of it. Even during the six months this year when Swift paused operations to prepare for the boost attempt, scientists felt its loss, says astrophysicist Judith Racusin of NASA Goddard. Racusin worked with Swift during its early years before turning her focus to NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which launched in 2

Pope Leo XIV has submitted his mail-in ballot in Illinois, for the midterm elections, becoming the first-ever pope to vote in a US election.
"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Holy See Press Office said in a statement.
The Chicago-born pontiff is the first US citizen to hold the Vatican's highest seat, after his selection in May 2025.
Since then, he has clashed with the Trump administration over various issues, including immigration enforcement and the US-Israel war with Iran.
"Pope Leo XIV has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so," the press office said, including during his years in Peru.
The US midterm elections will determine which political party controls Congress and have a significant impact on the final years of Donald Trump's presidency.
Elections will be held nationwide on 3 November, but early voting has begun in most states.
According to NBC News, the Pope requested his mail-in ballot from the Will County Clerk's Office on 3 October.
Less than two weeks later, the Vatican announced he had surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung after he was diagnosed with lung cancer.
The Vatican confirmed last week that the Pope, aged 71, will travel as planned to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru in early November.
Tensions escalated between the Pope and the US president in April, after the Pope called for peace in the wake of US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
"I don't think he's doing a very good job," Trump said about the Pope afterwards.
"We don't like a Pope that's going to say that it's OK to have a nuclear weapon," he continued. "I'm not a big fan of Pope Leo."
Pope Leo followed with his own remarks later, saying: "The mission of the Church is to preach the Gospel, to preach peace," according to Reuters.
"If someone wants to criticise me for preaching the Gospel... I hope simply to be listened to because of the value of God's words."
In the final few days before the midterms, Republican and Democratic officials alike are sprinting across the country to boost their party's chances of success.
Polls suggest Democrats are the favourite to gain control of the lower chamber of Congress, called the House of Representatives, and are poised to win seats in Republican-leaning areas that overwhelmingly voted for Trump in the 2024 presidential election.
Democrats also appear to have a chance to win additional seats in the Senate, the upper chamber of Congress.
The gloomy outlook for Trump's Republican party has seen the president hold several rallies in states where Republican victories are typically all but guaranteed.

46f519a3f663.text: By — Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press By — Simran Parwani, Associated Press Simran Parwani, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/millions-more-americans-vote-ahead-of-election-day-as-early-voting-jumps-across-senate-battlegrounds Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Early voting jumps across Senate battlegrounds as millions more Americans vote ahead of Election Day Politics Updated on Oct 30, 2026 1:17 PM EDT — Published on Oct 30, 2026 10:44 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Early voting is significantly outpacing the last midterm election, with millions more Americans casting ballots in advance and particularly sharp increases in states hosting competitive Senate races, according to an Associated Press analysis of voting data five days before Election Day. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The surge is especially pronounced in Texas, where voters are deciding closely watched Senate, House and governor's races. More than 6.3 million Texans had voted early as of Wednesday, compared with 4.2 million at the same point four years ago, a 50% increase. Advance voting has also increased more than 30% from the same point four years ago in Maine, Michigan, North Carolina and Kansas, states with competitive Senate races. In South Carolina, where voters are choosing a successor to the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, early voting is up 83%. Data comes 5 days before Election Day The data, compiled by the AP, offers a glimpse of early voter participation five days before an election that will determine control of Congress and other key contests. Across the country, more than 43 million Americans had voted early in person or returned mail ballots, nearly 10 million more than in 2022. The figures cover 47 states and Washington, D.C., compared with 48 states and the nation's capital four years ago. WATCH: Democratic and GOP strategists assess midterm landscape in final week In states that provide information on voters' party affiliation, about 6.8 million Democrats and 5.2 million Republicans have cast ballots early. Those figures do not account for all early voters nationwide or indicate which candidates received their votes. The increase comes as voters prepare to decide control of Congress two years into President Donald Trump's second term, with Republicans holding the House and the Senate. The turnout has been Texas-sized Voters have turned out in droves during Texas' two-week early in-person voting period, which ends Friday. In Harris County, which includes Houston, 862,700 people had voted as of Wednesday, compared with 564,500 at the same point in 2022. The surge comes in a county that has reliably voted Democratic in recent elections, though by varying margins. In 2024, Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris defeated Trump by nearly 6 percentage points in the presidential contest, while Democratic Senate candidate Colin Allred carried the county by roughly 11 percentage points over Republican Sen. Ted Cruz. This year, Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton faces Democrat James Talarico in a closely watched Senate race, while Republican Gov. Greg Abbott is seeking reelection against Democrat Gina Hinojosa. Hundreds of millions of dollars have poured into the Senate race as Republicans fight to defend a state where Democrats have not won a statewide election in more than three decades. Trump visited Texas earlier this week, his third trip to the state in a month. Early voting surges across Senate battleground states Republicans are defending a 53-47 Senate majority in a midterm election in which the battleground map has expanded significantly, with Democrats hoping to pull off upsets in states that have long favored Republicans. In South Carolina, where Trump won by nearly 18 percentage points in 2024, early voting has surged 83% compared with the same point in 2022. The state has open races for governor and U.S. Senate this year. READ MORE: What our final poll before Election Day says about midterms and Trump In Kansas, where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces Democratic Methodist megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton, early voting has increased 34%, with roughly 83,000 more ballots cast than at the same point four years ago. Michigan and Maine, both of which have closely watched Senate races, are also seeing increases. In Maine, where Republican Sen. Susan Collins faces Democratic former state Senate President Troy Jackson, early voting is up 44%. Michigan has recorded roughly 409,000 more early votes than at the same point in 2022, a 32% increase. Voters in Michigan approved early in-person voting in November 2022, making this the first midterm election in which it is available statewide. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 008ed0e01a14.text: By — Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/binance-flags-potential-security-issue-says-approximately-6-3-billion-impacted Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Binance flags 'potential security issue,' says approximately $6.3 billion impacted Economy Oct 30, 2026 10:25 AM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said Thursday it's investigating reports of a potential security issue as its founder said the incident "does look like a hack on Binance." The company said late Thursday the estimated total impact was at more than $6 billion, which could be one of the most significant of such security incidents on record. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. It wasn't immediately clear the extent of the damage hackers might have been able to cause, and Binance had not explicitly confirmed that funds had been pilfered. The company said its teams are "working around the clock" to resolve the issue. "Rest assured that user funds are completely safe," a Binance spokesperson said in a statement. WATCH: News Wrap: Democrats block crypto bill, demand limits on Trump's investments "Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information," the statement continued. The company wrote on its X account that the estimated total impact sat at around $6.3 billion. It said it has worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with roughly $3 billion frozen on-chain so far. "Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions," the company wrote. "We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak," it added. Binance said it will share more technical details once the investigation is complete and when the facts are "fully verified." "Our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets," the company wrote in a separate post earlier Thursday. WATCH: News Wrap: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance pleads guilty in securities investigation Binance also said all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while it conducts security checks, freezes funds and works with law enforcement. Stablecoin providers Tether and Circle each said they froze funds Thursday in response to the incident. Jeremy Allaire, co-founder and CEO of Circle, wrote on X that the company had frozen the equivalent of more than $800 million in currency associated with the incident "in coordination with law enforcement." Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X that the company froze the equivalent of more than $1.5 billion in currency related to "a potential Binance exchange hack." The price of bitcoin dropped 3.2% Thursday evening to under $79,000. READ MORE: How crypto, real estate and watches added up for Trump last year Binance was founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao, who in 2023 pleaded guilty to a felony related to his failure to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as CEO. President Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025. Zhao posted on X on Thursday that "User funds are safe!" but added that the incident "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that while he doesn't manage Binance anymore, "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered." Zhao was released from prison last year after being sentenced for violating the Bank Secrecy Act. He was the first person ever sentenced to prison time for violations of that law, which requires U.S. financial institutions to know who their customers are, to monitor transactions and to file reports of suspicious activity. Prosecutors said no one had ever violated the regulations to the extent Zhao did. Zhao and Binance have been key supporters of some of the Trump family's crypto enterprises. AP writers Chan Ho-him and Barbara Ortutay contributed. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Top Republicans are directing the Federal Election Commission to investigate Democratic Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltolaâs role in the effort to prop up a spoiler candidate with the same name as her opponent, incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, according to details first shared with Semafor.
On the heels of new reporting from The New York Times this week that detailed the efforts of national Democrats and the Peltola campaign to draft Dan J. Sullivan into the Senate race, the National Republican Senatorial Committee is asking the FEC to probe both the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Peltolaâs campaign and refer the matter to the Justice Department if the FEC determines âthese violations were knowing and willful.â
The new complaint calls on the body to âsanction to the fullest extent of the law all the violations it finds.â
The NRSC previously asked the FEC to probe the other Dan Sullivan in June, but the new reporting on the race has prompted the GOPâs campaign arm to expand its request. The new complaint is supplemental and contains new details and allegations.
âIt is now clear that Respondent Sullivanâs sham candidacy was the product of a months-long âballot composition Projectâ run by agents of Ms. Peltola and her campaign committee, Alaskans for Mary (together,the âPeltola Campaignâ), and financed by multiple super PACs,â the complaint reads.
With the midterms now days away, the complaint is part of an urgent effort to discredit Peltola in a must-win Senate race that could easily determine the upper chamberâs majority. The Justice Department is also investigating the matter.
The DSCC noted in a response that the FEC is without a quorum. A spokesperson said the GOPâs complaint is âpart of the Republicansâ dangerous effort to interfere in the Alaska Senate race, fully weaponizing the Department of Justice against political opponents and threatening to refuse to certify the election because they know their candidates are deeply unpopular on the issues that matter to voters.â
Republicans are worried the existence of a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot will cost the two-term incumbent votes in the stateâs race, which uses a unique ranked choice system to tabulate the votes. Alaskaâs moderate Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski said that ârecruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong. Alaskans deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign.â
The new complaint alleges that federal laws were violated since Dan J. Sullivan was recruited âbecause of his name for the deliberate purpose of misleading Alaska voters into voting for the wrong candidateâ and that Peltola allies inappropriately coordinated with outside groups to aid him. The complaint also alleges that âSullivan was not the only spoiler candidate that the Peltola Campaign attempted to recruit to run,â naming Gerald Heikes, who is also on the ballot.

Even before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.
The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.
One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.
This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.
On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lÃ¨se majestÃ© law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.
This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending.
"To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."
The past six years have seen the most extensive use of lÃ¨se majestÃ© in Thai history, in response to unprecedented student protests in 2020 which for the first time called for a public discussion of the role of the monarchy. Two hundred and ninety-four people, including 20 under the age of 18, have been prosecuted, receiving prison sentences of up to 50 years. Dozens of them are still on trial.
Most of those charged under this law are denied bail and kept in jail, even though their court cases can last several years. The standard defence of the law given by Thai officials is that it "reflects the culture and history of Thailand, where the monarchy is one of the main pillars of the nation, highly revered by the majority of Thai people".
Article 112 of the Thai criminal code simply reads, "Whoever defames, insults or threatens the King, the Queen, the Heir-apparent or the Regent, shall be punished with imprisonment of three to 15 years."
In practice, though, the law has been interpreted to cover a much wider range of comment about the monarchy, and a much wider range of figures. Saying anything negative about any member of the royal family, about the institution of the monarchy, even about long deceased kings, or in one case, the king's dog, has resulted in prosecutions.
"If you ask me what the text of the law says, I can tell you," says Akarachai Chaimaneekarakate, assistant director of Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, which helps defend those accused of breaking it. "If you ask me how the courts interpret the words "defame" or "insult", I don't think I can give you a definition, because it's so ambiguous, it's so vague. Even questioning the law itself, for example, can constitute lÃ¨se majestÃ© under Section 112."
From his cell in the Bangkok Remand Prison, where he has been for the last three years, Arnon has been writing to his young daughter and son.
"Dear Pran and Karl, my beloved children,
The winter wind has not only brought us cool weather, but also brings back stories from the past. I miss the time we travelled outside Bangkok that first winter after Karl came into this world. It was such a magical time for me. I shall miss it every winter I spend here until I regain my freedom."
Hearings like the one Arnon attended weeks before Friday's verdict are the only times he has seen Karl since he was a baby.
Karl is shy at first, but soon he's happy to be picked up and shown off to the other prisoners. His 10-year-old sister Pran sometimes visits their father in prison, and often draws and paints him.
But Arnon and Lookwa, his partner, think Karl is too young to visit. For now, Karl thinks the court is just where his dad works. A group of supporters has come too, filling the little courtroom. They mingle cheerfully with the prisoners, laughing and exchanging gossip before the judges walk in to start the hearing. It is an improbably informal setting for men facing one of the most feared charges in Thailand.
The effect of the law has been to smother any public discussion about the monarchy. Until six years ago, opinions on it were only ever whispered in private. In one notorious case a taxi driver was jailed because a passenger reported what he had said while riding in his cab.
That changed on 3 August 2020.
That year younger Thais had become increasingly frustrated with the conservative government led by coup-leader Gen Prayuth Chan-ocha. The year before millions had given their votes to a new party, Future Forward, which promised sweeping reforms, but in February 2020, the Constitutional Court dissolved the party on a technicality. The arrival of the Covid pandemic prevented any protests for three months, but as infections in Thailand started to fall, students began holding rallies calling for an end to the military's role in politics. Arnon Nampa argued this did not go far enough.
In the garb of Harry Potter, he gave a speech saying it was time to talk about the opaque power and wealth of the monarchy. He criticised King Vajiralongkorn's decision to take personal control of the vast assets held by the Crown Property Bureau, and over important units of the army.
In a single speech Arnon shattered a taboo which had hung over Thai society for the whole of its modern history. For the rest of that year the student-led protests continued, with increasingly bold demands for changes to the monarchy.

A US immigration agent has been charged with felony for allegedly hitting a man with a vehicle earlier this month in Texas, a prosecutor announced.
The prosecutor said US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer Mario Alberto Morales was indicted by a grand jury on a charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon.
Morales is accused of running over a Mexican national who was living in the US without legal documentation, leaving him with multiple leg fractures and a hip injury.
An ICE spokesperson dismissed the indictment as "nothing more than a political stunt" and described the allegations as "reckless and false".
The indictment comes amid the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration and a series of violent incidents involving federal agents that have resulted in injuries and deaths.
If convicted, Morales faces between two to 20 years in prison for the second-degree felony, according to Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare.
Teare said Morales pursued a vehicle driven by Miguel Parra-Hernandez, a 48-year-old Mexican national who has lived in Texas for more than 30 years without legal documentation, on the morning of 10 October.
Parra-Hernandez and another occupant fled the vehicle on foot before Morales "aggressively steered his vehicle" into the Mexican national, Teare said at a news conference in Houston on Friday.
He said Parra-Hernandez had no criminal record and was not subject to a deportation order.
"Not only did he hit Mr Hernandez, he ran over both of his legs, leaving him seriously injured and hospitalised to this day," Teare said.
Morales then called 911 to report that Parra-Hernandez had hit his car.
Teare said that ICE was allegedly pursuing a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, a Mexican national and undocumented immigrant, who has apparently been dead for nine years.
Immediately after the incident, an ICE spokesperson told the BBC's US media partner CBS News that Parra-Hernandez had run in front of the immigration agent's vehicle.
Following the indictment, ICE rejected the allegations brought by the grand jury - a panel of citizens empowered to determine whether there was sufficient evidence to bring criminal charges.
"This is nothing more than a political stunt by Houston sanctuary politicians," an ICE spokesperson said in a statement to the BBC.
"Allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE," the spokesperson said, adding that the men and women of ICE "are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct".
The statement added that federal officers acting in the course of their duties could only be investigated by other federal agencies. The spokesperson insisted that local governments did not have the authority to run such an investigation.
District Attorney Teare stressed that he had the utmost respect for law enforcement and believed that undocumented individuals who were violent felons should be deported.
He said he hoped the prosecution would not only deliver justice for Parra-Hernandez and his family but also send "a loud and clear message to every ICE officer who feels that they have a free pass to terrorise our streets".

Congressional leaders and Maryland regulators continue to pressure the Trump administration for information about the ongoing jet fuel leak at Joint Base Andrews. Both want immediate action that will stop the contamination that continues to threaten Piscataway Creek and nearby communities more than seven months after the incident was reported.
The latest calls follow recent Inside Climate News reporting showing that water testing across several locations on and around the base detected that “diesel-range” hydrocarbons, a category that includes jet fuel, were still entering Piscataway Creek despite assurances from the base that it halted the leak. The reporting also found that the base had not pinpointed the source of the leak, frustrating regulators and hampering cleanup efforts.
Approximately 32,000 gallons of jet fuel leaked across multiple dates and locations earlier this year, according to a letter lawmakers sent Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink in May. Of that amount, about 10,000 gallons were reportedly contained, while an estimated 22,000 gallons entered the environment, contaminating soil and Piscataway Creek.
The creek connects the base, located in Prince George’s County, Maryland, to the Potomac River near Fort Washington Park. Nearby Piscataway Park provides public access to the creek and river for fishing and recreation.
The Maryland Department of the Environment, which has enforcement authority under state environmental regulations, said it was not notified of the leak until March 23, when fuel odors and a sheen were observed near the creek’s headwaters, and the base did not report the full extent of the discharge until April 8.
The MDE then ordered the base to conduct an emergency soil investigation, install monitoring wells and remediate contaminated soil. The base’s delay in reporting the spill, despite its obligation to do so, prompted concerns and criticism from lawmakers and environmental advocates.
In their latest letter to Meink, sent Oct. 28, members of the Maryland congressional delegation criticized the cleanup efforts, saying “the Air Force has failed to fully contain the fuel spill” as demonstrated by the MDE’s water testing, calling it “unacceptable.”
“The Air Force must take immediate action to completely contain the spill and stop all sources of continued fuel discharge into the environment,” the lawmakers said, urging swift action to remediate contaminated soil and groundwater.
The letter was signed by nine of the delegation’s 10 members: U.S. Sens. Chris Van Hollen and Angela Alsobrooks and U.S. Reps. Steny Hoyer, Kweisi Mfume, Jamie Raskin, Glenn Ivey, Sarah Elfreth, April McClain Delaney and Johnny Olszewski, all Democrats. It warned that the spill threatened the health and well-being of people living along and recreating on Piscataway Creek.
The letter called the cleanup delay “especially concerning,” noting that the spill adds to pre-existing contamination in Piscataway Creek from other base activities, including legacy PFAS runoff. “Piscataway Creek is also part of a landscape that is sacred to the Piscataway people, and the waterway runs by important cultural and historic sites,” the letter said.
The lawmakers asked Meink to respond by Nov.12 with a plan for how Joint Base Andrews would stop further contamination of Piscataway Creek, address evidence of fuel escaping temporary containment berms and account for the estimated 22,000 gallons potentially released into the environment. They also sought a timeline for full cleanup, an update on the subsurface investigation and assurances that future leaks would be addressed promptly.
Responding to the questions about the legislators’ concerns over cleanup failures and the ongoing spill, a Joint Base Andrews spokesperson said heavy rain can carry “trace amounts” of previously spilled fuel from contaminated soil into Piscataway Creek. “This is not an active release from the fuel infrastructure,” the base maintained.
In written comments, the spokesperson said that containment, recovery and monitoring was continuing, with pressure testing expected to begin in the next few weeks and an updated subsurface investigation plan submitted to MDE. But the spokesperson provided no firm cleanup completion date, and added: “There is not yet a fixed completion date for all remediation measures.”
In separately emailed comments, an Air Force spokesperson said: “Our top priority is resolution and mitigation of the effects of this leak.” Responding to the lawmakers’ Nov. 12 deadline, the spokesperson said, “The Air Force will respond directly to Sen. Van Hollen’s office.”
In a May 6 letter to Meink, Congressional leaders raised concerns about the delayed disclosure of the spill’s full volume and inadequate initial containment measures. They asked for a briefing and written answers on the extent of contamination, cleanup plans and measures to prevent future leaks and keep regulators and the public informed.
Subsequently, the Air Force arranged a staff-level briefing for Van Hollen’s office in late September. But Congressional sources told Inside Climate News at the time that the senator was not satisfied with the responses the Air Force provided and his office will be requesting more information in the coming weeks.
The lawmakers are not alone in pressing the Trump administration for answers and demanding robust cleanup actions.
Also on Oct. 28, MDE Secretary Serena McIlwain upped the pressure by conveying her own concerns to JBA leadership.
It was troubling, she wrote, that despite seven months of back and forth between her staff and the base, “the source of the releases and the actions necessary to prevent further contamination remain unanswered.”

63c9dc02b17f.text: By — Larry Neumeister, Associated Press Larry Neumeister, Associated Press By — Ali Swenson, Associated Press Ali Swenson, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/judge-orders-3-taxpayer-funded-trump-administration-ads-to-be-pulled-from-tv-social-media Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Judge orders 3 taxpayer-funded Trump administration ads to be pulled from TV, social media Politics Oct 30, 2026 6:57 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — The federal government must pull three taxpayer-funded Trump administration ads that appear to have been made for political or propaganda purposes, including one touting the president's claim that every American will get $5,000 if Republicans keep control of Congress in the upcoming election, a judge ruled Friday. U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, in ordering the government to take down the advertisements entitled "$5,000 to Americans," "Every Democrat Voted Against No Tax on Tips," and "Cost of Socialism." She declined to pull several other ads. READ MORE: After taxpayer-funded ads glorifying Trump sparked backlash, he says his super PAC will pay instead She said the three ads must be taken off official government websites, including social media sites such as YouTube, Instagram and the like. Rochon also ordered the cancellation of any plans for the airing or distribution of the ads through authorized third parties, including by President Donald Trump's flagship super PAC, MAGA Inc. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Rochon was nominated to the court by then-President Joe Biden, a Democrat, and once served as a law clerk for Trump's sister, the late Maryanne Trump Barry, a longtime federal appeals court judge. Responding to the ruling, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said: "This Biden-appointed activist judge issued a lawless order to stop the administration from sharing patriotic videos." Rochon ruled during a hearing in which she considered expanding a temporary restraining order she issued two weeks ago, when she banned a series of ads that glorify Trump and echo his political messaging going into the midterms. The plaintiffs sought the removal of at least 13 ads, but Rochon only ordered that the three be pulled, at least for now. She noted that the Government Accountability Office has observed that there are instances when the president's office is entitled to inform the public of its policies, justify its policies and respond to attacks on its policies. Rochon said the plaintiffs were seeking to restrict the office in ways that were "broad and far reaching" and she found herself concluding that the government will ultimately prevail legally with regard to many of the ads. The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have made to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they don't try to help the public benefit from specific government programs, according to the plaintiffs. After Rochon issued the order, she noted that she was doing so on a Friday afternoon and that the government would have no excuse to delay taking them down immediately. A government lawyer acknowledged that he would be able to immediately notify relevant individuals responsible for taking down the ads. "Everyone is here. Everyone can hear my order. No one is at the theater," the judge quipped in a reference to excuses offered by government lawyers when her recent order, issued over a weekend, wasn't immediately obeyed. Rochon said irreparable harm could result to the plaintiffs if she didn't ban the ads while the court case proceeds, though she noted that she could reverse herself and restore the ads or ban additional ads after hearing more evidence in the coming weeks. "This court can neither postpone an election nor turn back the clock," Rochon said after concluding that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claims regarding the ads and would suffer harm if they were not taken down. "This temporary restraining order will stop the administration's wanton disregard for the law while the court hears the full case," said Bradley Girard, a lawyer with Democracy Forward. "Congress has made clear that partisan ads cannot be funded with taxpayer dollars, and we are proud to work with this coalition to earn today's result." In court papers, the coalition's lawyers wrote that Congress did not appropriate funds to the president's office "to run a PR shop to help the President's allies and attack his perceived ideological opponents." Assistant U.S. Attorney Jeffrey Oestericher wrote in response to the plaintiffs that there was nothing wrong with White House staff compiling advertisements to "inform the public about his policies and to rebut attacks on those policies and his Administration." Associated Press writer Michael R. Sisak contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.
