(AP) — A business jet carrying nine people nose-dived into a South Florida neighborhood Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes before crashing near a busy roadway. All passengers on board were killed, the nation's transportation secretary said. Video recorded by people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the aircraft plunged from the sky, before striking near the roadway and exploding. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as people milled about, expressing shock that it landed only feet from homes and only inches from passing vehicles. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site. READ MORE: California helicopter crash kills 2 people, leaves 2 hospitalized and 1 missing Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on X on Sunday that the Learjet 60 crashed in Palm Beach County at 12:50 p.m. and called it a "horrific tragedy." The Federal Aviation Administration is sending a team to support the National Transportation Safety Board's investigation into the cause, he said. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said the crash left a crater in the ground and spewed debris. There were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured or killed, he said. "It was a cataclysmic plane crash," DeSantis told reporters at the scene on Sunday. "It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road." Rain pounded the region on Sunday. A flood watch due to excessive rainfall was in effect through Monday afternoon, the National Weather Service said. The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Authorities did not immediately say what caused the jet to go down or who was on it. The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 11 kilometers) when pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation and requested to climb 2,000 feet (about 610 meters). Moments later, the plane entered a steep dive, first 10,000 feet per minute, then 20,000 feet per minute and up to 30,000 feet per minute, speeding the plane beyond its design limits, according to air traffic control recordings and flight tracking data. A pilot declared an emergency and issued distress calls. The plane banked sharply to the right before it crashed steeply into the ground. READ MORE: Firefighting helicopter crashes near Yosemite, killing both pilots Minutes before the crash, the pilot reported ice accumulating on the jet and turbulence that was jolting it by as much as 700 feet, according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net. "We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence," the pilot told controllers. But the situation rapidly deteriorated. After encountering precipitation and requesting to climb, the pilot declared an emergency as the aircraft began losing altitude at an alarming rate. "We're descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday - we're descending 10,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed. "We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed, before delivering a devastating acknowledgment of what was about to happen. "We're going to crash into the ground." Jim Reynolds, a spokesperson for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, said it was a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on the flight. Local authorities are evacuating about 600 people from a nearby mobile home community while federal officials investigate the crash. A rare humanitarian ceasefire in Ukraine's front-line Kherson region that allowed civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky has ended.
The localised ceasefire was due to end at 22:59 Ukrainian time (21:00 GMT) on Sunday. While the truce had held since it was implemented last week, fighting had continued elsewhere.
On Sunday evening, Ukraine's air alert system was apparently hacked, the country's air force said, warning of radiation over Kyiv - a reference to a possible nuclear attack.
The Air Force message read: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had struck energy infrastructure in four regions overnight on Saturday, leaving hundreds of thousands of homes without power. Some connections were restored on Sunday.
Another overnight strike killed two people, including a 13-year-old girl, in the Vinnytsia region, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine said.
Meanwhile, Ukraine hit a major missile fuel producer in Russia's Rostov region, which caused a fire and damaged four production facilities, Zelensky said.
In Ukraine, repair works to restore power continued throughout the day. Most customers in the Dnipropetrovsk region had their connections restored by early evening, but more than 60,000 were still without power, the governor said.
Because of regular attacks on energy infrastructure, emergency power cuts have been introduced across the country. Even in the capital Kyiv, electricity is cut off for most of the day, and water supplies are also disrupted.
Zelensky said in a social media post that the intensity of Russian strikes has been "extremely high" over the past week, adding that Russia was "trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic missile interceptors".
He added that "every day" Ukraine communicated its need for Patriot missiles - the only effective weapon for downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles - to the US, Europe and other partners. He thanked countries for their support so far and longer-term commitments, but called again for more immediate aid.
The limited pause in hostilities, which started on Tuesday, was brokered with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo.
It was originally confined to the city of Oleshky, which has been occupied by Russia since the first days of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and was expanded across the wider region of Kherson.
Oleshky had been trapped on one side by the Dnipro river and the other by Russian forces, with routes out mined and subject to drone attack.
Residents trapped there were suffering severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with many resorting to cooking garden weeds to survive.
The truce allowed for Oleskhy residents to evacuate if they wanted, and there were emotional scenes on Saturday of reunions between loved ones who hadn't seen eachother for years.
There are Ukrainian military positions just 5km (3.1 miles) from Oleshky, but evacuees had to travel through Russian-occupied territory to southern Russia, where they flew to Belarus, before finally being driven across Ukraine's northern border.
The oldest evacuee was 94 years old, while the youngest was one, according to Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman.

Chris Murphy is in the hospital after having a stroke, his office says Politics Nov 1, 2026 4:20 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Sen. Chris Murphy is in the hospital after having a stroke and is "awake and alert" as he receives treatment, the Connecticut Democrat's office said Sunday. Murphy's chief of staff, Allison Herwitt, said in a statement the 53-year-old senator "started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son's hockey game" on Saturday. Please check your inbox to confirm. "He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke," she said. "He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment. The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery." Murphy was elected to the House in 2006 and to the Senate in 2012. Several Republican senators, including Chuck Grassley of Iowa and Pete Ricketts of Nebraska, also offered prayers for Murphy. President Donald Trump said he was "really surprised" to learn about Murphy's stroke. "Nobody wants to have that," he said. Murphy has been traveling the country in support of House and Senate candidates as his party races for majority control. On Friday, he posted that he had been campaigning in his home state for Gov. Ned Lamont. Last week, Murphy posted from Minnesota campaigning with Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic nominee for Senate. The final sprint before Election Day capped Murphy's whirlwind trip to the Middle East at the start of October for meetings with several leaders, including Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. In early September, Murphy completed his annual "walk across Connecticut," covering about 70 miles over four days, talking with residents about their concerns along the way. "Thinking of my great friend & colleague, Chris Murphy," wrote Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., in a statement Sunday. e1aa62e17343.text: By — Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/israeli-officials-say-elections-wont-be-undermined-and-suspects-in-bribery-case-are-freed Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Israeli officials say elections will stand after Netanyahu claimed Arabs stole vote World Updated on Nov 1, 2026 4:54 PM EST — Published on Nov 1, 2026 2:57 PM EST TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's efforts to question last week's elections weakened Sunday as officials said the vote would not be undermined by the allegations and a court ordered suspects in one case released. In an image that indicated officials were on the same page, the head of Israel's elections committee was shown sitting between Israel's attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet intelligence service for a statement making clear that even if claims of foreign interference raised last week are substantiated, the vote would stand. Netanyahu's Likud party has said, without giving evidence, that Arab-led parties "stole" the elections in which Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority of seats in parliament. By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appears to be trying to block any potential alliance in the opposition with the Arab parties that could force him from office. WATCH: What Israel's election deadlock means for Netanyahu and the region Likud has cited a handful of cases, including the arrests of three political activists before polls opened on Oct. 27 with envelopes of cash, allegedly to bribe voters. Two days later, police arrested four more suspects. Police said the suspects were connected to the Islamist party Ra'am, which denied that it was involved. A judge on Sunday questioned or rejected police requests for further restrictions on the three suspects. Police later said one was released subject to unspecified "conditions" and another was ordered to remain on house arrest for eight days. The detention of the third suspect was extended for two days. Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra'am party, which won eight seats in the Knesset, denounced the arrests as undemocratic and "an attempt to influence the election results." Netanyahu suggests joining with Arab parties is treason Netanyahu saw his parliamentary bloc of allies drop to 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, down from a peak of 68 in the outgoing parliament. A bloc of parties led by his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, won 48 seats, while Arab-led parties, including Ra'am, won the remaining 19 seats. Together, those two blocs opposing Netanyahu have enough seats to form a new government, though it remains unclear whether they will agree to do so. The results are due to be officially certified this week, and President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday will begin meeting with each of the parties elected to parliament after that to see who they prefer to be the next prime minister. READ MORE: Israel's election results are in. Here's what could happen next Following those consultations, he will choose the candidate — most likely Netanyahu or Eisenkot — who he believes has the best chance of forming a coalition government. That would set the stage for weeks of negotiations. If they are unsuccessful, Herzog could ask another candidate to try. Otherwise, the country would be plunged into a new election early next year. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for Eisenkot to join with Arab parties. Some Israelis agree. A few dozen people protested outside Eisenkot's home on Sunday night. "We have a tiny country, a very tiny Jewish country. We want to keep it as a Jewish country," said one protester, Shoshana Idasis. Other, larger rallies in recent days have called for a Jewish-Arab coalition. Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of trying to delegitimize the vote Likud also has alleged foreign interference in the vote. The Shin Bet security service, at the request of Israel's election commission, has opened an investigation. But the head of the elections committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said that "our position is that even if the suspicions are substantiated, this would not undermine the integrity of the electoral process or the election results as a whole." Likud quickly issued a statement asking how the committee chief can acknowledge there are serious allegations while saying there will be no effect on the final outcome. Eisenkot on Sunday accused Netanyahu of launching an "orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results" by insinuating that Qatar had supported opposition parties to unseat Netanyahu. Eisenkot said that Shin Bet briefed him on the investigation into foreign interference. WATCH: Retired Israeli general on what the election results tell us Qatar has denied funding any activities meant to influence the election's outcome. Many Israelis see the Gulf Arab country as a patron of Hamas, and allegations of its influence have roiled Israeli politics in other cases, including one in which close aides of Netanyahu allegedly accepted money from Qatar while working for the prime minister's office. Netanyahu's opponents have accused him of using scare tactics and trying to create a narrative to further discriminate against Arab-led parties and Israel's Arab citizens, who make up 20% of the population. Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Joint List of Arab parties, which won 11 seats, noted last week that more than half the content published by Likud and Netanyahu on election day was directed against Arab voters as a tactic to encourage right-wing Israelis to vote. "In moments of crisis, he reverts to his familiar tactic: racist incitement and the delegitimization of the Arab public," he said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. The Pentagon’s IT agency wants to bridge network gaps in the Pacific
“The old ways of connecting with partners are simply no longer sufficient,” says INDOPACOM deputy commander.
HONOLULU—Lags in communication could undermine even the most advanced technology available, the deputy chief of Indo-Pacific Command warned Thursday.
“If we field cutting-edge compute and advanced software applications, but retain rigid, multi-layered bureaucracies requiring hours to authorize time-sensitive engagements, then we've negated our technological overmatch,” Lt. Gen. George Rowell, deputy commander of INDOPACOM, told attendees at TechNet Indo-Pacific. “No competitor on Earth can match America's network of capable allies and partners. That network is our greatest advantage. It is our strategic center of gravity. But the old ways of connecting with partners are simply no longer sufficient.”
Upgrading military networks in the Pacific so the U.S. can quickly share battle details with allies has been a key priority in recent years. The command recently deployed the Pacific mission partner network, a unified version of a series of bespoke networks for individual allied or partner nations in the region. Throughout the year, the command has tested the network in military exercises, where it has shown progress and allowed better coordination, with fewer devices to toggle between.
Still, there are still gaps that need to be addressed to improve communications with allies and partners.
“We're in the middle of a transition right now,” said Col. Michael Hlad, who leads the Defense Information Systems Agency’s regional field command in the Pacific. “We are migrating to a data-centric environment, helping our partners understand what does it mean to be zero trust? What are the key items that we need to agree on, let's say, from an identity standpoint, a data standardization standpoint?”
While some nations are more technologically aligned, such as the Five Eye partners, the plan is to build a data-sharing environment malleable enough to bring in other nations as well.
“I don't know what the coalition of the future necessarily looks like,” Hlad said. “So how are we, DISA, building a coalition environment that is agile and common enough that we can bring in those partners instead of making it brittle…where it's just bilateral or just multilateral? We've got to bring that agility to [Indo-Pacific Command] as well as our partners, so they're able to integrate for an [humanitarian assistance and disaster relief] scenario as well as a high-conflict scenario of the future.”
Getting to that common digital ground means agreeing on what tools and methods to use.
There must be “clear standardization of what that common architecture looks like,” Hlad said. “This only works if we get the data right. And we are still siloed.”
In addition to improving communication with allies and partners, one of DISA Pacific's top priorities is to improve data transfer, speed, and security in the region.
“How do we have better transport resiliency in the Pacific so that we can make sure that the critical feeds and data are where we need them?…How do we deliver those for the warfighters in the Pacific so the data is closer to the operational need?” Hlad said.
The field command recently unveiled the Regional Network Operations Security Center Pacific—which aims to increase network support for INDOPACOM’s headquarters.
“That's an enhanced [network operations center]. That's an enhanced [security operations center]. That's a regional service support desk, and that's some data fusion capabilities that were not resident in this theater to synchronize,” Hlad said.
The idea is for the center to respond to connectivity challenges, including when undersea cables cut out and during electromagnetic spectrum or application disruptions.
The center has yielded a 20 percent personnel increase to assist in solving those connectivity problems, Hlad said.

In the last weekend before the pivotal midterm elections, Donald Trump has made a final pitch to voters in hopes of keeping Republicans in control of the US Congress.
Trump held rallies in Florida, Iowa and Kansas - states he won in past elections - in a sign of Republicans' defensive stance in Tuesday's elections.
Facing voter frustration over rising prices, particularly fuel, Trump sought to tamp down such concerns and shift focus on attacking Democrats, saying they would "bankrupt" families if elected.
Polls suggest that Democrats have a good chance at winning at least partial control of Congress, which would act as a check on Trump's power and upend the last two years of his presidency.
Trump has been campaigning non-stop across the country ahead of the election - even in areas that were once thought to be safe Republican strongholds.
Throughout the weekend, Trump made the case for his party at rallies in Kansas, Florida and Iowa as well as at tele-rallies for candidates in states including Michigan, Ohio and Pennsylvania.
In previous years, Trump easily won Florida, Iowa and Kansas - once considered reliably Republican states - but the president's visits there in the final days of his election drive highlighted just how competitive these states have become in determining control of Congress.
Trump told supporters he had transformed the country, saying Democrats had left the US in a "dark age" but under his command, "we quickly turned it into the golden age of America".
Trump is facing a backlash over the cost of living. Prices have gone up, particularly for fuel, groceries and health care, since the war in Iran began over eight months ago. At these rallies, Trump appeared to have two aims: to change the subject from those issues and use fear to turn out the Republican vote.
At rallies in Florida and Iowa, he highlighted his policies on trade and immigration and said if Democrats were given power, they would "open the border", "bankrupt your family", "take away your guns" and "mutilate your children". He played video montages of Democrats criticising ICE and supporting transgender rights.
In the room at the rallies, supporters cheered, but there has also been disquiet among some Republicans over Trump's appeal with more moderate voters.
Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries said this weekend that he was "very confident" his party was on course to win control of the House of Representatives, as senior Democrats including former President Barack Obama made final appeals to voters.
A forecasting tool from Harvard University that analyses and compiles multiple polls and historical data suggests that Democrats have a 96% chance of taking the House and a 76% chance of taking the Senate.
A national poll from NBC News posted this weekend suggests that registered voters prefer a Democrat-controlled Congress by a 7-point margin, leading Republicans 52% to 45%.
But along with the last-push campaign stops, this weekend featured a dramatic turn in the Senate race in Michigan - a tightly contested seat currently held by Democrats.
Haley Stevens, a sitting congresswoman who lost the Democratic Senate nomination to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday.
The move led to widespread condemnation from fellow Democrats and praise from Republicans, including Trump who called her "very brave".
In Alaska, home to another crucial Senate race, a judge on Sunday dismissed an attempt by the Trump administration to delay certifying election results if the Republican incumbent candidate loses due to two candidates appearing on the ballot with the same name.
In the lead up to the election, Trump and his administration have repeatedly cast doubt on both the credibility and security of the vote, despite evidence showing voter fraud is rare. The justice department has launched investigations or demanded votes be set aside in multiple US states.
The stakes are high for Trump, as midterm election results are seen as a measure of how satisfied Americans are with a president's performance.
In most midterm elections, the party that holds the White House typically loses seats in Congress to the opposing party - meaning Trump's Republican party has the most to lose.
Republicans, who currently hold a slim majority in both the House of Representatives and Senate, don't want to relinquish their party's majority in Congress, as losing any seats would hinder their ability to pass laws and shape policies.
Democrats, however, are keen to gain control from Republicans. Holding a majority would enable them to challenge Trump's agenda, give them investigative powers over his administration, and could also help them showcase their vision for America ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
For lawmakers, it's all about gaining or maintaining power and control, but it's Americans who will feel the impacts of their policies.
Who gets elected at the city, state, and federal level affects many aspects of voters' everyday lives, including the cost of gas, rising inflation and grocery prices, healthcare and abortion access, income and property taxes, and immigration.

The News
When Tucker Carlson co-founded the Daily Caller in 2010, it was to be the Republican Partyâs answer to The New York Times.
A few identity crises later, the publication has followed Carlson into a hard turn against Donald Trumpâs war in Iran, and against Israel â choices that have injected into the publication the digital energy of the new online right, and cost it the support of some of its backers.
âIâve had some of the most aggressive donor pressure over this â the single most aggressive donor pressure over this, of anything Iâve seen in journalism in 20 years,â Daily Caller publisher Neil Patel told Semafor. He wouldnât detail the cost of lost financial support to the Caller, which includes both a for-profit firm and the nonprofit Daily Caller News Foundation, but acknowledged that there had been costs.
The Caller has been a pillar of Washingtonâs conservative media scene since its launch, an important voice in internecine Republican conflicts and a pipeline of journalistic talent whose alumni include employees of both conservative and mainstream outlets.
Now itâs at the vanguard of a Republican civil war that Carlson has helped unleash.
âThe Iran war is a huge turning point for the conservative movement,â Editor-in-Chief Amber Duke told Semafor on Friday.
Nowhere has that shift been clearer than in the outletâs X feed since the United States went to war with Iran in February. The organization has taken to tweeting the price of diesel every day, emphasizing the warâs cost on drivers, and posts screenshots of Trumpâs posts about the war in Iran, adding spicy commentary.
âWhat if instead of âbanningâ a term, we stopped spending endless amounts of money on foreign wars?â the outlet wrote of Trumpâs command that AI be referred to as âsuper intelligence.â
The Daily Caller has similarly gone after Israel, questioning its decisions in the Middle East. It has blasted Benjamin Netanyahu and his policies, and repeatedly highlighted Israeli settler violence, particularly against children. The criticism has gotten the attention of pro-Israel hawks, who have accused the publication of antisemitism and crudely implied it is pro-Islamic propaganda.
âDaily Caller means Al Jazeera in Arabic,â Fox News host and commentator Mark Levin wrote.
The fissures at the Caller âÂ and in the broader conservative movement âÂ began widening when the activist Charlie Kirk was assassinated last September, according to most of the nine current and former Caller employees who I spoke to over the last week. The movement that had united around Donald Trump devolved into a frenzy of unfounded conspiracy theories, many blaming Israel for Kirkâs death.
The podcaster Candace Owens drove those theories, infuriating her former employer, Daily Wire founder Ben Shapiro. Shapiro laid into Owens for perpetuating what he said were antisemitic conspiracy theories, attacked podcaster Megyn Kelly for not condemning Owens, and criticized Carlson for what he described as a cozy interview with self-proclaimed white nationalist Nick Fuentes.
The Daily Caller, long a younger and slightly edgier outlet than other right-leaning publications like the Washington Examiner, The National Review, or even Breitbart, followed that online energy. Some on staff noted that former editor Dylan Housman left the publication the Friday before the Iran war started, and the tone shifted significantly following his departure. Duke, a former Caller staffer, replaced him and encouraged the publication to adopt an aggressive posture on social media.
Employees also said they sensed that Patel seemed to side with Carlson, Patelâs longtime friend and business partner. While Carlson has long been unaffiliated with the outlet, Patel retains business connections with Carlson, while Carlsonâs brother Buckley Carlson has served on the Daily Caller nonprofitâs board.
Patel told Semafor he is not involved in day-to-day operations at the Caller, on which he defers to Duke and others, and stressed that Carlsonâs stances had no bearing on the outlet.
Still, he said he encouraged the Callerâs leaders to remain independent and reflect the publicationâs values.
That reality for average Americans, he said, has turned against Trump.
âThings just arenât going that well today. I think if youâre at all looking at this objectively, itâs hard to make the case that things are going great in a lot of areas. And so if our coverage has changed, I think itâs changed just to reflect that,â he said.
Right vs. Right

In October, Semafor reported that the Daily Caller tweeted a cartoon of Bill Gates and the devil posing with disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein wearing an Israeli flag Speedo. The post was quickly deleted, but not before it caught the attention of Republicans who have grown increasingly concerned about the Callerâs anti-Israel turn. The publication told Semafor that while the post didnât meet the publicationâs standards, it hadnât been posted with any âmalicious intent.â
Other Caller alumni suggested to Semafor that the recent pivot could threaten what in the last decade has become an important talent pipeline and incubator for the right. The Daily Caller has brought up some of the most prominent young political media figures in America, some of whom have left the conservative media sphere (like CNNâs Kaitlan Collins and Semaforâs Shelby Talcott), and others who have built major franchises in independent media (like Breaking Pointsâ Saagar Enjeti) or moved into positions within the Republican Party apparatus.
The previous generationâs crowd is clearly uneasy with the new crop.

The News
On Oct. 10, an unhappy billionaire, Amy Griffin, confronted a former Today host, Billy Bush, at a celebrity wedding on the Hawaiian island of Lanai. Guests included Demi Moore and Tobey Maguire. It was the sort of thing that delights the entertainment media, even if you wonât often read about it in this column.
But this meltdown didnât break on Vanity Fair or TMZ. Instead, New York and LA society discreetly tuned in to the Instagrammer known as KatyinKC, who cited âmultipleâ sources at the wedding.
When I wrote about Griffin, the wife of a hedge-funder and author of a bestselling memoir, last week, I repeatedly heard that the wealthy and powerful figures in her social world are obsessed with KatyinKC. Her name is Katy Hoffman, and she is a 33-year-old registered dietitian and mother of two toddlers who works from the sofa in her comfortable Midwestern home.
Over the course of this year, Hoffman has become the chief inquisitor of Griffinâs story of abuse during a superficially perfect childhood in Amarillo, Texas. Hoffman has unmasked pseudonymous characters from her book, discovered key audio files, and given a hard-edged voice to the skepticism about Griffinâs account first raised by The New York Times.
Hoffmanâs Instagram account is the thing âwomen in the ballrooms and the Upper East Side and the Palisades and Brentwood are listening to,Â but not following,â said Bush, who was fired from Today in 2016 for a 2005 hot mic exchange with Donald Trump on Access Hollywood, and who now hosts the podcast Hot Mics with Billy Bush.
Social convention dictates that you not be caught liking Hoffmanâs posts or following her yourself. But she is âthe internet version of Nancy Grace,â Jolie Hunt, the CEO of a New York marketing and communications consultancy, told me.
Hoffmanâs videos across TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram offer regular glimpses of her own life. Sometimes she dances. Once she defended a local pizza joint from another influencerâs criticism. Her home is on display, too, a well-kept place with a wood-paneled den youâd immediately rip out in the Hamptons. She doesnât, one person I spoke to noted, seem like the sort of person who would be found on Lanai.
I called up Hoffman Friday to ask how sheâd become part of a new generation of social media sleuths, why she was so focused on Griffin, and, of course, her decor.
Hoffman got on the video call Friday wearing a T-shirt featuring the lovers in the TV show Heated Rivalry. She had just dyed her blond hair red. She grew up in the well-off suburbs of Des Moines âÂ her family loves to travel and sheâs been all over the world, if not Hawaii. She attended Iowa State, where she put her energy into her sorority and personal training (and certainly not journalism). She moved to Kansas City to start her career counseling people with eating disorders, but also developed a set of hobbies that, along with fishing and hunting, includes poking around public records.
âIâm just a nosy lady,â she told me. Sheâd be the one to tell her friends that the neighbor down the street had a lien on his house. She recalled being in a nutrition office at a local hospital where colleagues were talking about local radio personalitiesâ messy public divorce, and she looked up the court documents. She also closely followed the messy drama between the actors Blake Lively and Justin Baldoni; like many on social media, she grew skeptical of Livelyâs well-publicized claims and was persuaded by Baldoniâs responses. She posted to a tiny audience about them, and was briefly featured in an Atlantic article last April that asked: Who Reads Entire Lawsuits for Fun?
But Hoffman had long harbored this generationâs great American dream â to be a âcontent creator.â She had experimented with posting recipes and talking about her professional expertise, nutrition. One TikTok about Ariana Grande has 7.2 million views.
But she also edged into original reporting. When a process server in the Lively-Baldoni case was arrested trying to get into Kansas City Chiefs star Travis Kelceâs property to reach his wife, Taylor Swift, Hoffman drove to the nearby police station to get court records, posted them online, and watched the news spread. She became one of a pack of traveling social media analysts and partisans, attending hearings in New York in January and April.
The Griffin case, however, has been Hoffmanâs breakout moment, and it has thrust her a little closer to the world of professional journalism than she expected.
âIt wasnât until this case that Iâve really figured out being an investigative journalist a bit without any of the training or whatever,â she said, adding that she wasnât sure how to feel when she noticed New York Times and Wall Street Journal reporters sign up for the Patreon where she distributes the court documents sheâs turned up. She said she felt âintimidatedâ by the professional journalists who have started calling her up to swap notes.
Benâs view
Hoffman, who sometimes works from a small swivel chair in her childrenâs room, has followed a path from social video into the center of the swirling news cycles of true crime and celebrity. Her rise has echoes of podcaster Ashley Flowers and blogger Jessica Red Krauss â media outsiders who tapped into deep veins of public interest. But sheâs also an obsessive researcher whose focus and work ethic remind me a bit of CNNâs Andrew Kaczynski, were his focus celebrities rather than politics.
She has gone to elaborate lengths to follow hints in Griffinâs book through high school yearbooks and long-forgotten high school sporting events. Hoffman also noticed a link in a legal filing to a redacted audio recording of Griffinâs 2021 call to the Amarillo police department and posted it; later, she posted the unredacted audio, but wouldnât tell me how sheâd obtained that.
In other ways, she is pure social media. In one recent short video, Hoffman dances to a pop song, Nina Noxâs Good Without You, and closes by giving a middle finger to

13ef37218747.text: Some House Democrats want Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) expelled from their caucus after she crossed party lines to endorse Republican Mike Rogers for Senate on Sunday. Why it matters: It would be an extraordinary step that reflects the deep internal resentment towards Stevens within her own party. "I hope she doesn't return to work on Tuesday," Rep. Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.) told Axios, saying Stevens should be removed from the caucus. "Agreed," Rep. Marc Veasey (D-Texas) told Axios, arguing the endorsement "doesn't accomplish anything except hurt[ing] Haley" and that "she got bad advice." "I'd support that," Rep. Emily Randall (D-Wash.) said of removing Stevens from the caucus. Driving the news: Stevens infuriated colleagues on Sunday by endorsing Rogers over Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Stevens in the Senate primary in August. Stevens, a pro-Israel moderate, had been urging the more left-leaning El-Sayed to more forcefully denounce a super PAC ad partially blaming U.S. aid to Israel for rising prices. Stevens said the ad claimed "Jews are responsible for America's economic woes." El-Sayed pushed back in a statement saying Stevens "seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago." Stevens attended church with Rogers on Sunday and released a video to social media endorsing him. The two also held a joint press conference. What we're hearing: There has been private discussion about moving to oust Stevens, a senior House Democrat said, telling Axios, "That's what people want." Stevens was also removed from several House Democratic text chains, the senior lawmaker said. A second House Democrat told Axios: "I've heard people invoking the rule about not endorsing against Democrats." "Endorsing a Republican in a tipping point state is ridiculous, especially from a Democrat ... She should be removed from our caucus altogether," a third House Democrat said. Yes, but: Not everyone is on board with the idea — even those frustrated at Stevens. The senior House Democrat told Axios that, at the very least, "we need to wait and have the discussion after Tuesday." A fourth House Democrat said it's "too bad she chose to throw her career in Congress away so easily" but that the caucus "might still need her vote in the final two months before she's gone." Several lawmakers noted that Stevens is retiring anyway and that if El-Sayed wins, the point likely becomes moot. Stevens did not immediately respond to a text requesting comment on this story. The bottom line: "[I] am not letting it distract me from the work between now and Tuesday at 8pm," Randall told Axios.

Ukraine's air raid alert app was apparently hacked on Sunday and for a short time said the capital Kyiv was subject to a radiation threat, the Ukrainian Air Force has said.
The alert on Telegram read: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."
The Ukrainian Central Intelligence Agency said there had been a failure in the app, and urged people to use other sources of information to clarify the situation on the threat of air strikes.
A few hours later Russian authorities said its app was hacked. A Ukrainian espionage group claimed fake warnings of nuclear strikes inside Russia had been sent to users.
Russia has the world's biggest nuclear arsenal, and President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly suggested an openness to using all weapons at Russia's disposal.
The alerts, in Ukrainian, started at approximately 22:47 (20:47 GMT), with red-level air raids apparently issued nationwide. Additional warnings were issued in Kyiv, with the first reading: "Radiation threat. Radiation threat declared in Kyiv."
The next message, written in Russian, came at 22:48, which read: "Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don't worry, it's Oreshnik flying".
A third alert, at 22:49, again in Ukrainian, said "Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 22:49, a fourth alert stated there was a "Street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 23:53 a series of all clear messages were then delivered to users' phones, which were connected to each of the previous Kyiv alerts, individually declaring each threat clear.
In a separate post on Telegram, the Ukrainian Central Intelligence Agency said that due to the Air Alert application, the Radiation Hazard signal was played on loudspeaker devices in the Lviv region, and added there was no threat of radiation hazard.
If the alert app is not working, Ukraine's Centre for Countering Disinformation advises the public to turn on notifications on their smartphones, pay attention to sirens, and to only read official sources
Several leaders of other regions also posted on Telegram that the app had apparently been hacked and there was no local threat.
"Everything is calm in the region for now," said Svitlana Onyshchuk, the governor of the Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast. The app had reported a red-level air raid alert for the oblast in Ukraine's east, between 22:50 and 23:57.
The Vinnytsia regional head, Natalya Zabolotna, said there had been a cyber-attack on the Air Alert app and posted a warning on Telegram not to click on the link in the message, which could be a phishing attempt.
The Air Alert app is supported by the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine, and informs users instantly about the beginning and end of defence alerts. The ministry had earlier said the app was temporarily disabled for maintenance after it had "apparently been compromised". It urged residents to turn on their smartphones' emergency notifications so they could receive state-issued distress signals.
A few hours after the false alerts in Ukraine, Russia's ministry of emergency situations said its app had been subjected to "a massive cyberattack" which sent "fake information to the public".
No further details were given by the ministry or state media.
Ukrainian news outlet, UNN, reported the hack sent fake alerts of a nuclear threat inside Russia.
Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian held territory, said on its Telegram page that the app had been hacked, accompanied with laughing emojis.
A screenshot of a purported emergency alert published by Atesh, which has not been verified by the BBC, told users to "urgently" stock up on provisions for three weeks and take cover in basements. It also used obscene language. Atesh has been contacted for comment.
The alerts occurred just minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in Ukraine's front-line Kherson region, which was implemented last Tuesday and officially ended at 23:00 Sunday.
Fighting had continued elsewhere while the Kherson ceasefire was in place, to allow civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The News
Democratic party leaders have found themselves unable to stave off an embarrassing schism in Michiganâs must-win Senate race, a crisis that may offer a glimpse of internal battles to come.
Days of frantic shuttle diplomacy and attempts to organize a joint appearance by erstwhile Senate primary rivals Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens culminated in Stevensâ surprise Sunday endorsement of Republican nominee Mike Rogers.
Stevens appeared with Rogers at a Black church in Detroit less than 24 hours after vowing to colleagues that she would back El-Sayed, winning praise from President Donald Trump and calls for her eviction from the House Democratic Caucus. But perhaps the most stunning aspect of the crackup was how hard senior Democrats had worked to avoid it.
Party leaders like Reps. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., and Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., were pushing hard to get El-Sayed and Stevens on the same page for a show of unity going into Tuesdayâs critical elections. Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., said on national TV hours before Stevensâ defection that she had personally assured him on Saturday night sheâd be backing El-Sayed.
Raskin told Semafor in an interview Sunday: âI was blindsided, and I feel dumbfounded by the whole thing.â
While the Senate race remains very close, itâs not clear how much Stevensâ turnabout will affect the final balloting. She has, however, laid bare deep divides within the party â principally over Israel and the establishmentâs relationships with the left wing.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffriesâ statement backing El-Sayed after the flap did not mention Stevens, a member of his caucus, by name. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who had initially favored her as a better general election candidate than El-Sayed, called her endorsement of Rogers a âdespicable betrayal.â
Many in the party believe leaders were powerless over Stevens: âI certainly donât think itâs somebody elseâs fault, other than Haley Stevens,â said a Michigan Democratic operative.
Yet Michigan, where El-Sayed was struggling to win over some Jewish and Black voters even before this week, is now set among the first-in-the-nation Democratic nominating states. And the partyâs inability to come together during the final week of the election is likely to haunt it well into the 2028 primary.
what happened
Stevens kept her allies and staff in the dark through the whole process as she privately insisted she would keep backing Democrats, including El-Sayed.
As she and El-Sayed squabbled publicly over the last week, a few of her staff reached out to her discouraging her from endorsing Rogers, according to a source whoâd worked on her race. Stevensâ response, according to the source: âOmg why would you think I would do that?!!â
By Sunday, many of her staff had resigned, slamming her Rogers endorsement.
âShe lied to the people that she says she respects,â said the Michigan Democratic operative.
El-Sayed, who had implored Stevens not to campaign with him last week, brushed aside the news. âNone of this matters,â he told reporters in Detroit.
Michigan party chair Curtis Hertel Jr. said Sunday on X Stevens was expelled from the state party. Meanwhile, national party leaders across the board were united in saying they supported El-Sayed.
what happens next
Stevens faces rough waters ahead. She appears to have violated House Democratic caucus rules banning campaign activity for non-Democrats, and some in the caucus want to punish her. Itâs not immediately clear whether Jeffries and Stevens have talked.
The Stevens-El-Sayed crackup had been building in the months since she lost to him in the primary. Stevens and other Michigan Democrats kept their distance from El-Sayed over his association with controversial streamer Hasan Piker and his positions on Israel.
The feud accelerated over the closing weeks of the campaign when Cenk Uygurâs Rebellion PAC began running the anti-Israel ad that would eventually convince Stevens to endorse Rogers. Now, Uygur says he never imagined that outcome when he aired it.âIt wound up creating the perfect storm because it caused two weather fronts to collide,â Uygur told Semafor. âThe establishment hated it with a passion and the internet loved it with equal passion. Thatâs what caused this explosion.â
Nicholas and Davidâs view
Democrats are closing their campaigns this cycle with fairly unified, populist messaging about âaffordabilityâ and âcorruptionâ that helps the super-rich stay wealthy. Underneath that messaging is a feud between the partyâs left flank and centrist arm thatâs bound to erupt after Tuesdayâs results.
If El-Sayed loses, there will be a fight over blame between Democrats who spent tens of millions of dollars to support him and progressives whoâll argue that the party establishment canât be trusted when leftist candidates win a nomination. This is in the air already, given Andrew Cuomoâs decision to run a third party campaign after losing the Democratic primary to democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani.
But if El-Sayed wins, his faction of the party will be able to say he did it in spite of the opposition of pro-Israel Democrats. That will weaken pro-Israel Democratsâ ability to say, as AIPAC does, that their agenda is âgood policy and good politics.â Thatâs in the air too, with Democrats already gearing up to challenge Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., whoâs stopped campaigning for other Democrats after feuding with pro-Palestine activists.

The Democratic Party has high expectations as it heads into these pivotal US midterm elections.
A historically unpopular Republican president, an American public unhappy with the rising costs of food and bills, and months of favourable polls point to a good night for them on Tuesday.
Democratic candidates lead in well over the 218 seats needed to flip control of the lower chamber of Congress, the House of Representatives, the polls suggest. And they are tied or narrowly ahead in the key Senate races.
A recent New York Times poll had the Senate race in South Carolina, a state Donald Trump won by 18 percentage points in 2024, as a tie. Recent CNN surveys put the Democrats ahead in Texas, Kansas and Maine.
But are the polls accurate?
Recent US political history is littered with examples where public opinion polls, even ones just days before an election, were off the mark. Trump outperformed predictions on his way to White House victories in 2016 and 2024. His narrow defeat in 2020 came after most surveys indicated a more comfortable win for Democrat Joe Biden.
Earlier this year, polls suggested Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was poised for a double-digit win in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. Instead it was 1%. In Wisconsin's Democratic primary for governor, the candidate that had a polling lead that approached 20 points lost by a fraction of a percent.
According to Clifford Young, president of Ipsos Public Affairs, which conducts political and market research surveys, polling has become difficult in recent years because it's harder to reach Americans as they abandon their land lines and screen their calls. And many of those who pollsters do contact have become less willing to participate.
"Conservatives, especially those on the far right, are much more anti-establishment by nature," Young says. "And they don't participate in anything. They hate the system. That's the challenge."
If Republican voters are being undercounted in a systematic way, and polling companies don't take that into consideration when constructing their voting models, it could skew their data towards the Democrats.
That's one of the reasons why it has become trickier for pollsters to predict what the electorate will look like.
One explanation for why Trump overperformed in previous presidential elections is that his supporters â many of whom were not regular voters â flocked to the polls in higher-than-expected numbers.
That unpredictability is one of the main contributing factors to those notable recent polling misses, even if the margins in most reputable polls were only off by a few percentage points.
In a close race, those few points can make the difference between victory and defeat for a candidate. And this year, many of the key Senate races are within those narrow margins.
In recent years, midterm general election polls have proven to be more accurate, in part because Trump - and his unique ability to draw disaffected Americans to the polls - was not on the ballot.
In 2022, they suggested Democrats would defy conventional expectations and avoid an electoral wipe-out despite Biden's low approval numbers.
While the party lost control of the House of Representatives, the margins were slim and Democrats maintained control of the US Senate.
While this year's primary results did provide bigger surprises, Young says that nominating contests have historically been volatile, with voters more likely to make up their minds at the last minute. It shouldn't be seen as an indication that the current crop of general election polls are off the mark.
It's common for the party of the president to have a bad night in the midterms.
One of the most notable examples in recent years came in 2010 when Republicans flipped more than 60 House seats and made gains in the Senate.
It came off the back of an economy struggling to recover from the financial crash and conservative fears over President Barack Obama's healthcare reforms. A defeat had been predicted by the polls but not quite on that scale.
The roles are reversed this time, with the Democrats in opposition and the economy on the minds of voters. But there are a number of reasons why Democrats may not have as good a night as history might suggest or as some might expect, given Trump's low approval rating.
Firstly, much of the territory in play in this election Trump conquered with ease in the presidential election just two years ago. It's like a home game for Republicans.
Then there have been changes to House election boundaries over the years that have meant fewer seats switch between parties.
Thirdly, there are fewer swing voters due to the deeper polarisation of the country. Some experts describe the electorate as calcified.
There's also the cash advantage Republicans have enjoyed which has given them hundreds of millions of dollars to spend on attack ads in the final weeks.
Polling models try to capture shifting fundamentals. And a well-designed poll is built to anticipate issues that may make it less than reliable.
Individual polls do have a built-in margin of error â a statistical level of uncertainty based on the sampling size compared to the population as a whole. Taken as an aggregate, polling averages and not individual surveys can provide a more accurate prediction.
At the moment, even the kind of polling lean we saw in recent presidential elections would suggest Democrats are likely to have a good night on 3 November. And polling inaccuracies can go both ways. In last year's state and special elections, Democrats outperformed most surveys as it was their voters who turned out in unexpectedly larger numbers.
The sight of Trump holding rallies in the final days of the campaign in states he won comfortably in 2024 will have lifted Democrats' hopes that Republican internal polling has conservative candidates in trouble.
There's always the chance that voters change their minds right up until election day, however.
Sometimes there are late shifts that can alter the d

- Published
Prosecutors in France have launched an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at police during unrest, French media reported.
An image of a police officer with his leg on fire during a clash with protesters in Paris on Saturday has prompted outrage and follows weeks of street protests in France that have also seen demonstrators injured.
The officer, who suffered burns to his ankle and minor injures to his hand, told French newspaper Le Figaro it was a "particularly sophisticated" incendiary device.
Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said throwing a molotov cocktail at a police line was "what I call a murder attempt", adding officers were working to find the perpetrators.
Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated across France in largely peaceful protests on Saturday, the latest in a series of youth-led protests that began in late September demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially schools.
Following previous clashes and looting, thousands of police officers were deployed across the country over the weekend, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 770 arrests on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.
But police said no one had been arrested for the attack caught on camera that set a police officer on fire, AFP reported.
The officer - part of the National Gendarmerie, a national law enforcement force that is technically part of the military but under the control of the interior ministry - said his unit "suddenly found ourselves facing several hundred hostile, well equipped adversaries".
Speaking to French newspaper Le Figaro, he said police were yet to identify the liquid used but that the incendiary device "had a far greater burning capacity than a standard Molotov cocktail".
"We faced hostile individuals who are not protesters," he said. "These adversaries are there with the intent to harm those who represent the state."
Fourteen other officers sustained wounds ranging from minor to serious, he said, adding some were struck by paving stones. The unit was supposed to be on leave but had been urgently recalled to police the weekend protests, he said.
French protest organisers, the Gilets Jaunes, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".
France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off, but French newspaper Le Monde has reported that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.
Protests also took place in Germany and Italy over the weekend, as mainly youth-led protests continue across parts of Europe, with varying demands but broadly linked to a focus on cost-of-living issues and public services.

A judge has tossed a lawsuit by the Trump administration that sought to delay certifying results in Alaska's crucial Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses.
The suit by the US Department of Justice argued that having two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the ballot could cause "voter confusion" and take support from incumbent Republican Dan S Sullivan.
The judge ruled that the federal government doesn't have authority to force Alaska to segregate and investigate any ballots in the three-way race between Sullivan, Daniel J Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola.
The Alaska Senate contest is considered one the closest in the Tuesday midterms, where control of Congress will be up for grabs.
"The United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy," US District Judge Sharon Gleason wrote in the ruling.
Alaska voters have the right to a secret ballot, she wrote, adding that regardless, such a move by the justice department would be too late as it is only days before the midterm election. Many voters have already cast their ballots in early voting and postal voting.
After the ruling, the justice department said it would file to appeal. It said in a statement that the court dismissed the federal case on "procedural grounds but did not dispute the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters".
"Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes," the statement continued.
Asked about the lawsuit last month, President Donald Trump said he had directed the justice department to file it.
"All of a sudden he decides to run for the Senate, and his name is Dan Sullivan. One is Daniel S., one is Daniel J. The Daniel J. is the fake," Trump told reporters.
Daniel J Sullivan, the little-known candidate running with no party affiliation, had previously told The New York Times he has voted both Democrat and Republican in the past.
Senator Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican, and his allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.
Then last week, controversy erupted when The New York Times reported that Democrats on Peltola's team worked with people who tried to recruit spoiler candidates in the Senate race.
Peltola has denied she knowing anything about an alleged "scheme" that led to the two Dan Sullivans standing in the race.
The Alaska race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest in the upcoming US midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress for the last two years of Trump's presidency.

266f64ef4558.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/freezers-at-supermarkets-in-several-european-countries-hit-by-apparent-cyberattacks-ruining-food Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Freezers at supermarkets in several European countries hit by apparent cyberattacks, ruining food World Nov 2, 2026 10:31 AM EST STOCKHOLM (AP) — Supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg and Estonia were hit Monday by problems with freezers and fridges that apparently were caused by cyberattacks, forcing some to dispose of ruined food. The problems follow a case last month in which attackers remotely took control of refrigeration systems in hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France, sending temperatures soaring. READ MORE: Cyberattacks disrupt refrigeration systems at European supermarkets In Sweden, ICA Group supermarket chain spokesperson Gustaf Nilsson told news agency TT that "a limited number" of stores were affected overnight by an incident that affected refrigeration and freezing systems. He declined to give a specific number. The ICA Kvantum branch in Sjöbo in southern Sweden wrote on its Facebook page that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and set to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit). It said it was working to discard the affected items. The Coop chain said that six of its stores in central Sweden had problems with their fridges and freezers, TT reported, though it didn't immediately have details. The Delhaize chain said that an "IT incident" had affected refrigeration systems in several dozen of its stores, mostly in Belgium but also a few in neighboring Luxembourg. "In the affected stores, the range of fresh and frozen products is temporarily somewhat limited. Our distribution centers are operating normally, and there has been no disruption to deliveries to our stores," spokesperson Sarah De Meester said. The Carrefour supermarket chain in Belgium said a "cyberattack targeting refrigeration installations only had an extremely limited impact," affecting 15 of its more than 700 stores. (AP) — Lindsay Clancy returns to court Monday in a bid to dismiss the charges that she murdered her three young children. Watch the hearing live in the video player above. The hearing Monday is the second time the Massachusetts mother has been in court since her trial ended with a deadlocked jury in September after jurors were unable to agree on a verdict. Prosecutors have yet to announce whether they plan to retry Clancy. They could choose to retry her on first-degree murder charges or pursue lesser charges, including second-degree murder or manslaughter, or drop the case entirely. READ MORE: Judge denies motion asking for Lindsay Clancy to be found not guilty due to lack of evidence Clancy has never disputed killing her three young children in 2023, but her lawyer has argued she had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behavior. Prosecutors have acknowledged that the 36-year-old Clancy had mental health problems but said she acted deliberately and understood her actions were wrong. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The focus at Monday's hearing in front of Judge William Sullivan is expected to be on a motion from the defense to dismiss the charges on double jeopardy grounds. They argue that the court did not need to declare a mistrial. Instead, it could have questioned the lone holdout juror Michael Desronvil, or the jury foreperson, regarding reports that he was refusing to follow court instructions with regards to reasonable doubt and failing to follow the law as he was instructed. That could have led to Desronvil being removed, thus avoiding the need for a mistrial. Since the trial ended, Desronvil said he was certain of Clancy's guilt but that no one would listen to him. Prosecutors, in their motion to dismiss, argue that double jeopardy "does not bar the Commonwealth from seeking justice on behalf of the three victims." READ MORE: Key things to know about Lindsay Clancy's case after judge declares mistrial They argue it was unnecessary to investigate Desronvil, whom they don't name but describe as the dissenting juror, because the foreperson complaint did not allege "any personal issue, bias, or extraneous attributable to the dissenting juror." Singling that juror out, they argued, for an investigation "surely would have led to judicial coercion" and the "impermissible intrusion into the substance of the jury's private deliberations." The other motion expected to be discussed is the Commonwealth's request for a gag order that would bar attorneys and their supporters "from making extrajudicial statements to the media that would have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing the criminal proceeding." Attorney Kevin Reddington has given a series of interviews since the mistrial and held walking news conferences almost every day during the proceedings. Prosecutors, in contrast, never talked to reporters. In response, Clancy's lawyers said this motion would amount to prior restraint since it is barring speech before it occurs. "The government bears a heavy burden to justify such an order," Laura McConnell, who was hired by Clancy's defense team, wrote. "There is no jury and it is unknown whether one will ever be impaneled. There is no trial date. The motion should be denied." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".
He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.
Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.
"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.
The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).
It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.
In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.
Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.
In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost â¬100,000 (Â£83,500) worth of produce.
The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".
In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit.
A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the ICA branches located in SjÃ¶bo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.
In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.
The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.
The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.
In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.
A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.
A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.
Additional reporting by Shiona McCallum

5d4efdecf004.text: By — Will Weissert, Associated Press Will Weissert, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-trump-delivers-last-pitch-before-midterms-at-reflecting-pool-site-of-botched-renovation Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Trump delivers last pitch before midterms at Reflecting Pool, site of botched renovation Politics Nov 2, 2026 9:55 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump is making his closing pitch of the midterm elections at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, pushing his slow, expensive and problem-plagued efforts to repair it back into the spotlight on the eve of Election Day. The president is expected to speak at 2 p.m. EDT. Watch live in our video player above. In comments to reporters as he deplaned from Air Force One for a Sunday rally in Iowa, Trump said his speaking at the site would "show how beautiful it is." READ MORE: Candidates make final midterm stops as early voting surges "We might hold it tomorrow or something," the president added, without giving specifics. Hours later, the White House formally announced he'd be giving a speech there Monday afternoon. Please check your inbox to confirm. Rather than using Monday to travel to key states and try to energize his "Make America Great Again" supporters as his Republican Party tries to maintain control of Congress, Trump opted for an event at a Washington renovation project that has been embarrassing and contentious. The unusual move marks a departure from Trump's month-long race to stage more than 25 rallies in largely conservative areas, hoping the GOP can overcome his own low approval ratings and polls predicting that the Iran war, high energy prices and cost of living increases could spell a strong election night for Democrats. READ MORE: Judge permanently dismisses Trump administration's case charging ex-Olympian with Reflecting Pool vandalism Trump wrote on his social media site that his Sunday evening rally in Kansas — which followed his Iowa visit — was "my last stop." The president spent a lot of time at those rallies talking about his second-term focus on molding the White House and the surrounding nation's capital in his own image. He crammed the Oval Office with gold flourishes, demolishing the East Wing to construct a sprawling ballroom, converting the Rose Garden into a patio space reminiscent of his Mar-a-Lago estate and erecting a sprawling South Lawn helipad. Trump also closed the Kennedy Center after failed attempts to add his name to the building, has planned a towering arch just outside the city and is pushing to revamp a century-old public golf course. WATCH: Trump should 'take stock' and 'own' election outcome, Sen. Tillis says He has bristled at criticisms from former President Barack Obama and other Democrats that he's spent too much time focused on construction projects — insisting that renovations relax him and that he does them quickly and without requiring too much planning time. Trump said the Reflecting Pool fix would be fast and inexpensive His Reflecting Pool saga began in April when Trump said he wanted to change its color and would use contractors he knew to fix the monument in mere days and for about $1.5 million before Independence Day. The repairs wrapped up nearly three months behind schedule and the budget ballooned to more than 10 times Trump's early estimate — and that's assuming no more additional work will need to be done in the future. READ MORE: A midterm crossroads for both parties eyeing the beginning of the end of the Trump era Trump had initially declared the work was complete in June. But after unveiling the overhaul, the pool was soon choked with algae blooms, and its "American-flag blue" liner began peeling off in sections. The pool was quickly drained anew for repairs in mid-July. Trump has repeatedly blamed vandals, but the office of U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia — former Fox News host and longtime Trump ally Jeanine Pirro — said the problems were caused by shoddy workmanship. In his comments Sunday, Trump continued to insist that the Reflecting Pool "was vandalized badly." He said that security cameras have since been added to stop that. WATCH: How does The Associated Press call 2026 midterm election winners? 4 things to know Still, a particularly ignominious moment came when the Justice Department charged former Olympian David Hearn with intentionally damaging the Reflecting Pool — then abruptly dropped the case this summer — determining he was not responsible. A judge later permanently dismissed it. That prompted Trump to fume that Pirro "choked," and that he was "disappointed with Jeanine Pirro, really disappointed. A Wizz Air flight travelling from London Luton Airport to Sofia has been escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet to Budapest after a mid-air bomb threat.
The aircraft was forced to make an emergency landing at Budapest Liszt Ferenc International.
Authorities there "carried out the necessary security checks on the aircraft and passengers", a spokesperson for Wizz Air said.
The airline later confirmed an inspection had been "completed and nothing was found", adding that the plane would depart again shortly. Hungarian Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendis confirmed his country provided the fighter jet to escort the flight.
According to flight tracking website FlightAware, Wizz Air flight 4302 departed Luton at 08:33 GMT and was due to arrive in the Bulgarian capital at 13:25 local time (11:25 GMT).
But the website said it landed in Budapest at 12:09 local time (11:09 GMT).
In a post on social media, Ruszin-Szendis said that after receiving the bomb threat, the Wizz Air flight had requested permission to land at the airport in Budapest.
"Within minutes, a Hungarian Defence Forces Gripen fighter jet took to the skies and provided an escort for the passenger aircraft", he said.
After this, the jet returned to its base and police took charge of the incident, he added.
The airline said that after the plane made the emergency landing, it taxied "to a designated stand" where the security checks were carried out.
Wizz Air added that it was "cooperating fully with the authorities", and that the safety of passengers and crew "remains our highest priority".
